First 43052 characters: Monotone Function Estimation for Computer Experiments
abstract: In statistical modeling of computer experiments sometimes prior information is available about the underlying function. For example, the physical system simulated by the computer code may be known to be monotone with respect to some or all inputs. We develop a Bayesian approach to Gaussian process modelling capable of incorporating monotonicity information for computer model emulation. Markov chain Monte Carlo methods are used to sample from the posterior distribution of the process given the simulator output and monotonicity information. The performance of the proposed approach in terms of predictive accuracy and uncertainty quantification is demonstrated in a number of simulated examples as well as a real queueing system application.
Introduction: Deterministic computer models are commonly used to study complex physical phenomena in many areas of science and engineering. Oftentimes, evaluating a computational model can be very time consuming, and thus the simulator is only exercised on a relatively small set of input values. In such cases, a statistical surrogate model (i.e., an emulator) is used to make predictions of the computer model output at unsampled inputs. To this end, a Gaussian process (GP) model is a popular choice for deterministic computer model emulation . The reason for this rests largely on the ability of the GP to interpolate the output of the simulator, the flexibility of the GP as a non-parametric regression estimator and its ability to provide a basis for statistical inference for deterministic computer models.An important property of GP models that makes them attractive in some settings is that the partial derivative processes are also GPs with covariance functions that can be derived from the original process (see for e.g. , Section 9.4). Indeed, when the simulator output includes derivatives, they can be used to improve the accuracy of the emulator . In some applications, derivative information is available only in the form of qualitative information - for example, the computer model response is known to be monotone increasing or decreasing in some of the inputs. Incorporating the derivative information into the emulator in such cases is more challenging because the derivative values are unknown. The problem of using the known monotonicity of the computer model response in one or more of the inputs to build a more accurate emulator is the main focus of this paper. Although our approach can be applied in situations with observation error, we focus primarily on GP emulation of computer experiments.While a rich literature exists on monotone function estimation, interpolation of monotone functions with uncertainty quantification remains an understudied topic. Examples of related work are monotone smoothing splines, isotonic regression, etc. See for e.g. , and . Also work has been done on incorporating constraints in general and monotonicity specially into Gaussian process regression as discussed below. In a related framework, constrained Kriging has been considered in the area of geostatistics . While some of the existing methods may be modified to be used in the noise-free set-up none of them directly address monotone interpolation. On the other hand, there exist tools for monotone interpolation that do not provide uncertainty estimates. See for e.g. . considered monotonicity assumptions for GP models for noisy data. They incorporate the monotonicity information by placing virtual derivatives at pre-specified input locations, thereby encouraging the derivative process to be positive at these points. They use expectation-propagation techniques to approximate the joint marginal likelihood of function and derivative values. Point estimates for the hyper-parameters are obtained by maximizing this approximate likelihood.In this paper we initially take an approach similar to to build an emulator, given the computer model output and monotonicity information. Our approach is different in two respects. First, we focus on deterministic computer experiments where interpolation of the simulator is a requirement. Constructing a monotone emulator is more challenging in the deterministic setting than the noisy setting. The problem in our case lies in generating sample paths from the GP that obey monotonicity and also interpolate the simulator output. In the noisy setting, where the GP need not interpolate the observations, sampling from the GP is easier. Second, we sample from the exact joint posterior distribution rather than relying on an approximation. In doing so, we provide fully Bayesian inference for all parameters of the emulator as well as the predicted function at unsampled inputs, instead of using plug-in estimates of the parameters, thereby underestimating the posterior predictive uncertainty. We also take advantage of the flexible parametrization of monotonicity information to facilitate efficient computation. We show that when the monotonicity constraints are more strict, virtually all the posterior mass of the distribution for the derivatives falls in {{formula:b16d8c92-5a89-4486-893b-d01469e80937}} . The end result of the proposed approach is an emulator of the computer model that uses the monotonicity information and is more accurate than the standard GP.An advantage of approaches which use derivative sign information at specific locations in the input space, is that they offer flexibility in incorporation of monotonicity information. For example, by specifying that derivatives are positive with respect to a particular variable, at particular locations, we have the flexibility to make predictions of the response that has monotone relationship with a predictor in just a subset of the range of the predictor.A related Bayesian approach to monotone estimation of GP models has been independently developed in . Similar to this paper, the sign of derivatives at user-specified locations is assumed known. Two modeling approaches are taken: i) an indicator variable formulation, which can be seen as a limiting case of a probit link of (also used in this paper), and ii) a conditional GP model, which allows zero or positive derivative values. Unlike , who uses plug-in estimates of GP parameters, we conduct full inference for GP parameters as well as function and derivative values. We also demonstrate applications with more than one input dimension. The extension to higher-order derivatives which considers, is not developed here. While uses Gibbs sampling to sample from the marginal posterior with the covariance parameters held fixed at their maximum likelihood estimates, we employ a sequentially constrained Monte Carlo (SCMC) algorithm that permits sampling from the full posterior in fairly high-dimensional scenarios. propose a GP based method for estimating monotone functions that relies on projecting sample paths obtained from a GP fit to the space of monotone functions. They use the pooled adjacent violators (PAV) algorithm to obtain approximate projections. While the projections of interpolating GP sample paths into the space of monotone functions are not generally guaranteed to interpolate the function evaluations, the PAV algorithm can be modified to generate monotone interpolants. However, there are two drawbacks to this method; firstly, inference cannot be made about the GP model parameters by projecting GP sample paths since the posterior distribution of the covariance parameters is affected by the projection. Secondly, sample paths generated by the PAV algorithm are often non-smooth since monotonicity is gained by flattening the ridges and valleys resulting in flat segments followed by occasional rises. “Box-like" credible intervals are obtained from the projected interpolants with truncation from below and above to exclude violating sample paths. These credible intervals can remain unchanged for a range of different coverage probabilities, making their interpretation difficult.The article is organized as follows. Section 2 presents two motivating examples. The first illustration demonstrates a situation where the unconstrained GP performs poorly. We also describe a motivating application involving a queuing system. New methodology for GP emulation of monotone computer models is proposed in Section 3. The monotone interpolation variant of the SCMC algorithm that samples from the full posterior is explained in Section 4. In Section 5, some insight and guidelines on the construction of the derivative design is provided. Two simulated examples illustrate the performance of the method in Section 6, and a simulation study is described in Section 7. The proposed method is applied to the queuing system application in Section 8, and we finish the paper with some concluding remarks in the subsequent section.
Illustrative example: Consider the simple monotone function in Figure REF , sampled at {{formula:b3580042-ffa7-4cd5-9975-6ebe9c998e5b}} design points. A GP model provides estimates of the function evaluations and uncertainties at unsampled points (Figure REF ) (we leave the details of GP models until Section REF ). {{figure:0266c826-60ea-4973-813f-2435e72866d5}}This example illustrates several issues. Suppose that the function is known to be monotone increasing. Since the GP model does not incorporate monotonicity information, the posterior predictive distribution in Figure REF includes sample paths (the gray curves) that decrease. Furthermore, 95% credible intervals in the range {{formula:7fb1c5a7-7cc2-45ea-b157-23f60d2a3bda}} are relatively wide (Fiqure REF ), reflecting the wide variety of sample paths suggested by the GP model. While it is unlikely that an experimenter would run a design with such a large gap between the fifth and sixth design points (i.e., {{formula:29431eb2-e077-4c55-a808-46e3061bb166}} ), sizeable gaps are likely to occur in practice in higher input dimensions - especially when the usual run-size recommendations for computer model emulation (e.g., ) are adopted.If the experimenter knows beforehand that the computational model is monotone (increasing in this example), this information should be used to rule out some of the non-monotone proposals for the emulator. We will see (Section REF ) that using our proposed methodology, most of the posterior mass can be concentrated on increasing functions and the posterior predictive uncertainty can be reduced (Figure REF ).
Queuing system application: The example that motivated this work is a computer networking queuing system in and . Consider a single server and two first-in-first-out queues of jobs arriving stochastically at rates {{formula:93808890-0486-4b96-901b-92d5ed9943ac}} and {{formula:59c47a75-2493-4d20-9938-19d8664e4e81}} (denoted as {{formula:b95c0aab-dc38-4569-87be-67497d69c98f}} and {{formula:45368a04-3009-4075-9442-54453f7ca72e}} in ). The queues have infinite capacity buffers for the jobs waiting to be served. To make decisions on which queue to serve, a server allocation/scheduling policy is used to maximize the average amount of work processed by the system per unit of time . As mentioned by , the queuing system also captures essential dynamics of many practical systems, such as data/voice transmissions in wireless networks or multi-product manufacturing systems.A performance measure of the system is the average delay for the jobs to be served, as a function of the arrival rates {{formula:4d4e3ebf-084e-49cb-a625-1667e295ccbb}} and {{formula:de7a6042-5d24-4537-9829-19a34f615297}} . This average delay is not available in closed form and is evaluated by a computational model that simulates the system. Details of the simulator are discussed in .An important characteristic of this queuing process is that the average delay is a monotone increasing function of the job arrival rates. The increase is negligible for small {{formula:a17b4924-b34e-42db-b890-fdb372a31900}} and {{formula:72e7cd27-e99c-4c36-b0f8-c118d7a1c585}} , yielding a nearly flat function, but eventually the average delay increases exponentially as the arrival rate(s) increase. With such behavior in the response surface, predicting the average delay at unsampled input rates is a challenge. The monotone GP model introduced in Section REF will serve as a guide for improving inference in this context.
Gaussian process models with monotonicity information: We begin this section with a brief review of GP models and use of derivatives in GP regression. Next, new methodology for emulation of monotone computer models and a sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) algorithm for this setting are introduced.
Gaussian process regression: Let {{formula:4f90e77d-9f63-47a4-9248-0f67f953bf5c}} be the function encoded in the computer model that is evaluated at {{formula:12135b49-2cc9-4384-beab-32471c9e69cd}} design points (or input locations) given by the rows of the {{formula:149bd24e-1405-46d0-b8bf-56ea5991f35d}} design matrix {{formula:e7066c74-c0c4-444d-9e33-e71ea00f49d2}} , where {{formula:a7c8efba-7440-4490-a6bd-e789ab205406}} . It is standard to assume that the response surface for the computer model is a realization of a GP . In practice, this amounts to placing a prior distribution over the class of functions produced by the simulator.Denote the vector of computer model outputs as {{formula:081d8940-413e-44ab-b771-841273dadb9f}} , where {{formula:0dd62e06-3877-4382-86ec-2e1a6431a57e}} ({{formula:76e8754b-3a60-47a8-8722-dd6799e23490}} ). We specify {{formula:3dbd8fd3-c642-4f15-a2ac-06868fa77392}} be a zero mean (without loss of generality) GP with an anisotropic, stationary covariance function. Therefore, {{formula:3215bbdd-229e-40a0-9468-b72c3b901524}} is a realization of a mean zero multivariate normal distribution with a covariance matrix {{formula:8a3d63ec-baf3-4189-918e-4a1e2ec711fa}} whose {{formula:4a72f59a-e2d0-4999-bf32-7b1c2137cb0e}} th element is given by {{formula:ded8151d-c923-4a1e-87ca-9cadcf3f369e}}where {{formula:a041a72c-4db0-4ea3-952b-93c8380f0813}} is the vector of length scale parameters in each dimension and {{formula:b4b21bff-d8b0-4d55-8d7c-af6e2efa1548}} is the constant variance. We choose {{formula:12659432-3b91-426f-b4aa-6c9b8684670c}} from the Matern class of covariance functions that are of the form {{formula:fafb709e-8be8-45fd-8912-0096c595d63b}}where {{formula:a11e37ee-b4dd-4b49-88fd-27a7366d1862}} is the gamma function, {{formula:14d38ef5-080b-428e-8131-106424a29b4a}} is the modified Bessel function of the second kind, and {{formula:046af37b-d2e7-474e-9665-50c431980681}} is a non-negative parameter. The Matern correlation function is {{formula:fbb0763f-a9c6-444b-a501-e7bca979e3e2}} -times mean square differentiable if and only if {{formula:aaf5766c-6b62-42b9-b14a-af00f0dc6873}} . We choose {{formula:4fda4f11-37ab-4a6e-991b-55e10a51dcad}} .This choice of the Matern covariance function over the commonly used squared exponential family avoids numerical instability, often observed when inverting the covariance matrix, by removing the restriction of infinite differentiability. Note that twice mean square differentiability is a requirement to be able to obtain the covariance function for the derivative process and is likely to be the level of smoothness one can safely assume in practice.Following the above specification for the GP, the conditional distribution of {{formula:bd59e96c-4bd0-4bb8-af08-635c4c6205f0}} at any unsampled input {{formula:62bdd524-c4ef-42d7-b114-fbffbe170851}} , given the evaluations and the covariance parameters, is given by {{formula:964d5c93-eab7-47d0-ae4f-67285e00a560}}where {{formula:894c214e-8798-4616-acc9-4608615f314e}} {{formula:04ac3a14-d00f-487b-8a12-c4a4811f7d2b}}and {{formula:8a5b7a13-8576-45f9-91dd-571d9cb0885e}} is the {{formula:ba9cb27e-9212-4385-a4c0-ee07a69b1c3a}} -vector of correlations between the observation at {{formula:43fa60bb-6a9a-4199-a1bc-3d870faf9e2e}} and the observations at the design points, {{formula:d42e0a9d-2f01-433a-9d66-80672b3e6486}} . The mean {{formula:0c2c316f-e98c-47ab-8363-5166bc397a86}} is often used as the prediction of the computer model response at {{formula:0ce58251-8860-442b-8556-e3b9a12eca3e}} (i.e., {{formula:94eec457-a5f6-4a47-8e00-25ecfc075176}} ) .We take a Bayesian approach to make inference about the GP parameters, {{formula:cbccd798-ae68-47a6-9bf8-e66aa7bdc439}} and {{formula:aa05d800-805f-4e3d-bbbc-8c3b61487deb}} , instead of replacing them by their maximum likelihood point estimates . Assuming a prior distribution, {{formula:db87f126-ca54-4109-95aa-10a428119455}} , the joint posterior distribution of the GP parameters and {{formula:9cbe47a1-2c33-49e8-bcfe-4ade9787098b}} is given by {{formula:e46dfd44-81b6-49e0-af90-532c3bcfd4b5}}where the first term on the right hand side of (REF ) is given by (REF ) and the second term is the likelihood. We delay discussion of the specific choices of prior distributions until Section .
Derivatives of a Gaussian process: In the context of computer model emulation, a more efficient emulator can be obtained by combining the model response and derivatives when the derivatives are observed . Results relating the GP and observed partial derivatives are presented in this section. Of course, in our setting the partial derivatives are not observed, but we treat the derivatives as unobserved latent variables in the next section - doing so will allow us to incorporate monotonicity information into the emulator.Consider the partial derivative of the GP, {{formula:31547746-7c91-434b-8c0f-5068520fb715}} , with respect to {{formula:3c1aeea9-ff25-4472-afed-8fd222f2d200}} (i.e., the {{formula:015e36ba-6a8e-4411-bf49-993dd0a3982a}} input dimension). Denote this derivative function by {{formula:d1dbf908-59cd-476b-9c02-eb8c430b70ad}} . Since differentiation is a linear operator, the partial derivatives of a GP are also GPs .The means and covariances of the derivative function can be obtained by differentiating the mean and covariance of {{formula:1a0fcdf9-bd42-4ec1-b7b2-78be08a419d7}} ( ,page 83), i.e., {{formula:7949a116-cdfd-4af2-81de-c683c46ee6a3}} {{formula:70e00ff5-4a62-4267-9b2d-81f6d2f6575a}}and {{formula:97711951-2e15-4264-868b-eb978ac5bdd9}}The analytic formulas for the derivatives of the Matern covariance function that we use are given in Appendix . Let {{formula:3e0a7643-65bc-4a69-85d1-5d50b5113f0f}} be a set of input points where derivatives have been observed (note that {{formula:1fd6933e-473f-494a-8546-276d73bdbdf2}} does not necessarily have any points in common with {{formula:a17d3e2c-2d88-4e27-a821-2dd7cbe47965}} ). Furthermore, denote the vector of partial derivatives in the {{formula:01d634db-9060-48f9-9392-cf81c03db71a}} input dimension, observed at {{formula:92beb975-82b1-4474-9d57-3019f92aacad}} as {{formula:23f24c09-a9e3-406c-b0bf-271a02a49ac9}} , where {{formula:55fd22e5-5eab-4fc2-b017-fc6133c1f04f}} ({{formula:169e0162-5563-4940-81ff-0a3c22171ea0}} ). The joint distribution of simulator evaluations, {{formula:d969b92d-767d-495d-82e8-861488f8c8f8}} , at the design matrix, {{formula:f9d80d41-47c1-4ca9-a1d5-a486cbf5a6c6}} , and partial derivatives, {{formula:868b39ba-373e-4ab9-8770-e781a0c5a413}} , at a set of points given by the matrix {{formula:761435ba-bb27-40ac-8fd7-2eb2c14678f7}} , given the GP parameters follows a multivariate Gaussian distribution, {{formula:c2e161f9-555d-4247-8b77-705b437361c8}}where {{formula:c99ef9e6-c668-4fb0-a315-0d8aeb9a8629}}and {{formula:92132b5b-e165-4ff1-be79-c80d7f4dc9ef}}Note that the four blocks of {{formula:9c5c4279-320e-41a9-a020-77b0eba0c4dc}} are covariance matrices whose components are obtained by applying the covariance functions to the points in {{formula:89a2f525-9267-4c0e-9cda-29c598d3b566}} and {{formula:3292f946-3a1d-40c9-81be-c0611a5d4118}} . Partial derivatives with respect to more than one dimension could be included analogously.
Incorporating monotonicity information: In some computer model applications, the simulator output includes derivatives with respect to some of the input dimensions . In our setting, the experimenter knows beforehand that the simulator response is monotone in some, or all, of the inputs, but only knows the sign of the derivatives. The magnitude of the derivatives are unknown.Consider, for example, the one-dimensional illustration given in Section REF . Suppose that in addition to the seven function evaluations, it is also known that {{formula:e308aefa-0fe9-4974-acdc-0ae245ef57f5}} , but the values of the partial derivative are unknown. Figure 1(b) shows the prediction intervals using the usual GP, while Figure 1(c) illustrates the prediction intervals using the methodology we will propose shortly. Clearly, the prediction intervals are smaller when the derivative information is used in the predictions.In this section, we propose methodology to construct a more efficient emulator than the usual GP when the response is monotone in one or more of the inputs, but where the derivative process is unobserved. We consider the case where the function is strictly increasing with respect to the {{formula:9d51bbe2-6c54-4386-9671-e1744609dc02}} input. The strictly decreasing case is handled similarly by replacing {{formula:1332b9f8-22a1-43b9-a25e-b8abf8813902}} with {{formula:0f7a47c0-8a97-4a76-b2e3-3cf59340fe4e}} .With no constraints imposed, the derivatives of the GP, outlined in the previous section, take values in {{formula:2a9f7852-2d71-471d-9076-6922d74d2c68}} . proposed a method to impose the positivity constraint on the derivatives at a set of {{formula:3375cd1a-a573-4fff-8cb2-eb016973d8f7}} specified inputs {{formula:33aa6ee6-8625-4ce6-9cb1-9559c60c8f14}} . Although the constraints at {{formula:558ff37f-d8e3-4c45-8b78-46ed87da91b4}} input values do not guarantee monotonicity everywhere, with enough well-placed points, monotone functions are made highly probable. They used a probit function that links the monotonicity information with the derivative values that are treated as unobserved latent variables. Building on their notation, let {{formula:276e22e1-7ff8-4a71-b9bb-18dd9358b428}} be a binary random variable that is equal to 1 when the derivative in the {{formula:c01fbaee-dadb-48b4-afea-b7c17bbbe54f}} input dimension is positive at {{formula:764d3acc-6da3-4dfe-8730-a0e9c07b2732}} and 0 otherwise. While Bayesian inference for unconstrained GP regression can be made using basic MCMC algorithms based on Metropolis-Hastings steps, the addition of the constraints to the model creates sampling challenges that disqualify the existing MCMC algorithms as efficient sampling tools. The main reason is that under the constrained model, given the covariance parameters, {{formula:cb0d9eb5-8d20-4b69-b61a-606d1754d1c3}} and {{formula:26ef8f62-9089-44b3-81ab-0ec77a464cb3}} are no longer Gaussian processes and their distribution cannot be obtained in closed form. Therefore, inference about the function and its derivatives is made based on point-wise sampling. Under point-wise sampling, the dimension of the state space gets large with the size of the prediction set and the number of locations at which derivatives are constrained. MCMC sampling from such a space will be inefficient.Another factor that contributes to the difficulty of sampling from (REF ) is the restriction imposed on the support of the posterior distribution by the monotonicity constraints; an MCMC approach based on accept/reject steps is likely to be very inefficient when the support of the proposal distribution is very different from that of the target distribution. The filtering sequence is defined based on the strictness of constraints. Starting from an initial distribution under which the constraints are relaxed fully or to an extent that sampling is feasible, the restriction is imposed gradually on the distributions to eventually obtain a sample from the fully constrained target distribution. Sequentially Constrained Monte Carlo for Posterior Sampling: In this section we outline the sampling algorithm adapted from for the unobserved function values, {{formula:34b98a00-a7c5-4da3-9419-1fc5fed7224a}} , derivative values, {{formula:8ef47596-9f9b-433f-8168-8f893c4c83df}} , and covariance parameter values, {{formula:4b65899e-4833-474d-88d7-3fa4872e5320}} , from the posterior distribution, (REF ). While Bayesian inference for unconstrained GP regression can be made using basic MCMC algorithms based on Metropolis-Hastings steps, the addition of the constraints to the model creates sampling challenges that disqualify the existing MCMC algorithms as efficient sampling tools. The main reason is that under the constrained model, given the covariance parameters, {{formula:cb0d9eb5-8d20-4b69-b61a-606d1754d1c3}} and {{formula:26ef8f62-9089-44b3-81ab-0ec77a464cb3}} are no longer Gaussian processes and their distribution cannot be obtained in closed form. Therefore, inference about the function and its derivatives is made based on point-wise sampling. Under point-wise sampling, the dimension of the state space gets large with the size of the prediction set and the number of locations at which derivatives are constrained. MCMC sampling from such a space will be inefficient.Another factor that contributes to the difficulty of sampling from (REF ) is the restriction imposed on the support of the posterior distribution by the monotonicity constraints; an MCMC approach based on accept/reject steps is likely to be very inefficient when the support of the proposal distribution is very different from that of the target distribution. While the constraints define an explicit soft constraint on the derivative function space, the effect of this constraint on the covariance parameters' distribution is not obvious and therefore it is not trivial to define a proposal distribution that is likely to generate values for these parameters with high posterior probability.To overcome these difficulties we use a variant of Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) samplers . SMC samplers take advantage of a sequence of distributions {{formula:c9776a36-6aeb-499c-a0f0-5be512b3d467}} that bridge between a distribution that is straightforward to generate from (e.g. the prior) and the target distribution. introduced a variant of SMC, referred to as the sequentially constrained Monte Carlo (SCMC), for the case that sampling from the target distribution is challenging due to imposition of constraints. The filtering sequence is defined based on the strictness of constraints. Starting from an initial distribution under which the constraints are relaxed fully or to an extent that sampling is feasible, the restriction is imposed gradually on the distributions to eventually obtain a sample from the fully constrained target distribution. The Derivative Input Set : The GP model for derivatives in Section REF and the mechanism for including monotonicity information via derivatives in Section REF make the assumption that derivative information is available at a “derivative input set", {{formula:690fab1e-dd3a-441d-b5e7-cc6ad1f36c88}} . At each {{formula:bb890eab-95d6-45be-884a-78eb8a742a4c}} , we assume the soft constraint {{formula:7a26fed6-56ca-4b52-b2ab-cac929c30e6f}} , which via (REF ) induces a probability that {{formula:eb5d20dd-8c4b-4cc7-96a0-b7b01631f896}} . That is, instead of assuming that the derivative of the GP is positive everywhere, the model assumes that there is a (large) probability that the derivative is positive at a specified set of points.To estimate the monotone GP, the derivative input set must be specified. The SCMC algorithm described above permits working with relatively large derivative sets since SCMC is proved to be stable as the dimensionality of the state space increases . Therefore, using a space filling design to construct a derivative set that assures imposition of the monotonicity constraints uniformly over the input space is a reasonable strategy. However, one may restrict the derivative set to regions that probability of occurrence of negative derivatives is high, as suggest, to save computation time.Under the unconstrained GP model the derivatives are Gaussian processes, and the point-wise probability of negative derivatives can be obtained analytically for fixed covariance parameters. For Example 1, Figures REF and REF show this probability together with the mean and expected derivative function of the Gaussian process evaluated at the posterior mean of the covariance parameters. {{figure:eb80a4c3-a7d1-4e51-be77-c668eb97b77d}} recommend sequential addition of points where the probability of occurrence of negative derivatives is the largest. developed a sequential algorithm for selection of the derivative locations based on this idea with an upper bound on the size of the derivative set predetermined with consideration of computational limitation. use maximum likelihood estimates for the covariance parameters and are able to iteratively calculate the probability of negative derivatives analytically under the constrained model to determine where to place the next derivative point. Starting from an unconstrained GP (Figure REF ) derivatives are constrained at locations added in the gap one at a time from left to right. Non-eligible sample paths are filtered from the posterior by addition of each derivative point to eventually obtain a trimmed collection of posterior sample paths that satisfy positivity of derivatives at ten locations (Figure REF ). {{figure:7154f5b9-49ec-454a-86ff-15505d07d7e1}}The choice of the derivative input set can be extended to the case where monotonicity is required in two or more inputs. Therefore, we will use a different derivative input set, {{formula:2bb48bdb-2a1c-438f-9ba0-6a459ec18e13}} , {{formula:9e25633c-62c0-489e-8ebe-4be48ff9ed62}} for each of the {{formula:09ab8440-08a1-4c53-bb90-1ff2b5310dad}} input dimensions in which the underlying function is assumed to be monotone.As a straightforward extension to the one-dimensional case we place the partial derivatives in the neighborhood of the prediction point, on the corresponding slice, parallel to the corresponding axes (see, for e.g., Figure REF ). The system response is monotone in each of the inputs: one would expect to wait longer if the arrival rate in the queue is larger.The input region to be investigated is not rectangular . Instead the region of interest, after scaling, is a subset of the unit square where the expected delay is finite. The proposed methodology is evaluated using this setting. Predictions at four input locations, {{formula:aaf05358-34ac-4bf6-918b-e565999b1de5}} , are made and compared to the true system response. We chose these points because they are in a region of the design space where the response surface changes quite rapidly. This is a challenging emulation problem because such non-stationary behavior is difficult to model with a stationary GP. The derivatives are constrained at the locations shown by the red dots in Figure REF - that is four points along each axis in the neighborhood of the prediction locations. {{figure:e884aa0e-c3e9-44dd-963a-87fad46e2538}}{{figure:2300048b-c7ae-4c16-a210-5556bf797cb0}}The proposed monotone interpolator and the unconstrained GP are applied to this application. However, the posterior uncertainty is so large for the unconstrained GP as to be almost uninformative. Notice that both approaches overestimate the response at prediction point {{formula:05fd4c7d-290b-4a47-ab35-acd5f1843319}} . This is due to the rapid change in the response. {{figure:85789110-22e4-4e70-a3a2-eb26f9c32ebf}}Both models find this queuing application challenging. The response surface (Figure REF ) is very flat for much of the input space and increases rapidly near the boundary of the input region. This is not the behavior of a simulator that is easily modeled by a stationary GP. Overall, taking monotonicity into account helped reduce the predictive MSE and also the uncertainty in the predictions.
Conclusion: In this article we have developed a methodology for the incorporation of monotonicity information into the GP emulation of a deterministic computer model. Through the mechanism of a link function, monotonicity information is encoded via virtual derivatives (binary indicators of derivative sign) at points in a derivative input set. Some guidelines for construction of the derivative input set are proposed; an online specification of the derivative design that can be incorporated into the sampling algorithm is currently under investigation. Full inference for unsampled values of the function and its derivatives are available via the constrained SMC algorithm. Notably, by sampling GP parameters, {{formula:f9fe8329-9c77-4208-89b7-d3836fab6979}} and {{formula:3b7b0aa6-4912-45a7-9a70-7ae59a167f27}} , a more realistic representation of uncertainty is provided than would be obtained from plug-in estimates of {{formula:73edbe4e-e3b4-48bd-96c2-e9c5e12b4f10}} and {{formula:da640525-ff48-4e56-9695-85e87334f9ab}} . Through examples, a set of simulations, and a queuing application, we demonstrate improvement in prediction uncertainty while respecting monotonicity information.The proposed methodology will be most effective in situations where monotonicity of the function is not clear from the data. As Example 1 indicates, when the training set has gaps or holes, the lack of nearby data points may lead conventional GP models to estimate a non-monotone relationship. As the queuing application suggests, another challenging situation arises when the true function is monotone but nearly constant. In both these situations, incorporating monotonicity information into the model is helpful, since the conventional GP model may infer a non-monotone relationship.In some prediction scenarios (e.g. point D in Figure REF ), the monotonicity constraint may impact coverage of credible intervals. Although credible intervals from the unconstrained model have higher coverage, they are of little value because the intervals are wide enough to be uninformative. One may gain back some prediction uncertainty by relaxing the model assumptions in the proposed method. In our framework, this can be done by either relaxing the monotonicity assumption to some extent or relaxing the interpolation requirement. The former is done by choosing a smaller monotonicity parameter allowing for (small) positive probability for the occurrence of negative derivatives while the latter is performed by adding a nugget which allows for positive uncertainty at the evaluation points.As input dimension increases, efficient computation will become more of a consideration. If derivatives are constrained in {{formula:9bb9bd58-fd19-4508-9a93-7323b640a5b9}} input dimensions, then monotonicity information is required in each of these inputs. Increasing {{formula:7f9c35d8-0e89-4b59-90cb-760fe63f02e6}} has the effect of increasing the size of the covariance matrix in (REF ) that has to be inverted with each evaluation of the likelihood. This can slow down the computation considerably. However, the SMC, in comparison to MCMC, has the advantage of being easily parallelizable and is shown to be stable as the dimensionality increases, thereby, being able to handle fairly high dimensional scenarios.

question: How do measurements of two-particle correlations in Au+Au collisions at sqrt(s_NN) = 200 GeV, after subtracting contributions from elliptic, triangular, and higher-order flow harmonics, constrain the extent to which triangular flow—generated by event-by-event fluctuations in the initial collision geometry—can account for observed away-side double-hump structures across different collision centralities?
answerWithPaperReferences: Paper 1003.0194 introduces the concept of participant triangularity, which quantifies the triangular anisotropy of the initial nuclear overlap geometry arising from event-by-event fluctuations in participant-nucleon collision points. Using the AMPT model, the authors demonstrate that this initial triangularity generates triangular flow (v3), and that this triangular flow contributes dominantly to the third Fourier coefficient of two-particle azimuthal correlations, producing the observed ridge and broad away-side features [Paper 1003.0194]. Building on this understanding, Paper 1209.0044 presents PHENIX measurements of two-particle correlations in Au+Au collisions at sqrt(s_NN) = 200 GeV, where contributions from v2, v3, and v4 are subtracted using the ZYAM method to study the remaining non-flow correlations [Paper 1209.0044]. The PHENIX data show that after subtracting these flow harmonics, the away-side double-hump structure disappears in most-central collisions, indicating that higher-order flow (including triangular flow) can largely account for the correlation structure in this regime. However, the away-side double hump persists in mid-central collisions even after the subtraction, suggesting that additional physics beyond higher-order flow harmonics is required to fully explain the observed structures in that centrality range [Paper 1209.0044].
answerWithoutPaperReferences: Event-by-event fluctuations in the positions of participating nucleons create a finite triangular anisotropy, known as participant triangularity, in the initial geometry of heavy-ion collisions. Transport model calculations show that this initial triangularity generates triangular flow (v3), which manifests as a significant contribution to the third Fourier component of two-particle azimuthal correlations and produces ridge and broad away-side structures. Experimental measurements of two-particle correlations in Au+Au collisions at 200 GeV subtract the contributions from elliptic, triangular, and higher-order flow harmonics using the zero-yield-at-minimum method. These measurements reveal that the away-side double-hump structure vanishes in most-central collisions after the subtraction, indicating that flow harmonics including triangular flow can account for the structure in central events. However, the double hump remains in mid-central collisions even after removing these flow contributions, demonstrating that triangular flow alone cannot fully explain the observed away-side structures across all centralities and that additional mechanisms must be present.

Two particle correlation measurements at PHENIX
abstract: Measurements of two particle azimuthal correlations in relativistic heavy ion collisions are useful tools to dissect the interplay between hard-scattered partons and hot dense medium. Correlations with trigger particle selection relative to second order event plane are sensitive to the path-length dependence of parton energy loss and to the influence of the medium on jet for high and intermediate transverse momenta pairs, respectively. To study the parton-medium coupling, it is also crucial to obtain correlations with rejection of contributions from higher harmonic flow. We present current results of second order event plane dependent correlations as well as correlations in which contributions from higher harmonic flow have been excluded in Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=200$ GeV measured by PHENIX.
Higher harmonic event planes and flow: In previous understanding of relativistic heavy ion collisions, it has been assumed that the spatial geometry of the participant nucleons shows almond-like shapes and considered that the generated hot and dense medium mainly expands in the direction of short axis of almond-like shapes.Recent studies with AMPT model simulations and experimental measurements revealed that, in addition to ellipticity, there are triangularity, squarity as well as higher-order deformation in the initial collision geometry originating from its fluctuations, giving thus rise to higher-order flow harmonics, i.e. anisotropy of particle productions relative to each harmonic event plane, over wide rapidity range. The effects due to fluctuations of initial collision geometry play an important roll for the understanding of space time evolution of the medium created in heavy ion collisions.The amplitude of flow harmonics {{formula:d1b42f0e-e9d9-4fc6-a883-05da3a0ac1df}} is defined as {{formula:066c8c5d-59f0-46ff-91df-9a6d947cadbf}}where {{formula:9c9e6c70-e731-4ec6-9799-e7eccb361653}} is the particle azimuthal angle and {{formula:e6d29321-0034-4226-a73e-773d2641b981}} is the direction of the nth harmonic event plane in transverse plane.The {{formula:f401eb39-5188-43a5-a49f-ade20a91e663}} of hadrons within {{formula:8a0f8d7a-716d-4d49-ac9c-e36018ecd24b}} is measured with the event planes determined in {{formula:a1d10aff-d495-4c89-8999-0e8499f022b1}} to ensure a sufficient pseudo-rapidity gap between particle and event planes to reduce non-flow correlations, such as those due to jet production.
Two particle correlations: Two particle correlations are calculated by dividing the relative angular distributions of real event pairs with those from mixed events, and applying proper normalization: {{formula:bbfba2c4-b2d5-46cc-a955-122320f89390}}where {{formula:770da4b6-4ea2-4b22-8d6e-203e6b1a4634}} is the trigger particle azimuthal angle and {{formula:99c7a064-b1a1-43c6-aef0-91188a1fa812}} is the associate particle one. Correlations have been measured with particles tracked at mid rapidity in the range {{formula:417568fb-abb2-45de-aa6f-ff54107c2250}} without rapidity gaps between trigger and associate particles. In the correlations, the contributions from jet survives, thus allowing us to study to the interplay between hard-scattered partons and medium.In addition to inclusive trigger correlations, the study of two particle correlations with additional selection of the azimuthal angle between the trigger particle and the second order event plane provides a useful tool to control the path length which parton propagate. This studies produce measurements sensitive to the path-length dependence of parton energy loss with high momenta pairs and to the influence of medium effects with intermediate momenta pairs.The correlations include the contributions from collective flow. The flow shapes can be estimated from experimentally measured event plane resolutions and the Fourier coefficients {{formula:40ac64a3-f6ee-4454-8343-ea1aa7a3cb59}} . Their contribution is subtracted with the normalization factor determined by ZYAM method .
Two-particle correlations versus event plane at high pt: The {{formula:10705551-5b3d-48d2-a39f-ad4166d83478}} -hadron correlations with neutral pions in the {{formula:4aa63562-62a3-4495-8260-7cec4ccc5978}} range {{formula:59f01d95-65cc-419a-9d57-c42f06db0d19}} GeV/c as trigger particles and hadrons in the range {{formula:fcae2007-62f9-47f3-8026-4f652377f852}} GeV/c as associated particles are shown in the left panel of Fig. 1 for Au+Au collisions at {{formula:43bb88df-db2d-44d2-aee0-e08660735498}} GeV and in the centrality range 20-60%, where path length can be well controlled. Two sets of data points are shown, corresponding to different intervals of the angle between the trigger particle and the second order event plane.Right panel of Fig.REF shows the integrated yield in near and away side of triggered correlations, normalized to the yields in {{formula:2601c238-697f-4dc2-aa25-d2de887dd8e9}} collisions as a functions of the relative angle between the trigger particle ({{formula:10420ad9-617d-4037-a532-42846a97e034}} ) and the second order event plane ({{formula:9fa14578-895d-4d62-85c4-b41cbfe5d456}} ). Here the collective flow contributions from {{formula:7849bd41-a049-4e3a-a791-9c6c5a0367d7}} and {{formula:508b8d2e-65ba-455d-ba8a-32a066df14c7}} harmonics are subtracted, while {{formula:354f7791-395d-434d-b51a-7b032b50783b}} and {{formula:44b43d5a-c0a5-4ada-b6eb-d675a7514f17}} are not subtracted. However the omission of higher {{formula:87cf3d83-86f1-4f27-a6c3-baf896f38720}} is not significant in correlation measurements with high momenta pairs, since the ratio of jet signal over flow contribution is large enough.While the near side yield is consistent with the yield in {{formula:39beb840-c454-4525-bc34-f0a88890eb2d}} collisions within the statistical and systematic uncertainties, the away side yield is significantly suppressed compared to {{formula:d58d1ba0-cb4c-415f-b045-884e0fc25680}} collisions. The away side yield is monotonically decreasing as the angle between the trigger particle and the second order event plane increase, that is parton path length increases.
Two-particle correlations versus event plane at intermediate {{formula:93d35ef1-a00f-46da-8a5c-6d6705633aee}}: Fig.REF shows the hadron-hadron correlations in polar coordinates for trigger particle in {{formula:b717b6bb-8088-4e29-90a2-4833b42564e6}} GeV/c and associated particles in {{formula:4111a56e-75d8-4edc-bc5d-a91588429a12}} GeV/c in Au+Au collisions at {{formula:648eda05-a410-414e-94d6-e2a86e31016e}} GeV, with the additional selection on the angle of the trigger particle with respect to the second order event plane. Also in this case contributions from {{formula:1aae4170-c5f5-4acf-9a35-10207f1a54c6}} and {{formula:a267a053-3792-4eef-9485-7e4d3883cf15}} are subtracted from correlations with ZYAM method. In the left panel, the correlations are shown for the case of trigger particle in the out-of-plane region, while the case of in-plane trigger particle is shown in the right panel.The open symbols (in blue) show the correlations where the trigger particle is selected in left side of event planes, while the closed symbols (in red) show the correlations where the trigger particle is selected in right side of event plane. The ellipse at the center (in green) represents the medium shape. The red, blue, and black arrows indicate the direction of the trigger particle and of the event plane, as well as orange arrows indicate the direction in which correlation yields are more pronounced.Focusing on the away side shape of left-triggered correlations from event plane, the yield in longer path length tends to be larger than that in shorter path length side in the case of trigger particle exiting out-of-plane, while, for the case of trigger particle in the in-plane region, the yield in shorter path length side tends to be larger. Out-of-plane triggered correlations are dominated by surface emission of particles, however in-plane triggered correlations are overwhelmed by penetrating emissions. These observations indicate a non-monotonic behavior of the away side yield as a function of parton path length, which is inconsistent with the monotonic trends seen in high momenta pair correlations shown in Fig.REF .This non-monotonic behavior in triggered correlations is preserved even including {{formula:7b08fcfd-b7c2-4860-8f93-8630280e8752}} terms to flow contribution subtraction. Since the correlation between second and third event planes is weak and contributions from {{formula:6b37e1f3-b7c2-4a78-92e5-b8642d06c61f}} is almost independent of the angle between the trigger particle and the second order event plane, and the same amplitude of contributions from {{formula:5b93b360-5755-4625-a119-cecdbc69df33}} is subtracted in any correlations with different trigger particle angle relative to second order event planes.
Two-particle correlations with {{formula:94ffc0f1-a663-4eb3-ae8c-070be0556430}}  contribution subtractions: Fig.REF presents the hadron-hadron correlations for trigger particle in {{formula:ee6a23ca-7c6b-4a24-a72d-98c1f9ae8b10}} GeV/c and associated particles in {{formula:5cb9399d-9d69-45e4-9fc3-ffa2af32b356}} GeV/c without selecting on the angle between the trigger particle and the event plane. The {{formula:b5a79b4d-f3f4-42a0-8ca0-f4670fabb565}} , {{formula:587f01bd-e2b6-44f2-aa60-5a57b94cf693}} and {{formula:0720781d-f503-4fae-be3b-ec7573264d12}} are subtracted. The subtraction of contributions from {{formula:d9beb674-040a-4526-bb7b-362c58317af6}} and {{formula:0b9b95a9-aba5-4985-8ef9-e47cd2e33414}} reduce {{formula:87f76c4b-dce2-46ce-9146-d462ff2868ac}} and {{formula:39e7490e-ad3f-417a-87c0-a3fb4d996863}} components in correlation functions, resulting in the disappearance of the away side correlation yield in most-central collisions, as seen in correlations with rapidity gap between pairs measured at the LHC . However, away side yield and double humps remain even after the {{formula:f06c5590-ff88-44ba-8c6f-a0962f06b275}} contribution subtraction in mid-central collisions.The remaining amplitude of {{formula:7f9462cc-ec57-48f8-a579-97d1f7c74585}} which is estimated by the {{formula:5c5026c2-f729-4f5f-888a-b92a2c8257e0}} components in flow subtracted correlations is roughly equivalent to the amplitude of already subtracted {{formula:6323294a-66dc-4a91-bec2-464073baea0d}} . It is difficult to explain away side double hump structure in mid-central collisions only with higher order flow harmonics {{formula:41574180-c63e-4f21-a0db-1d69dac18222}} .
Summary: Two particle correlations with trigger particle selection relative to second order event plane have been measured at high and intermediate transverse momenta pairs. While away side yields in high momentum pair correlations shows a monotonic suppression as a function of path length, yields from two particle correlations at intermediate momentum show a non-monotonic behavior. Two particle correlations without selection on the trigger particle angle relative to the event plane and with subtraction of :the contribution from {{formula:3bebfc9e-f294-473a-9984-17b04ba9192a}} flow coefficients show the disappearance of double hump structure in most-central collisions. However, the away side double hump structure is still present in mid-central collisions. It is difficult to explain the remaining away side double humps in mid-central collisions in the context of higher order flow harmonics.

question: What is the asymptotic form of the density of states in the second tangent space of a random matrix product state manifold as a function of quasiparticle spacing, and how does the bond dimension D influence this result, when the underlying Haar integrals over the unitary group are evaluated using the combinatorial framework that maps such integrals to invariants of tensor representations?
answerWithPaperReferences: [Paper 2109.14890] introduces Weingarten calculus, a method that converts the problem of integrating polynomial functions over compact groups (such as the unitary group) into computing certain matrices associated with tensor invariants, effectively providing an analogue of Wick calculus for Haar-distributed matrices. [Paper 2401.13740] applies this framework to evaluate the Haar integrals appearing in the second tangent space of random matrix product states. By using the well-known expressions from Weingarten calculus, [Paper 2401.13740] computes the transfer operators in the replicated space and derives the density of states ρ(x), finding that it asymptotically behaves as ρ(x) ~ 1 + (D²-1)e^{-x/ξ}, where D is the bond dimension and ξ is the correlation length of the reference MPS. Equivalently, for integer spacing j, ρ(j) ~ 1 + (D²-1)/d^{j-1}. Thus, the bond dimension enters quadratically in the correction to the uniform density of states.
answerWithoutPaperReferences: The density of states in the second tangent space of a random matrix product state manifold can be computed by evaluating Haar integrals over the unitary group using a combinatorial framework that maps such integrals to problems involving tensor invariants and associated Weingarten matrices. Applying this framework to the transfer matrix structure of random MPS yields an asymptotic density of states that behaves as ρ(x) ~ 1 + (D²-1)e^{-x/ξ}, where D is the bond dimension and ξ is the correlation length of the reference state. For discrete quasiparticle spacing j, this corresponds to ρ(j) ~ 1 + (D²-1)/d^{j-1}, indicating that the bond dimension D contributes a quadratic correction to the uniform background density.

Paper 2109.14890 provides the former but contains no information about MPS or the density of states result, while Paper 2401.13740 provides the latter but does not explain the underlying integration framework in sufficient detail to answer the conceptual 'what framework' part. First 37719 characters: The Weingarten Calculus
abstract: This is a short introduction to Weingarten Calculus. Weingarten Calculus is a method to compute the joint moments of matrix variables distributed according to the Haar measure of compact groups.
Introduction: Every compact topological group supports a unique translation invariant probability measure on its Borel sets — the Haar measure. Haar measure was first constructed for certain families of compact matrix groups by Hurwitz in the nineteenth century in order to produce invariants of these groups by averaging their actions. Hurwitz's construction has been reviewed from a modern perspective by Diaconis and Forrester, who argue that it should be regarded as the starting point of modern random matrix theory . An axiomatic construction of Haar measures in the more general context of locally compact groups was published by Haar in the 1930s, with further important contributions made in work of von Neumann, Weil, and Cartan; see .Given a measure, one wants to integrate. The Bochner integral for continuous functions {{formula:a1e9a3cf-12d8-4ae3-bbc3-bc2fc02ea5bf}} on a compact group {{formula:04502a13-8139-4337-acf6-5c9895b68624}} taking values in a given Banach space is called the Haar integral; it is almost always written simply {{formula:0e250b21-b616-469f-af8f-6b3d1b45e7f5}}with no explicit notation for the Haar measure. While integration on groups is a concept of fundamental importance in many parts of mathematics, including functional analysis and representation theory, probability and ergodic theory, etc., the actual computation of Haar integrals is a problem which has received curiously little attention. As far as the authors are aware, it was first considered by theoretical physicists in the 1970s in the context of nonabelian gauge theories, where the issue of evaluating — or at least approximating — Haar integrals plays a major role. In particular, the physics literature on quantum chromodynamics, the main theory of strong interactions in particle physics, is littered with so-called “link integrals,” which are Haar integrals of the form {{formula:a7fbdb7f-aafb-408f-a21f-fd6dad34fac0}}where {{formula:ca00395d-16cf-4c94-83a9-0c3926e12134}} is the compact group of unitary matrices {{formula:51454746-09ca-4dba-aa22-22b179eea2db}} Confronted with a paucity of existing mathematical tools for the evaluation of such integrals, physicists developed their own methods, which allowed them to obtain beautiful, explicit formulas such as {{formula:8325992d-0e42-443c-9e96-bbc8b1df0ef7}}an evaluation which holds for all unitary groups of rank {{formula:1f55f448-8555-4ccb-8ba9-5223df89b9c6}} Although exceedingly clever, the bag of tricks for evaluating Haar integrals assembled by physicists is ad hoc and piecemeal, lacking the unity and coherence which are the hallmarks of a mathematical theory.The missing theory of Haar integrals began to take shape in the early 2000s, driven by an explosion of interest in random matrix theory. The basic Hilbert spaces of random matrix theory are {{formula:3d3e096c-1b2d-455d-9594-848897f9d61e}} and {{formula:c90d241a-3250-4449-ac2f-ac6bfa4cda68}} where {{formula:f04fe169-ab02-442e-995f-b0e1ddfc5133}} is the noncompact abelian group of Hermitian matrices {{formula:ef2514e9-80e1-4364-8c36-643c8a2f88b6}} equipped with a Gaussian measure of mean {{formula:d9d3d4e1-9ea4-4217-aea5-4bbf00303c9f}} and variance {{formula:4f623c76-4538-4679-a4bc-e7901c6ff30e}} , and {{formula:2618fa6c-2cc2-45a3-8a4a-4e2259800b4a}} is the compact nonabelian group of unitary matrices {{formula:f5ac497a-22c3-4d86-96a2-d5c6944cb96d}} equipped with the Haar measure, just as above. Given a distribution on matrices, the basic goal of random matrix theory is to understand the induced distribution of eigenvalues, which in the selfadjoint case form a random point process on the line, and in the unitary case constitute a random point process on the circle. The moment method in random matrix theory, pioneered by Wigner () in the 1950s, is an algebraic approach to this problem. The main idea is to adopt the algebra {{formula:6e65d0ed-a8f8-4faf-b15d-d0f9f4f1cad3}} of symmetric polynomials in eigenvalues as a basic class of test functions, and integrate such functions by realizing them as elements of the algebra {{formula:a42a4485-8fe5-445a-a11e-e7095851cc51}} of polynomials in matrix elements, which can then (hopefully) be integrated by leveraging the defining features of the matrix model under consideration. The canonical example is sums of powers of eigenvalues, which may equivalently be viewed as traces of matrix powers; more generally, all coefficients of the characteristic polynomial are sums of principal matrix minors.It is straightforward to see that, in both of the above {{formula:0fc756a3-550c-41b6-9fd3-365a584c6ad4}} -spaces, the algebra {{formula:0a183ef9-18e1-4cc2-9adc-6aa19f50ec12}} of polynomial functions in matrix elements admits the orthogonal decomposition {{formula:8ed92227-1a6f-49e4-9782-dfdd05f86582}}where {{formula:3d145e00-dd77-46a9-8610-d48a4c4e2147}} is the space of homogeneous degree {{formula:84e3d777-e0d7-4b75-956f-1e8ec76288eb}} polynomial functions in matrix elements. Thus, modulo the algebraic issues inherent in transitioning from {{formula:5cb28a33-4226-45ca-ad62-0b8bad6a7fa8}} to {{formula:da7f8d1f-f3d7-4989-9daa-c37771d79b53}} the moment method boils down to computing scalar products of monomials of equal degree, so expressions of the form {{formula:a0fed8ac-60fc-4f06-84c8-71141e8fae11}}and {{formula:64560e86-af92-46e7-b188-88522a6aaad0}}In the Gaussian case, monomial scalar products can be computed systematically using a combinatorial algorithm which physicists call the “Wick formula” and statisticians call the “Isserlis theorem.” This device leverages independence together with the characteristic feature of centered normal distributions — vanishing of all cumulants but the second — to compute Gaussian expectations as polynomials in the variance parameter {{formula:8966a056-e4e3-45e1-91c0-0cf7c3bcc48b}} . The upshot is that scalar products in {{formula:f723ee3f-774d-4f8e-bb0c-8bed79eadc21}} are closely related to the combinatorics of graphs drawn on compact Riemann surfaces, which play the role of Feynman diagrams for selfadjoint matrix-valued field theories. We recommend () as an entry point into the fascinating combinatorics of Wick calculus.The case of Haar unitary matrices is a priori more complicated: the random variables {{formula:483b5867-da64-401c-81b8-ccc6ab8778ba}} are identically distributed, thanks to the invariance of Haar measure, but they are also highly correlated, due to the constraint {{formula:ee93314b-e9f2-4b96-bc73-675c51105209}} Moreover, each individual entry follows a complicated law not uniquely determined by its mean and variance. Despite these obstacles, it turns out that, when packaged correctly, the invariance of Haar measure provides everything needed to develop an analogue of Wick calculus for Haar unitary matrices. Moreover, once the correct general perspective has been found, one realizes that it applies equally well to any compact group, and even to compact symmetric spaces and compact quantum groups. This compact group analogue of Wick calculus has come to be known as Weingarten calculus, a name chosen by Collins to honor the contributions of Donald Weingarten, a physicist whose early work in the subject proved to be of foundational importance.The Weingarten calculus has matured rapidly over the course of the past decade, and the time now seems right to give a pedagogical account of the subject. The authors are currently preparing a monograph intended to meet this need. In this article, we aim to provide an easily digestible and hopefully compelling preview of our forthcoming work, emphasizing the big picture.First and foremost, we wish to impart the insight that, like the calculus of Newton and Liebniz, the core of Weingarten calculus is a fundamental theorem which converts a computational problem into a symbolic problem: whereas the usual fundamental theorem of calculus converts the problem of integrating functions on the line into computing antiderivatives, the fundamental theorem of Weingarten calculus converts the problem of integrating functions on groups into computing certain matrices associated to tensor invariants. The fundamental theorem of Weingarten calculus is presented in detail in Section 2.We then turn to examples illustrating the fundamental theorem in action. We present two detailed case studies: integration on the automorphism group {{formula:5bcb40a6-79c5-4daa-ab2a-5e2e44fd2d4e}} of {{formula:aaac9080-9216-457a-9b5d-8b0003ef338f}} distinct points, and integration on the automorphism group {{formula:1de03ea0-8578-436e-9a68-ec8f91f2e19b}} of {{formula:b8700bfb-fea8-45fd-add5-3cfef5cf791a}} orthonormal vectors. These are natural examples, given that the symmetric group and the unitary group are model examples of a finite and infinite compact group, respectively. The {{formula:1bb7f39f-06e4-4fcd-8c09-f354def35a2e}} case, presented in Section 3, is a toy example chosen to illustrate how Weingarten calculus works in an elementary situation where the integrals to which it applies can easily be evaluated from first principles. The {{formula:848cc25c-3b98-4aff-97e4-afae7855667a}} case, discussed in Section 4, is an example of real interest, and we give a detailed workup showing how Weingarten calculus handles the link integrals of {{formula:a82630e4-a6f1-4811-ad4b-a6a77aabb3ae}} lattice gauge theory.Section 5 gives a necessarily brief discussion of Weingarten calculus for the remaining classical groups, namely the orthogonal group {{formula:1025d445-69c3-4b26-b290-a582a55f663c}} and the symplectic group {{formula:cfdd67b9-3bbd-4632-8849-9256ffce4a42}} both of which receive a detailed treatment in (cite our book). Finally, Section 6 extols the universality of Weingarten calculus, briefly discussing how it can be transported to compact symmetric spaces and compact quantum groups, and indicating applications in quantum information theory.
The Fundamental Theorem: Given a compact group {{formula:705cb79e-9af7-4e25-a3d1-cf1508324095}} , a finite-dimensional Hilbert space {{formula:a173f455-a6b7-4f53-a7bc-22a09ac20acd}} with a specified orthonormal basis {{formula:b3eca92e-2fe5-4768-a0e7-8412a12f83f3}} , and a continuous group homomorphism {{formula:9f33158e-fd3a-4289-ab39-f5be25e845ea}} , let {{formula:94028d6b-8c5f-44a7-8620-9ded492f0a60}} be the corresponding matrix element functionals, {{formula:c39b2993-fd6d-44c4-8ce4-3c45f94f2e08}}The Weingarten integrals of the unitary representation {{formula:6329af89-d9c7-4c87-a011-e86dce722ef5}} are the integrals {{formula:f2849a56-e959-4a57-81ac-d5c522414111}}where {{formula:5925a468-31f8-4315-990c-35b212d11132}} ranges over the set {{formula:dac68ede-be9c-47a2-9e77-83cbcf4edf7a}} of positive integers, and the multi-indices {{formula:09a0c942-3e65-4e03-afb3-1b83c54eb7e9}} range over the set {{formula:0b83ee95-f980-4a39-b73c-2ceb4d2036d3}} of functions from {{formula:eb6a1c00-4837-4fe2-b923-47b2cb180388}} to {{formula:933a2419-66d7-433c-a083-56b8339bb2db}} . Clearly, if we can compute all Weingarten integrals {{formula:cb919d35-5c96-4394-9cfc-ff67e5bfba4e}} , then we can integrate any function on {{formula:80a076d2-c002-4d98-a33a-1b73f4906029}} which is a polynomial in the matrix elements {{formula:42dcaf05-c001-4348-ac88-1608a11af249}} This is the basic problem of Weingarten calculus: compute the Weingarten integrals of a given unitary representation of a given compact group.The fundamental theorem of Weingarten calculus addresses this problem by linearizing it. The basic observation is that, for each {{formula:cc211415-98c0-49c9-a578-e726cf6cb89f}} the {{formula:700c637e-6c49-487f-a6b4-6a6053a14339}} integrals {{formula:73da5987-2e5c-4a41-95a7-5ba2b7daccba}} , {{formula:1f924e7a-1663-4425-9696-04c273c257a8}} , are themselves the matrix elements of a linear operator. Indeed, we have {{formula:0239ae24-ebde-4a9b-b414-51e2a88577a5}}where {{formula:b02e2e38-2539-4251-a75d-6d2e53703940}}is the orthonormal basis of {{formula:208cc892-32e0-4bdc-a3ef-85581e57af00}} corresponding to the specified orthonormal basis {{formula:de20798f-bb03-4521-abd0-145aca284e6e}} in {{formula:d5676932-9c63-4ed1-b7ad-7915028f5cc2}} , and {{formula:0d446cfd-ddd6-4fcb-bab4-46993ce91c87}}are the matrix elements of the unitary operator {{formula:7bf77d7f-321e-4624-acbc-5cf65c8b6038}} in this basis. By continuity, we thus have that {{formula:ceb0d1bc-5fe9-4854-b8b8-7a0e0a0ddc35}}where {{formula:ea5ce555-3594-4fa2-b55c-e674ff14423b}} are the matrix elements of the selfadjoint operator {{formula:e0557511-b933-4e0f-ad08-9208d740743c}}obtained by integrating the unitary operators {{formula:0eca0755-a7f5-404c-9a33-e8a88b8330a2}} against Haar measure. The basic problem of Weingarten calculus is thus equivalent to computing the matrix elements of {{formula:b2a2af66-4d5f-4351-833e-044a5235ca75}} , for all {{formula:6ee7e0e2-0f65-4e42-97d0-f56a41e08945}}This is where the characteristic feature of Haar measure, the invariance {{formula:120ca268-3211-409c-81b3-a8eb34f7aa45}}comes into play: it forces {{formula:2f07f2d1-796b-40b3-9a82-22d3c5586800}} Thus {{formula:146fa228-c7d8-4431-b0ab-df14556906bc}} is a selfadjoint idempotent, and as such {{formula:760f2b66-1e22-4c63-9156-da62af0553b8}} orthogonally projects {{formula:1b303842-839c-4aa1-991b-57e8289dc3f1}} onto its image, which is the space of {{formula:eb0c82de-4821-4364-821e-3e1d97f3fdaa}} -invariant tensors in {{formula:3a8aedb7-169d-4397-a61b-c78fd938653c}} {{formula:3c70f564-753c-45e6-8843-ad9eeba7d71b}}Thus, we see that the basic problem of Weingarten calculus is in fact very closely related to the basic problem of invariant theory, which is to determine a basis for the space {{formula:0218b912-440a-496d-b59c-5e1ac2c2ce27}} -invariant tensors in {{formula:692dc9bf-e5e3-48c1-8c56-09818c5f6be0}} for all {{formula:91ceaa81-7ad5-4c6b-a364-2b693575a76c}}Indeed, suppose we have have access to a basis {{formula:9dec9950-9251-4456-a148-93d6824e9e58}} of {{formula:95efad39-a9cc-4b60-8335-36fb6a15060d}} . Then, by elementary linear algebra, we have everything we need to calculate the matrix {{formula:cc1b3d67-1a13-4abf-b602-dc37bf74c590}}of degree {{formula:225324b1-ab9f-4493-b3fa-705111734d6f}} Weingarten integrals. Let {{formula:2c38aee2-1248-4888-a871-7177edd3c374}} be the {{formula:59569c47-f1c6-483f-9676-61bca8c991a7}} matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the basic invariants in the desired basis, {{formula:5c53711e-d74a-4698-9e85-da76e96cfef2}}Then we have the matrix factorization {{formula:700dd83f-f2dd-4cc0-be71-173e664eeef6}}familiar from matrix analysis as the multidimensional generalization of the undergraduate “outer product divided by inner product” formula for orthogonal projection onto a line. The {{formula:73b0533e-c754-499f-95ad-48327265ed8a}} matrix {{formula:9b1a25e0-3c9d-4100-bc4b-eca3fa25e3e7}} is nothing but the Gram matrix {{formula:f5f78f08-aa9a-4fe8-8c82-472897759de8}}of the basic {{formula:f7762bdd-80f7-42da-b6cf-b0ab6e699d6f}} -invariants in {{formula:c0897c6e-ceeb-4de8-825a-97ba73d3c3d5}} , whose linear independence is equivalent to the invertibility of the Gram matrix. Let us give the inverse Gram matrix a name: we call {{formula:36c98fcf-a00d-41e0-a073-98d7ac22136b}}the Weingarten matrix of the invariants {{formula:6685e016-d4b8-4858-9fbf-6e05b2e5d8ae}} Extracting matrix elements on either side of the factorization {{formula:5bb457e8-255a-4446-8b03-235cc9911fda}} , we obtain the Fundamental Theorem of Weingarten Calculus.Theorem 2.1 For any {{formula:d913191d-8565-4918-9298-0f1ceebd76ff}} and {{formula:bdaf9aef-cabe-4895-aad1-82b9856f523c}} we have {{formula:bbeaffd3-bfe6-454c-8ad7-593483ffbca8}}Does Theorem REF actually solve the basic problem of Weingarten calculus? Yes, insofar as the classical fundamental theorem of calculus solves the problem of computing definite integrals: it reduces a numerical problem to a symbolic problem. In order to apply the fundamental theorem of calculus to integrate a given function, one must find its antiderivative, and as every student of calculus knows this can be a wild ride. In order to use the fundamental theorem of Weingarten calculus to compute the Weingarten integrals of a given unitary representation, one must solve a suped up version of the basic problem of invariant which involves not only finding basic tensor invariants, but computing their Weingarten matrices. Just like the computation of antiderivatives, this may prove to be a difficult task.

The Gram matrix: In order to calculate Weingarten integrals of the adjoint representaiton of {{formula:aaa1b4f4-46f6-400d-b5b7-e619c7235e18}} we first need to solve the basic problem of invariant theory for this representation. A partial solution to this problem is well-known, and part of a classical circle of ideas, commonly known as Schur-Weyl duality, which relate the representation theory of {{formula:294fbec9-56cf-4f13-92e2-39e48b02dba5}} to representations of the symmetric groups {{formula:77f5a9d6-f9bc-4fe1-ace2-c66a1b65eff6}} {{formula:0bc25881-6e82-4c68-83aa-6757233307b4}} In particular, it is known that, after identifying {{formula:3c863f78-b7e5-42e2-aa3b-edf915e10c59}} with {{formula:c4806b7a-5a95-4667-b06b-bc53d16c200b}} the space of {{formula:be50f651-cb84-4f41-ae68-fea9a32494d2}} -invariants is spanned by the operators which act by permuting tensor factors, {{formula:0f81444d-faa5-49af-a136-20b49cd8d9a3}}Moreover, it is not difficult to compute the scalar product of any two of these operators: given {{formula:6e8ec28b-677d-4cdf-b67f-d2cd047b89ca}} one finds that {{formula:50178e7c-5e83-49b0-b74d-6e5d4442a2ca}}where {{formula:b3a34d13-daad-45cf-bccc-b5242a53b764}} is the number of factors in any factorization of {{formula:b996b69d-8f5a-4bea-9364-292ef0a2558f}} into disjoint cyclic permutations, so that the Gram matrix of these invariants is the {{formula:1b515921-c2c6-4ebc-ac24-e023fe3b8d8d}} matrix {{formula:db9cb676-8022-4f3f-a7e6-55f945f1c06c}}The reason we refer to this as a partial solution to the basic problem of invariant theory for the adjoint representation of {{formula:0364dd34-2663-4e96-bdd4-89e889a15657}} is that, although {{formula:816cd2c3-8c2e-4c34-96bc-fea0fd678a68}} is a spanning set of invariants, it is only a basis in the stable range, where {{formula:ac2190c6-dc8d-4270-8d10-802a1c993e03}} In the unstable range, {{formula:16a96fce-ec3e-4b6f-8288-1867ae25209e}} , the operators {{formula:d44fc3b0-35f2-4d89-896e-783c27cf8c11}} are linearly dependent, and their Gram matrix is singular. A satisfactory patch for this issue was found relatively recently by Baik and Rains (cite "Increasing subsequences and the classical groups"), who showed that {{formula:fda30130-3196-454b-a937-dd99affc3f0a}} is always a basis, where {{formula:e74d5472-d8e7-4964-8ceb-3d5cfe960f2e}} is the set of permutations of {{formula:63cd0489-a945-4bb9-91c0-88af821f98ce}} with no decreasing subsequence of length {{formula:4b8d5747-ca2e-47ca-93ad-d437c752a80c}} Thus, the Gram matrix which needs to be inverted in order to calculate the degree {{formula:6d4ef4bb-6aa6-4b34-a447-0cb119d8f54a}} Weingarten integrals of the adjoint representation is actually {{formula:1dd480e7-5a05-4488-82d6-78d2da207b0a}}In the unstable range, the Gram matrix {{formula:8a8ddd5b-e592-4839-9734-6417f26a693f}} must be computed numerically, but in the stable range we can view {{formula:42ed7288-5035-4527-b384-b37090830f34}} as a parameter, so that the Weingarten matrix {{formula:94ebd72c-c654-47bf-bed2-4ef58e8f04c9}} is a {{formula:84dfa5ca-2b8d-4b4f-b08b-99039b604312}} matrix whose entries are rational functions of {{formula:b5ecc48d-23c7-48fc-8aa1-20318e31effc}} To get a handle on what these functions might be, it turns out to be a good idea to reinterpret the Gram matrix from the viewpoint of geometric group theory. More precisely, let us identify {{formula:ae4e1a0c-01e9-47b2-a123-97c9cd2e10cd}} with its (right) Cayley graph as generated by the conjugacy class of transpositions; then, the geodesic distance between permutations {{formula:b64fec74-785c-4aff-9fda-ff962b9d2bb8}} is given by {{formula:135f5236-2f37-4827-a4d5-75ac340025a7}} where {{formula:64a8f082-210f-40de-b4ad-b6677f46e5f5}}is the word norm corresponding to the generating set of transpositions. Let {{formula:6f58cbcf-397a-4e18-bf78-5fa9b14e05d1}} be a complex parameter, and consider the {{formula:70b5f5d3-5775-40fb-a56d-7a0df1e8c9d7}} matrix {{formula:7ae06868-13dd-48e5-9edf-761843f4f798}}the {{formula:ee26b688-d6f1-4f63-a4d0-218854e9e731}} -distance matrix of the symmetric group {{formula:9c24de16-2044-4a97-92f5-de2297dc00e7}} The {{formula:7e5876d8-1753-46c5-9738-bba07c9a3ba7}} -distance matrix {{formula:41477c63-94be-4470-bad2-72fa9dc87de6}} is a natural analytic continuation of the Gram matrix {{formula:249e915d-216c-4d43-afc8-efe55068c90a}} — to recover the latter from the former, simply multiply by {{formula:51f11803-653e-40d7-ac76-e20bc137ff7b}} and then set {{formula:b76cd212-3f4f-40cf-b8bf-439b35101724}}Thus, the problem we face is that of understanding the {{formula:efbb4a0b-9b35-4164-8e0a-711b4c8484d9}} -distance matrix of the symmetric group sufficiently well that we can invert it. This may be addressed via harmonic analysis on {{formula:e0c10e05-e485-4e3f-8012-f2bde270bda8}} The basic observation is that {{formula:c4fba8e9-59da-4f99-9c85-3d530d558744}} is the matrix of the group algebra element {{formula:7fff990f-cd5a-40ce-a8c2-804dd696a5ad}}acting in the right regular representation of {{formula:271db628-2f5a-4d04-8fff-c297e160733f}} Moreover, {{formula:c75dc9e3-bd4d-464d-b3b2-fd76ed3eb24a}} is a central element in {{formula:91a24bbd-11a6-4a89-89fa-0992cfe6e2a4}} : in fact, we have {{formula:32bd8a80-f2db-45f1-8f3d-89a6c70a40ae}}where {{formula:7d676158-129f-41a5-891e-5cadfe5d1862}} is the sum of all points on the sphere of radius {{formula:d36d840d-8dc6-4eb7-98d3-1fbd1c159011}} centered at the identity permutation {{formula:74136aa5-8a9b-418f-9079-ff2832e24935}} or equivalently the sum of all permutations on the {{formula:4005c4fc-5e22-4374-8109-fa2e6689d8f8}} th level of the Cayley graph. Clearly, every such sphere/level is a disjoint union of conjugacy classes. The plan is thus to take the Fourier transform of {{formula:f965a716-2057-452b-95a1-11f203d0ff79}} , i.e. its image under the algebra isomorphism {{formula:a7d470be-1252-446f-a74d-42c50b524314}}where {{formula:f808be29-3044-43a6-9c98-e0914e3030c9}} is the irreducible representation of {{formula:249b6e2c-4481-4601-95de-0dde51a66f9d}} indexed by a given Young diagram {{formula:b7b21ff7-8b11-489c-bb82-0d8b5f76cd9e}} with {{formula:0a2e95b5-5264-4ff7-863f-97cc77417ead}} cells, and {{formula:f68c1057-879c-49b2-a3b8-f0537134d579}}Since {{formula:bca174c7-8d42-450d-8b9a-5359a856ca2e}} is central, Schur's Lemma guarantees that {{formula:867161c8-9742-4f46-b3c2-db74c7c29963}} will be a direct sum of scalar operators, which can then easily be inverted. In particular, the computation reduces to calculating the Fourier transforms of the levels {{formula:913bcab1-cf0f-4bc1-ae54-6c5b29f7f0c5}} of the Cayley graph.The computation of the Fourier transform of {{formula:aee94bee-b5cd-42e3-84d7-199c28e41fa6}} rests on a pair of remarkable discoveries in algebraic combinatorics made by the Lithuanian physicist Algimantas Adolfas Jucys (not to be confused with his father, the Lithuanian physicist Adolfas Jucys). The first of Jucys' discoveries is a unique factorization theorem for permutations. Let us call a factorization {{formula:8f321527-28ae-4569-9ad7-02b9d7b18e0e}}of a permutation {{formula:dee2b429-45d6-4f30-a905-c1c8e892f4c6}} into transpositions {{formula:a80fd5e5-c853-4b24-bdf5-247ea59e711c}} where {{formula:320b7971-9a14-42da-9444-89ced971946e}} , a strictly monotone factorization if {{formula:d97fa181-cde6-46e1-bb72-fac5ecfe6ec8}}Theorem 4.1 Every permutation {{formula:1cd04e1a-8c5a-4845-8a13-5864e393c94f}} admits a unique monotone factorization, and the number of factors in this factorization is {{formula:cf71e489-0bab-4a1a-8baa-11ed82fa739c}} {{figure:0e1dbc67-9154-4149-9088-6a82bd576cb3}}This result may be visualized as follows. Let us mark each edge of the Cayley graph of {{formula:a4180731-9116-4861-a352-cec3ab8fdcd9}} corresponding to the transposition {{formula:35ec88f0-4b3a-4534-b7bc-14dea0b22ccc}} with {{formula:00c2d452-e3a3-4374-b8f5-ad0fdbdfc97d}} the larger of the two symbols it interchanges. We call this the Biane-Stanley labeling of the symmetric group, since a version of it was considered first by Stanley and later by Biane in connection with the combinatorics of noncrossing partitions. Figure REF depicts the Biane-Stanley labeling of {{formula:5f5c671b-3115-4067-9903-89c472448efb}} Call a walk on {{formula:4e8a9fb2-2f43-482b-8552-ef47fe8d3496}} a strictly monotone walk if the labels of the edges it traverse form a strictly increasing sequence.
