Conclusions: We have shown that in many cases, it is possible to perfectly transfer an unknown quantum state along a pair of quantum chains even if their coupling is to some amount random. This is achieved using a dual-rail encoding combined with measurements at the receiving end of the chains. Since any scheme for quantum communication will suffer from some imperfections when implemented, the dual-rail is a powerful tool to overcome the decrease of fidelity.This work was supported by the UK Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council through the grant GR/S62796/01 and the QIPIRC.

Conclusive and arbitrarily perfect quantum state transfer using parallel spin chain channels
abstract: We suggest a protocol for perfect quantum communication through spin chain channels. By combining a dual-rail encoding with measurements only at the receiving end, we can get conclusively perfect state transfer, whose probability of success can be made arbitrarily close to unity. As an example of such an amplitude delaying channel, we show how two parallel Heisenberg spin chains can be used as quantum wires. Perfect state transfer with a probability of failure lower than P in a Heisenberg chain of N spin-1/2 particles can be achieved in a timescale of the order of N^1.7|ln(P)|. We demonstrate that our scheme is more robust to decoherence and non-optimal timing than any scheme using single spin chains.
Introduction: The development of reliable methods to transfer quantum states is of fundamental importance in quantum information theory. Usually, flying qubits such as photons, ballistic electrons and guided atoms/ions are considered for this purpose. However, converting back and forth between stationary qubits (of say a quantum computer or as held by the communicating parties) and mobile carriers of quantum information and interfacing between different physical implementations of qubits is very difficult and may not be really worth for short communication distances.An attractive alternative is to use a finite array of interacting but stationary qubits as an information bus. It would, however, not be very useful if the interactions between various pairs of stationary qubits have to be repeatedly switched on and off to perform the communication, because gating errors will then accumulate. Moreover, the local control required will be as high as that of a quantum computer. Only if we can utilize systems with permanently coupled material qubits (such as molecular spin chains), or systems without local control (such as Josephson junction arrays or optical lattices) with minimal global switchings, can we have a communication bus much before a quantum computer. In such schemes, both the amplitude and the phase damping (mechanisms of decoherence) can be ensured to be no worse than that of a single moving qubit, by ensuring that there is at most one excitation in the array during the communication process. With the above view in mind, recently the use of spin chains , , , , , , , , , , , and harmonic chains as quantum wires have been proposed.The initial system independent proposal was inspired by the natural setting for spin chain molecules (and optical lattices): regular arrays without local accessibility. Single spin encoding was assumed to avoid quantum gates. For this simplicity, its specific realizations is already being proposed . However, it allows only imperfect communication fidelity and necessitate the use of entanglement distillation from a large ensemble, which destroy its simplicity. Later approaches of perfecting fidelity require either the engineering of the couplings , , or an encoding of a qubit to several spins , . Independently, local measurements on each qubit along the chain , , have been proposed. The above deviate either from naturalness or from simplicity. We are thus sorely in need of a scheme which remains natural and simple, yet achieves perfect quantum communication. This is achieved in this paper by using a dual-rail encoding.The outline of the article is as follows. In Section , we suggest a scheme for quantum communication using two parallel spin chains of the most natural type (namely those with constant couplings). We require modest encodings (or gates) and measurements only at the ends of the chains. The state transfer is conclusive, which means that it is possible to tell by the outcome of a quantum measurement, without destroying the state, if the transfer took place or not. If it did, then the transfer was perfect. The transmission time for conclusive transfer is no longer than for single spin chains. In Section , we demonstrate that our scheme offers even more: if the transfer was not successful, then we can wait for some time and just repeat the measurement, without having to resend the state. By performing sufficiently many measurements, the probability for perfect transfer approaches unity. Hence the transfer is arbitrarily perfect. We will show in Section that the time needed to transfer a state with a given probability scales in a reasonable way with the length of the chain. Finally, in Section we show that encoding to parallel chains and the conclusiveness also makes our protocol more robust to decoherence (a hitherto unaddressed issue in the field of quantum communication through spin chains). {{figure:53329b2b-c3a6-41f2-821f-bb7a1b2e9ff6}}
Scheme for conclusive transfer: We intend to propose our scheme in a system independent way with occasional references to systems where conditions required by our scheme are achieved. We assume that our system consists of two identical uncoupled spin-{{formula:03b1698b-0284-499d-bfbd-cef366e682cb}} -chains {{formula:b9a99ef3-9ff6-4f7c-b09f-3f0352667de9}} and {{formula:f94b9f31-93bd-49d7-805f-699feb881061}} of length {{formula:86111b5b-50e8-4f2f-b1b4-fe8b6dc85a9b}} , described by the Hamiltonian {{formula:6c4a6450-47f8-4921-80cd-66e03439ca17}}The term identical states that {{formula:3cfb199e-5a31-4bba-8739-b472c67f07d0}} and {{formula:8cbeb56e-4513-4808-ac9f-6301465deaf9}} are the same apart from the label of the Hilbert space they act on. The requirement of parallel chains instead of just one is not problematic, since in many experimental realizations of spin chains, it is much easier to produce a whole bunch of parallel uncoupled , chains than just a single one.We assume that the ground state of each chain is {{formula:8a9a90a8-9a15-4755-8830-dd8192dc33c2}} , i.e. a ferromagnetic ground state, with {{formula:e220bad2-8fa5-4798-bf85-9ba18bd216df}} and that the subspace consisting of the single spin excitations {{formula:dd4708ef-74b9-4194-971b-6ba5a75ca17c}} is invariant under {{formula:276ecc0b-972e-4418-9dae-2bde87f14b70}} An arbitrary qubit at the site {{formula:7339a3ea-84e9-4657-94d2-548d8a0dd610}} of system {{formula:8acf0b7f-697f-4b2f-b7eb-a5fc04478d2b}} can be written as {{formula:5baed9f6-f7ea-4e88-b474-5e04bb18fdad}}The dynamics restricted to this subspace can be expressed in terms of the transition amplitudes {{formula:2907fdf7-0d45-4617-a8b0-922d15ee5e95}}The aim of our protocol is to transfer quantum information from the 1st (“Alice”) to the {{formula:25c4c19e-1c93-46a7-b1a8-b1bc5f324a40}} th (“Bob”) qubit of the first chain, {{formula:2269faa4-7278-4f9e-a8eb-bc7150459887}}To achieve this, we need {{formula:958a13a7-6bc1-4c9b-9797-9e63b2733d59}} (which is valid for a Heisenberg chain, for example ). An advantage of Heisenberg ferromagnetic chains over a non-interacting qubit array is that some XXZ anisotropy can make the states {{formula:1c4e3c5e-7d8c-4fea-b367-dc7e54175cda}} and {{formula:159219df-80e9-4d79-b755-66a8fe4ab410}} stable against excitations at finite temperatures . Even a small anisotropy in the coupling {{formula:3be0ef9f-474e-4c7a-a129-f347ca28c8bd}} may suffice (as {{formula:ebaef23b-6034-4961-a215-e14a0653063d}} itself can be as high as {{formula:cd32f7dc-49c2-43c7-a357-db667e7dbd7f}} ). Alternatively, one can prevent thermal excitations by applying an uniform magnetic field to the chain.The initial state of the system is {{formula:9b74803d-b266-44c3-ade7-e8df3be2acdc}} . The first step of the protocol is to encode the input qubit in a “dual-rail” by applying a NOT gate on the first qubit of system {{formula:7d208279-9506-4b8c-a9fc-0fc9e98304c0}} controlled by the first qubit of system {{formula:f82022a8-fd47-4222-b8de-6e24ccfe7d3c}} being zero, resulting in a superposition of excitations in both systems, {{formula:d8fcaa26-7805-4284-95d9-8006c5853598}}This is assumed to take place in a much shorter timescale than the system dynamics. Even though a 2-qubit gate in solid state systems is difficult, such a gate for charge qubits has been reported . For the same qubits, Josephson arrays have been proposed as single spin chains for quantum communication . For this system, both requisites of our scheme are thus available. In fact, the demand that Alice and Bob can do measurements and apply gates to their local qubits (i.e. the ends of the chains) will be naturally fulfilled in practice since we are suggesting a scheme to transfer information between quantum computers.Under the system Hamiltonian, the excitation in Eq. We can decode the qubit by applying a CNOT gate at Bob's site. The state thereafter will be {{formula:f76d0b17-2e86-4ba4-8ae7-6de775d41237}}Bob can now perform a measurement on his qubit of system {{formula:8408c7bd-b598-4c72-b815-107b75169e1e}} If the outcome of this measurement is 1, he can conclude that the state {{formula:5417660a-ca47-467c-98e2-10d21e8e5530}} has been successfully transferred to him. This happens with the probability {{formula:a6dd7fb0-c2d6-40ae-91d4-881d5be40646}} If the outcome is 0, the system is in the state {{formula:f641cdfb-86a4-4c4e-9beb-d7ac32a5490b}}where {{formula:40163546-066c-4d78-891b-353efcf275f0}}is the probability of failure for the first measurement. If the protocol stopped here, and Bob would just assume his state as the transferred one, the channel could be described as an amplitude damping channel, with exactly the same fidelity as the single chain scheme discussed in . But success probability is more valuable than fidelity: Bob has gained knowledge about his state, and may reject it and ask Alice to retransmit. However, as we will show in the next section, this is not necessary.
Arbitrarily perfect state transfer: Because Bob's measurement has not revealed anything about the input state, the information is still residing in the chain. By letting the state (REF ) evolve for another time {{formula:ee4d8cae-ab3d-4eda-964e-618f3c0c5249}} and applying the CNOT gate again, Bob has another chance of receiving the input state. The state before performing the second measurement is easily seen to be {{formula:f06e5a36-fadd-41d8-8b79-8ee33a175fb9}}Hence the probability to receive the qubit at Bobs site at the second measurement is {{formula:aa1b9f7f-acf1-4d0b-8359-9e67413b129f}}If the transfer was still unsuccessful, this strategy can be repeated over and over. Each time Bob has a probability of failed state transfer that can be obtained from the generalization of Eq. (REF ) to an arbitrary number of iterations. The joint probability that Bob fails to receive the state all the time is just the product of these probabilities. We denote the joint probability of failure for having done {{formula:f43dfdaf-d781-4b93-9849-674ce3cd730a}} unsuccessful measurements as {{formula:6dac3584-10fd-4d86-be52-c194f4125668}} . This probability depends on the time intervals {{formula:82080aa7-8145-490d-931a-6cad9a876f76}} between the {{formula:3960070e-2440-4427-8413-a169a9f3ff68}} th and {{formula:6232ce4e-ffe3-4e34-8471-289d424cba2a}} th measurement, and we are interested in the case where the {{formula:67c0fa53-3a0a-4e5a-b93c-d87f82f5c4a6}} are chosen such that the transfer is fast. It is possible to write a simple algorithm that computes {{formula:fbfd169f-ba68-4bd8-907c-a2e43f19c434}} for any transition amplitude {{formula:346bdbbf-c3bb-43d0-9135-4d73e230e8dd}} Figure REF shows some results for a Heisenberg spin-{{formula:f86839cc-8ee0-4d85-82d2-557019be2e2e}} -chain with equal nearest neighbor couplings, {{formula:b177961e-2144-47a7-9717-d3cc3b6ac370}}This model is exactly solvable, and the transition amplitude is given explicitly in . However, the results are valid for a wide class of anisotropies and in the presence of a uniform magnetic field, too. {{figure:452f8551-2925-4058-883c-18c0c8635e51}}An interesting question is whether the joint probability of failure can be made arbitrary small with a large number of measurements. Since {{formula:dc78c551-0f55-4006-8760-8ff3586f7cc2}} is a bounded, monotonic decreasing series, it must have a limit. In fact, the times {{formula:a02f7b93-0071-4c5b-a812-1ed73358ad38}} can be chosen such that the transfer becomes arbitrarily perfect. This has been proven in , where a generalization of the above scheme and a much wider class of Hamiltonians is considered. In the limit of large number of measurements, the spin channel will not damp the initial amplitude, but only delay it.
Estimation of the timescale the transfer: The achievable fidelity is an important, but not the only criteria of a state transfer protocol. In this Section, we give an heuristic approach to estimate the time that it needs to achieve a certain fidelity in a Heisenberg spin chain. The comparison with numeric examples is confirming this approach.Let us first describe the dynamic of the chain in a very qualitative way. Once Alice has initialized the system, an excitation wave packet will travel along the chain. As shown in , it will reach Bob at a time of the order of {{formula:285825cc-43f1-48af-afb7-ce0fd88fce30}}with an amplitude of {{formula:41d07e4b-355b-4e36-a9e7-1ab8b4621d8c}}It is then reflected and travels back and forth along the chain. Since the wave packet is also dispersing, it starts interfering with its tail, and after a couple of reflections the dynamic is becoming quite randomly. This effect becomes even stronger due to Bobs measurements, which change the dynamics by projecting away parts of the wave packet. However, {{formula:7b6a1543-46ba-4a1e-9ec1-e2d95b5a6d54}} (the time it takes for a wave packet to travel twice along the chain) remains a good estimate of the timescale in which significant probability amplitude peaks at Bobs site occur, and Eq. Therefore, the joint probability of failure is expected to scale as {{formula:d37a729e-a90f-41fe-9117-755b1c77ead9}}in a time of the order of {{formula:798719c1-ea96-4045-a028-2abf2411821d}}If we combine Eq. The best fit is given by {{formula:8a1b2af2-0a03-4967-9afa-22d9c6710faf}}englishWe can conclude that the transmission time for arbitrarily perfect transfer is scaling not much worse with the length {{formula:adc3a6e4-bba9-428d-9e60-4072fd4dcdf7}} of the chains than the single spin chain schemes. Despite of the logarithmic dependence on {{formula:18e98eb0-ac10-423a-affc-c0825bb4b7bf}} the time it takes to achieve high fidelity is still reasonable. For example, a system with {{formula:8b1fdb7d-8426-4d77-8da4-c3b86076f698}} and {{formula:c236acdc-f7f1-4adb-b8d2-7ecc0518a77d}} will take approximately {{formula:16d42aad-8068-4f7c-b0f8-210bebfb28e1}} to achieve a fidelity of 99%. In many systems, decoherence is completely negligible within this timescale. For example, some Josephson junction systems have a decoherence time of {{formula:03753cbe-4650-4fbf-bfbc-ff8a513235f3}} , while trapped ions have even larger decoherence times.
Decoherence and imperfections: If the coupling between the spins {{formula:9520b96e-036b-409b-8b09-e9a4257abfa4}} is very small, or the chains are very long, the transmission time may no longer be negligible with respect to the decoherence time (see Section ). It is interesting to note that the dual-rail encoding then offers some significant general advantages over single chain schemes. Since we are suggesting a system-independent scheme, we will not study the effects of specific environments on our protocol, but just qualitatively point out its general advantages.At least theoretically, it is always possible to cool the system down or to apply a strong magnetic field such that the environment is not causing further excitations. Then, there are two remaining types of quantum noise that will occur: phase noise and amplitude damping. Phase noise is a serious problem and arises here only when an environment that can distinguish between spin flips on the first chain and spin flips on the second chain. It is therefore important that the environment cannot resolve their difference. In this case, the environment will only couple with the total {{formula:9abb3082-5293-4ec7-be64-db0f882c9db9}} -component {{formula:592762ef-5df1-4e5c-8c07-7d573610d147}}of the spins of both chains at each position {{formula:406e246a-8bb4-47ed-8970-bc8c5fb5e0b2}} . This has been discussed for spin-boson models in , but should also hold for spin environments as long as the chains are close enough. The qubit is encoded in a decoherence-free subspace and the scheme is fully robust to phase noise. Even though this may not be true for all implementations of dual-rail encoding, it is worthwhile noticing it because such an opportunity does not exist at all for single chain schemes, where the coherence between two states with different total z-component of the spin has to be preserved. Having shown one way of avoiding phase noise, at least in some systems, we now proceed to amplitude damping.The evolution of the system in presence of amplitude damping of a rate {{formula:15eaec26-a513-430b-8e35-919803defad9}} can be easily derived using a quantum-jump approach . Like for phase noise, it is necessary that the environment acts symmetrically on the chains. The dynamics is then given by an effective non-unitary Hamiltonian {{formula:fb3b2e30-0fbc-4148-b048-fa18d1292072}}if no jump occurs, and the effect of a jump is given by the operator {{formula:66990e98-96e2-46b6-9375-7a5eb57b6d7b}}which will put the system in the ground state. As this can be solved analytically, we do not go into numerics. The state of the system before the first measurement conditioned on no jump is given by {{formula:af618ec1-5a6d-4365-a34c-87ab281c4cff}}and this happens with the probability of {{formula:4e4f075f-8620-4789-a2ba-9a2fe343e8d0}} (the norm of the above state). If a jump occurs, the system will be in the ground state {{formula:26e8bb2f-5057-4e69-93fc-3db8a8960af7}}The density matrix at the time {{formula:bea09ec6-5d2b-4bd8-a44d-48924b9ef076}} is given by a mixture of (REF ) and (REF ). In case of (REF ), the quantum information is completely lost and Bob's error check qubit will never show success. If Bob however measures a success, it is clear that no jump has occurred and he has the perfectly transferred state. Therefore the protocol remains conclusive, but the success probability is lowered by {{formula:df7d55a1-39ae-4282-8320-4d8675c0f981}} This result is still valid for multiple measurements, which leave the state (REF ) unaltered. The probability of a successful transfer at each particular measurement {{formula:ecc3035a-8f1f-4483-95b9-50ca56afc517}} will decrease by {{formula:e9de5553-6021-4cda-b41f-c719bf01006b}} , where {{formula:b8cf8ac9-8d48-45dc-a33e-8d2696815bb0}} is the time of the measurement. After a certain number of measurements, the joint probability of failure will no longer decrease. Thus the transfer will no longer be arbitrarily perfect, but can still reach a very high fidelity. Some numerical examples of the minimal joint probability of failure that can be achieved, {{formula:104f12f7-ea83-4ad4-a632-efd8220c66b0}}are given in Fig. REF . For {{formula:bc43042d-0532-4210-a7e3-54934aa30be1}} nearly perfect transfer is still possible for chains up to a length of {{formula:7307e27d-053a-4089-a7d4-ba0794766320}} . In a single Heisenberg chain using the scheme described in , this system could only achieve a fidelity of {{formula:32464da9-2d80-49d9-a244-c98df021af45}} when transferring an exitation. {{figure:a57486e8-6999-4afa-8825-3e7d549b0853}}Even if the amplitude damping is not symmetric, its effect is weaker than in single spin schemes. This is because it can be split in a symmetric and asymmetric part. The symmetric part can be overcome with the above strategies. For example, if the amplitude damping on the chains is {{formula:619061bf-8b13-4b77-9dd4-a9ae296efcd4}} and {{formula:79ea19d2-9c38-42f7-b91c-1498c1ae4681}} with {{formula:30748718-bba3-43e3-b30f-a8a7ad6d671a}} the state (REF ) will be {{formula:df28c8a3-3c58-4d0b-8c65-c888422906cb}}provided that {{formula:cf39aee1-448f-4236-b00a-ce1ec0ae710e}} Using a chain of length {{formula:af02c146-5023-4594-ad37-7091c1d4d769}} with {{formula:2c188f88-a731-4442-8898-c177491dd266}} and {{formula:5f22317e-d787-4c20-8810-cc39049be11d}} , {{formula:6c13dc8b-6ebc-4f32-8f02-83896559878c}} we would have to fulfill {{formula:a3cb813b-6176-43c9-8096-b1e24b2c14ee}} . We could perform approximately 10 measurements (cf. Eq. (REF )) without deviating too much from the state (REF ). In this time, we can use our protocol in the normal way. The resulting success probability given by the finite version of Eq. (REF ) would be 75%. A similar reasoning is valid for phase noise, where the environment can be split into common and seperate parts. If the chains are close, the common part will dominate and the seperate parts can be neglected for short times.Finally, let us mention another advantage of our scheme. In single chain schemes, Bob has to extract the state precisely at an optimal time to obtain it with high fidelity. Our scheme is robust to the errors in this. Even if Bob measures to extract his state at an incorrect (non-optimal) time, he will receive the perfect state conditional on his measurement outcome. If he is unsuccessful, he simply tries again, without having Alice to resend. Also, due to the conclusive nature of the protocol, once Bob has received the state, the rest of the channel is automatically in the ground state and does not need to be reset for the next transfer (as opposed to many of the existing schemes , , , ).
Conclusions: In conclusion, we have presented a simple and efficient scheme for conclusive and arbitrarily perfect quantum state transfer. To achieve this, two parallel spin chains (individually amplitude damping channels) have been used as one amplitude delaying channel. We have shown that our scheme is more robust to decoherence and imperfect timing than the single chain schemes. Even though the encoding is simple, it has made spin-chain based communications both realistic and perfect at the same time.Our strategy can be generalized to graphs interconnecting many different users, and to many other systems. As an example, we will now briefly mention how our scheme can be adapted to a single chain of qutrits. The correct generalization of the exchange interaction for a chain of 3-level quantum system is a SU(3) chain . For example, a chain of atoms with three internal levels, {{formula:e3f2a057-166e-4852-b738-cd70b7339708}} , {{formula:63a0c093-5065-47ec-97b0-18811c16aed6}} and {{formula:9277df60-6ba3-495a-8ecf-7d0c33f5e92b}} in an optical lattice, where the atoms can hop from site to site but more than one atom cannot occupy a single site, will form a SU(3) chain. If we relabel our parallel spin chain states {{formula:7707081a-69b9-4594-b216-b7d21cf3cb37}} by {{formula:2c853e17-2c7c-4029-85f7-a5790fe67a86}} , {{formula:72377a43-fe2c-4d0d-9572-b4b0cf6fa4c8}} by {{formula:4f0c6a72-6aa2-4dbc-8985-ccad3e6f6722}} and {{formula:61bbaf52-0821-443d-893f-7067b05445da}} by {{formula:354c04bc-d974-4740-8ad5-178d62cfb730}} , then our protocol can be mapped to a single chain of qutrits interacting via SU(3) exchange. Though the state is no longer encoded in a decoherence free subspace as before, in an optical lattice implementation, one can use three hyperfine ground states of atoms as {{formula:7eddcd02-b9c9-460e-a0af-6c70d46c77b7}} , {{formula:fa84d5c3-2046-40ad-9638-09ae972ec4f4}} and {{formula:cdaa2736-baba-4390-b8e4-bc8bde99fa81}} to completely avoid amplitude damping.This work was supported by the UK Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council grant Nr. S627961/01 and the QIPIRC.

question: How is the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) employed within a hybrid quantum-classical approach to address the unit commitment problem in power systems, and what results are obtained from simulations?
answerWithPaperReferences: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a variational quantum algorithm that alternates between a cost Hamiltonian and a mixing Hamiltonian to approximate solutions to combinatorial optimization problems [Paper A]. In the hybrid quantum-classical unit commitment algorithm, the QUBO subproblem, which arises from the unit commitment formulation, is solved using QAOA [Paper B]. The hybrid algorithm coordinates the QUBO subproblem with two other subproblems via a three-block alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). Simulation results on a ten-generating-unit system demonstrate that the hybrid algorithm achieves the same optimal commitment as a classical solver, validating the approach [Paper B].
answerWithoutPaperReferences: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a variational quantum algorithm that uses a parameterized quantum circuit to approximate the optimum of a combinatorial optimization problem. In the hybrid quantum-classical approach for the unit commitment problem, the QUBO subproblem is solved using QAOA, while the other subproblems are handled classically. The algorithm coordinates these subproblems using a three-block ADMM. Simulations on a ten-unit power system show that the hybrid algorithm can find the same optimal commitment schedule as a classical solver, confirming its effectiveness.
isNotSingleHop: The question is not single hop because it requires two distinct pieces of information: first, understanding what QAOA is and how it works (from the original QAOA paper), and second, knowing how it is specifically applied to solve the QUBO subproblem in the hybrid unit commitment algorithm (from the hybrid algorithm paper). Without the first step, one cannot comprehend the role of QAOA in the second step, and vice versa.
bridgeEvidencePaperText:
A Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
abstract: We introduce a quantum algorithm that produces approximate solutions for combinatorial optimization problems. The algorithm depends on a positive integer p and the quality of the approximation improves as p is increased. The quantum circuit that implements the algorithm consists of unitary gates whose locality is at most the locality of the objective function whose optimum is sought. The depth of the circuit grows linearly with p times (at worst) the number of constraints. If p is fixed, that is, independent of the input size, the algorithm makes use of efficient classical preprocessing. If p grows with the input size a different strategy is proposed. We study the algorithm as applied to MaxCut on regular graphs and analyze its performance on 2-regular and 3-regular graphs for fixed p. For p = 1, on 3-regular graphs the quantum algorithm always finds a cut that is at least 0.6924 times the size of the optimal cut.
introduction: Combinatorial optimization problems are specified by {{formula:f65499ef-67dc-48bd-a529-cbd253131543}} bits and {{formula:eb212d78-7b77-4dfe-bad1-5f6cbb9587e0}} clauses. Each clause is a constraint on a subset of the bits which is satisfied for certain assignments of those bits and unsatisfied for the other assignments. The objective function, defined on {{formula:2dafb493-1597-4283-9010-6489a14f9525}} bit strings, is the number of satisfied clauses, {{formula:363040cd-aa62-41ab-9036-6702d40f02f9}}where {{formula:404c6ac0-b538-4357-be55-5c9ebdf5f7a4}} is the bit string and {{formula:50f3b5a5-7bfa-47d0-bba3-f34a2948aa7f}} if {{formula:ccad66c2-9630-40c6-a324-ae512ee08bf1}} satisfies clause {{formula:3c2f38ac-6d0c-41d8-80ad-b763ed11dc63}} and 0 otherwise. Typically {{formula:acebe051-3f0e-4d2b-95f5-68239e7a2ed1}} depends on only a few of the {{formula:55d5e6ba-773f-4c1e-a6cd-4268bdfbdb26}} bits. Satisfiability asks if there is a string that satisfies every clause. MaxSat asks for a string that maximizes the objective function. Approximate optimization asks for a string {{formula:febce11b-1d4e-4c93-ac87-95ce62fae5c1}} for which {{formula:dd7b89f5-40ee-4f98-a49b-4b44bb53e17b}} is close to the maximum of {{formula:bbb29cdd-eca2-4219-9ffb-cfd697d0ebe8}} . In this paper we present a general quantum algorithm for approximate optimization. We study its performance in special cases of MaxCut and also propose an alternate form of the algorithm geared toward finding a large independent set of vertices of a graph.The quantum computer works in a {{formula:107e8263-a75f-4036-82b9-2e003246ad09}} dimensional Hilbert space with computational basis vectors {{formula:d8671ba9-3fa0-4939-851a-9cd1d8feba06}} , and we view (REF ) as an operator which is diagonal in the computational basis. Relation to the Quantum Adiabatic Algorithm: We are focused on finding a good approximate solution to an optimization problem whereas the Quantum Adiabatic Algorithm, QAA , is designed to find the optimal solution and will do so if the run time is long enough. Consider the time dependent Hamiltonian {{formula:a47f5ee8-db89-4fb7-9e19-53c5fbbf237f}} . Note that the state {{formula:a657d1e0-1473-44ae-b8db-2eb980f221e8}} is the highest energy eigenstate of {{formula:e942c844-9f6d-42ca-8199-89c25a6c8ecd}} and we are seeking a high energy eigenstate of {{formula:41e2b7a9-c670-41e8-8434-50cfaf30f780}} . Starting in {{formula:7e05fe6e-6049-48f0-a0f7-e5b9e1dda8e9}} we could run the quantum adiabatic algorithm and if the run time {{formula:b2aec8f6-bcd6-4124-ac9b-00e8ec41e01c}} were long enough we would find the highest energy eigenstate of {{formula:b32aa6a1-c73f-4c83-8e7a-40b6f724bca6}} . Because {{formula:6abe780b-6ada-4e71-8057-6ad1b73b08e8}} has only non-negative off-diagonal elements, the Perron-Frobenius theorem implies that the difference in energies between the top state and the one below is greater than 0 for all {{formula:9de4c4a6-2bf8-4d9b-a377-e52f6104cfe9}} , so for sufficiently large {{formula:a1b3662b-eb8d-4432-914e-618d52f0b142}} success is assured. For a given {{formula:3616591a-e303-4900-9522-69960c9ba313}} and a given {{formula:334ece8b-9396-4141-bf73-af47b352ed40}} produce the quantum state {{formula:6a9ecf02-ef6d-4186-9825-3395e9b8a1a8}} of (REF ). We view this as a continuous time quantum walk entering the big graph at a particular vertex . In the extreme case where the input graph has no edges, all strings of length {{formula:5aca06ef-ccd3-478e-9a89-b262d037225e}} represent independent sets so the Hilbert space dimension is {{formula:b1b59286-46d8-4515-a7ad-5a71158c020f}} . In the more general case we can view (REF ) as a succession of quantum walks punctuated by applications of {{formula:76d11090-9b6d-4932-b754-77195ce82b29}} dependent unitaries which aid the walk in achieving its objective. The algorithm of the previous sections can also be viewed this way although the starting state is not a single vertex.
Conclusion: We introduced a quantum algorithm for approximate combinatorial optimization that depends on an integer parameter {{formula:9f20f1e0-3459-4bdd-8f0b-c478383baed9}} . The input is an {{formula:13043fd3-6b40-4463-9000-cd4c6d7c8a98}} bit instance with an objective function {{formula:c993d452-2863-4454-9edc-96e2c40ef5e0}} that is the sum of {{formula:ef99d980-922f-4461-ab33-d36abb5ce7a2}} local terms. The goal is to find a string {{formula:129e7179-dd5a-4210-a524-359905c2263b}} for which {{formula:6504a962-0cd7-4eea-b22f-662e407ae633}} is close to {{formula:91599552-27e6-4306-95ae-c7d67c3cdfca}} 's global maximum. In the basic algorithm, each call to the quantum computer uses a set of {{formula:34e9016e-3936-4c94-a43e-8431e73cd026}} angles {{formula:de982abc-39f4-49e5-8ca8-5e7460d9d12a}} and produces the state {{formula:b0d6ecf4-b0bb-47b9-9257-f90c6092fbeb}}This is followed by a measurement in the computational basis yielding a string {{formula:f0887e2e-16e0-4d6e-87cb-7238820fc623}} with an associated value {{formula:b1b358ba-2da2-4217-a99e-fcc0905e935f}} . Repeated calls to the quantum computer will yield a good estimate of {{formula:29e383bf-635d-4259-b430-74155939844c}}Running the algorithm requires a strategy for a picking a sequence of sets of angles with the goal of making {{formula:c03f68cb-01fc-4a7e-b07c-473ec68c8e38}} as big as possible. We give several possible strategies for finding a good set of angles.In section II we focused on fixed {{formula:e5d7ffb4-cc43-42f8-b6ab-3467f5837525}} and the case where each bit is in no more than a fixed number of clauses. In this case there is an efficient classical algorithm that determines the best set of angles which is then fed to the quantum computer. Here the quantum computer is run with only the best set of angles. Note that the “efficient" classical algorithm which evaluates (REF ) using (REF ) could require space doubly exponential in {{formula:41c03d1a-6abb-4c6b-98e5-2c901f0b562f}} .An alternative to using a classical preprocessor to find the best angles is to make repeated calls to the quantum computer with different sets of angles. One strategy, when {{formula:6c7c2ac3-6402-41b8-960f-b2d97d8d619a}} does not grow with {{formula:3f8c4bad-9c10-4485-8891-a4c1e356758a}} is to put a fine grid on the compact set {{formula:103bee55-c84d-40e9-9e34-af6ea879e68f}} where the number of points is only polynomial in {{formula:c85c852e-4fae-45af-a1c2-d516daad4f32}} and {{formula:cce85dd1-20ee-459c-943d-6290dabb614f}} . This works because the function {{formula:b89b98cd-b40d-4aaf-8ef5-ebb33e38dc8f}} does not have peaks that are so narrow that they are not seen by the grid.The QAOA can be run on a quantum computer with {{formula:894b57de-64f4-4d57-8254-c9b852865e62}} growing with {{formula:bab152cc-5a42-49ce-a355-b2d879901bac}} as long as there is a strategy for choosing sets of angles. Perhaps for some combinatorial optimization problem, good angles can be discovered in advance. Or the quantum computer can be called to evaluate {{formula:4509c3c5-3796-4d47-acbb-127a0f549c8d}} , the expectation of {{formula:15a342a0-a4dd-4ade-b9aa-f8f31688688c}} in the state {{formula:b19f1f71-5c9b-4564-8792-f84165420df5}} . This call can be used as a subroutine by a classical algorithm that seeks the maximum of the smooth function {{formula:ae35cbea-2d20-4d48-87e1-5c132a62f391}} . We hope that either {{formula:3ee151e3-76d5-4e30-87dd-00f874e206e9}} fixed or growing slowly with {{formula:3b69c3ea-44f3-4696-b07a-e97a2059f656}} will be enough to have this quantum algorithm be of use in finding solutions to combinatorial search problems beyond what classical algorithms can achieve.

Hybrid Quantum-Classical Unit Commitment
abstract: This paper proposes a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm to solve a fundamental power system problem called unit commitment (UC). The UC problem is decomposed into a quadratic subproblem, a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) subproblem, and an unconstrained quadratic subproblem. A classical optimization solver solves the first and third subproblems, while the QUBO subproblem is solved by a quantum algorithm called quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA). The three subproblems are then coordinated iteratively using a three-block alternating direction method of multipliers algorithm. Using Qiskit on the IBM Q system as the simulation environment, simulation results demonstrate the validity of the proposed algorithm to solve the UC problem.
Introduction: Computing plays a pivotal role in power system modeling and analysis. As the mathematical challenges of real-world problems increase, progress in advanced computing technologies becomes more crucial . Though still in the early stages, algorithms performed on quantum computers promise to complete important computing tasks faster than they could ever be done on traditional computers . Despite substantial studies on quantum computing applications in a wide range of areas, its application to power systems has largely remained intact. This paper aims to perform a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm to solve the unit commitment (UC) problem, a computationally expensive problem for conventional computers.UC is a fundamental optimization problem in power systems operation. It aims to determine the commitment of generating units to supply the demand and meet technical constraints in a cost-effective manner. The UC problem is generally cast as a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP), which is expensive to solve using classical solvers. Solving advanced UC problems efficiently in a reasonable amount of time is of paramount importance . The computational burden exponentially increases as the number of generating units increases. Thus, developing effective approaches to handle the UC problem becomes crucial.There are a variety of solvers to solve or approximate mixed-binary optimization problems with classical or heuristic approaches. DIscrete and Continuous OPTimizer (DICOPT) is a program that solves MINLP problems by solving a series of nonlinear programming and mixed-integer programming (MIP) problems . BARON is a popular option for solving MINLP problems . This solver relies on solving a series of convex underestimating subproblems arising from the evolutionary subsection of the search area. IBM’s CPLEX is a famous mathematical solver that works based on branch-and-cut to find exact or approximate MIP solutions .Solving optimization problems using quantum computers is mainly restricted to quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problems . A few algorithms, such as quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) and variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) , are available to solve QUBOs. Given the mixed-integer nature of many practical optimization problems, we need to extend the quantum optimization techniques to cope with MINLP problems on current quantum devices. In this regard, to solve the UC problem, the authors in have proposed two modifications to enable using quantum algorithms:Adding slack variables to convert inequality constraints into soft equality constraints Discretizing continuous variables to h partitions to have pure binary variablesThe main drawback is that for solving a UC problem with N units, N(h+1) qubits are required, which is not practical.In this paper, a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm is proposed to solve the UC problems. We first decompose UC into three subproblems, namely a quadratic subproblem, a QUBO, and a quadratic unconstrained subproblem. The QUBO subproblem is solved using a quantum QAOA algorithm, and the other two subproblems are handled by a classical solver. We then use a variant of alternating direction method of multiplier (ADMM) to coordinate the QUBO and non-QUBOs (referring to quadratic and quadratic unconstrained subproblems) iteratively. Although the standard ADMM was originally developed for solving convex problems, recent studies , , have developed heuristic ADMMs that can be applied to a variety of nonconvex problems. We have used one of these variants, namely a three-block ADMM. Simulations are carried out using Qiskit on the IBM Q system, and the validity of the proposed algorithm is studied.
Unit Commitment: The UC formulation is a large-scale mixed-integer problem. Solving UC is computationally expensive because of generating unit nonlinear cost functions and the combinatorial nature of its set of feasible solutions. The UC solution determines the combination of units’ on/off status to meet the load at a time. UC a single time period is formulated as: {{formula:f5d4f65b-fe93-4af1-931d-b5ef48c6bfa5}}s.t. {{formula:a6ad1c29-f2c7-4b27-840a-6a73269fffe3}} {{formula:fcbf9fdc-2590-4654-8116-9108312b50b8}} {{formula:8c483d76-5e3a-4abd-b937-a7930482787d}}where {{formula:822e008e-d8e4-48f4-a91a-f7597c481553}} , {{formula:4edad9db-eb02-4a52-9d34-4a5eeebbdf6f}} , and {{formula:aefac3de-1a22-4766-8764-0de253f7bdf6}} are the fixed cost coefficients of unit {{formula:b4e7395b-3939-4284-ae33-6c11afacde72}} . {{formula:0b92eddb-130f-47c6-80ef-98da0b3779fd}} is a binary variable which is 1 if unit {{formula:03ddfac8-5ed6-4120-b7ad-bd91eca9e3f5}} is on and 0 otherwise. {{formula:97e8744b-907e-48b5-970c-b2b4f513771a}} is the power generated by unit {{formula:43362171-0b59-445f-b528-5c6a6d7a9793}} . However, this algorithm is guaranteed to converge under some restricting condition for large enough {{formula:c015526f-2036-44e0-903c-13ebfed51012}} .The assumptions under which Algorithm 1 converges to a stationary point of the augmented Lagrangian {{formula:a9356cd7-3b9f-4504-b256-0ee566e94813}} , are:(Feasibility). For two consecutive iterations and a constant {{formula:c31a1ef1-63c0-4bbc-bf39-c34081efd568}} , it is possible to have the condition {{formula:d8a589db-f9ff-4c82-adc8-a17d411c8c35}} for variable {{formula:22bfbd2e-4654-4c8c-bc03-811e0151f99f}} . This condition holds with a constant {{formula:526d46b3-9370-420e-b079-c2efbf171605}} . Note that this condition is true for variables {{formula:cdde9a37-6ab4-4213-940a-0877ebe9d2cb}} and {{formula:494ed52a-ca06-49b6-af8f-023506d67a58}} as well. (Objective regularity). This condition holds since objective (2a) is a convex function, and the set of constraints (1b)-(1c) and (2b) is convex .Moreover, if {{formula:28cb6f31-8a2a-48b8-936d-3249a6cb02d8}} is a Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz (KŁ) function, , it would converge globally. Therefore, Algorithm 1 converges to a stationary point of {{formula:30c27a81-2bd5-4e1e-9f36-61ca96564e71}} function with starting from any point and any large enough {{formula:07eb2e3d-f8b4-49a5-8052-9847d04e8d2d}} . 3B-ADMM algorithm [1] Initialize: {{formula:8963504b-0638-43f3-98fe-4ff7d3a34c85}} , {{formula:6ea664ca-afe6-48ca-a05b-e2bb3e16a11a}} , {{formula:d2ff8b91-4491-4305-91a9-2baa2ba915a1}} , {{formula:806bcd88-e694-4866-923e-294576c2bdad}} . {{formula:82af42cf-fd91-4934-b8e1-f116131916f7}} First block update:{{formula:ce623d6f-0fb3-4ae9-9408-d1f451386078}} s.t (1b)-(1c) and (2b). Return {{formula:ed38c744-c365-4858-bf60-30d33dcf0270}} .By fixing the variables {{formula:0160d791-b174-4e11-b489-4a8b0b35fb86}} , we will have a two-block ADMM and skip the third block update. However, having auxiliary variables {{formula:fc1f3811-a6d1-4d28-b13c-53f2abcc9ec3}} has two main advantages. Quantum Approximation Optimization Algorithm: While the two non-QUBO subproblems can be solved using a classical computing solver, the QUBO is solved using QAOA, which is a quantum computing-based algorithm. QAOA intends to approximate QUBO problems, which is a kind of combinatorial optimization problem. Combinatorial optimization is the process of searching for minima (or maxima) of an objective function whose domain is a discrete but large configuration space. Here, we want to minimize QUBO function {{formula:e28b4e00-795f-4dce-818f-6df0d8441788}} , where {{formula:2caaba72-c64b-4f42-b2bd-ee6aacbeb8b0}} denotes the set of variables {{formula:8262cdd6-416f-490c-8dd6-5f37d1cf1bb2}} . {{formula:fef8c177-a7bd-4c57-a115-0f33801921b8}} values can be {{formula:2809d540-2d93-4586-a6b4-707e56630f59}} or {{formula:187861f9-c8fc-4e43-a7c7-e782c75947e5}} . Therefore, to meet the standard form of QAOA, we have to convert our binary variables {{formula:b96a80ca-483b-4b3d-bbb0-d8a2e9f5f819}} as follows to take {{formula:8ff915c2-8b40-4083-b451-d4ed6bffbcb0}} : {{formula:0fc83566-9f0a-4d78-9ff4-001321045cf7}}QAOA acts on {{formula:fe10f8af-3fd7-4ee4-bd73-973b92af7070}} quantum-bits (qubit), where each qubit represents the state of one of the binary variables. Initially, this algorithm begins with all of the qubits initialized at state {{formula:6f2d5c02-6e1c-4f0f-b2f7-0da2b45a55c6}} . The next step is to put all qubits into an equal superposition by applying {{formula:ac09e3a2-0ea6-4cbb-a1ee-0f49705498e0}} , the Hadamard operator on each qubit. In the following, we aim to alter the amplitudes so that those with small {{formula:1b20b968-50e6-4071-8300-9d1f9d6a21fe}} coefficients will grow and those with large {{formula:bb0ade41-1458-42d4-af1b-446f8a91a97e}} coefficients will decrease. Thus, there will be a greater chance of finding a bitstring with a small value of {{formula:e8433135-dde7-4957-bd3b-d6cc8171213e}} when we measure the qubits. To this end, first, we apply the unitary operator, so-called cost Hamiltonian, {{formula:77ab5e50-2b5a-485c-95bb-c4943ca6a15e}} . {{formula:c166a111-0448-4897-9632-deec70ab6161}} is a variational parameter that we adjust its value to achieve the best possible results. {{formula:ca248b50-6951-4a36-b073-2b1843d687a8}} is a diagonal matrix in the computational basis that its elements correspond to all the possible values for the second block objective function. {{formula:18cc243e-1aea-4221-a1b9-09ae94495328}} consists of the Pauli-{{formula:f9d2cd70-a37c-4608-a6f2-6cd55c9cfcb9}} operator on each qubit based on the argument {{formula:627fd798-ecd7-43c2-a012-fb602ac61d91}} .So far, the result of this algorithm is a summation of all possible bitstrings, with complex coefficients that depend on {{formula:0e4db4ba-31ef-4490-85d2-b38115fce33e}} . Also, the probability of all bitstring is equal at this stage. Then we apply the second unitary operator, so-called mixing Hamiltonian, {{formula:5f6c8627-ffe3-4f31-86c7-d90dfd426a4e}} , where {{formula:384dff16-e4fc-4cfa-bdce-a155c81ddad3}} is a variational parameter, {{formula:f28c5e67-0506-49b2-ac9b-49c546e14020}} , and {{formula:ba8db10f-7295-4832-aa4e-360be5766cd1}} is Pauli-{{formula:6dae1c25-342d-487c-8a0a-b66710ea237f}} operator. This operator rotates each qubit {{formula:8e1d2c4f-591a-4f15-aec0-35352c59eb8c}} degree around the X-axis on the Bloch sphere. Unlike the previous operator, this is not a diagonal operator on the computational basis, and the probability of final states will not be the same for all bitstrings. This algorithm consists of repeating the first two steps {{formula:ebc77f04-5433-4808-b343-3b7c2fec0148}} times, where {{formula:4b73d461-919e-47f8-919a-a85a6ed83f56}} is the depth of the circuit regardless of how many qubits there are. Conclusion: An algorithm is proposed to solve the UC problem using a combination of quantum and classical computers. A reformulation strategy is presented to decompose the problem into a QUBO and two non-QUBO subproblems. The non-QUBO subproblems are solved on classical computers, while the QUBO subproblem is solved using QAOA, which is a quantum computing algorithm. To obtain the optimal solution for the whole UC problem, the solution of subproblems are coordinated iteratively using a three-block ADMM. An updating strategy for QAOA variational parameters is applied to make this algorithm achieve the best possible results.Simulation studies on a classical computer show the performance of the decomposition algorithm such that the results of the problem for different load levels match the results of a centralized classical solver. Moreover, when we solve the problem using the hybrid quantum-classical algorithm, we obtain the same results as those found by solving all subproblems in a classical computer.

abstract: The classical motion of spinning particles can be described without employing Grassmann variables or Clifford algebras, but simply by generalizing the usual spinless theory. We only assume the invariance with respect to the Poincare' group; and only requiring the conservation of the linear and angular momenta we derive the zitterbewegung: namely the decomposition of the 4-velocity in the newtonian constant term p/m and in a non-newtonian time-oscillating spacelike term. Consequently, free classical particles do not obey, in general, the Principle of Inertia. Superluminal motions are also allowed, without violating Special Relativity, provided that the energy-momentum moves along the worldline of the center-of-mass. Moreover, a non-linear, non-constant relation holds between the time durations measured in different reference frames. Newtonian Mechanics is re-obtained as a particular case of the present theory: namely for spinless systems with no zitterbewegung. Introducing a Lagrangian containing also derivatives of the 4-velocity we get a new equation of the motion, actually a generalization of the Newton Law a=F/m. Requiring the rotational symmetry and the reparametrization invariance we derive the classical spin vector and the conserved scalar Hamiltonian, respectively. We derive also the classical Dirac spin and analyze the general solution of the Eulero-Lagrange equation for Dirac particles. The interesting case of spinning systems with zero intrinsic angular momentum is also studied.
Introduction: The theory we are going to put forward concerns classical systems (CS's) in the most general meaning of the word, namely non-quantum systems. As special relativity allows, a CS can own “internal” degrees of freedom and a spin angular momentum. The set of CS's contains as a special subset, the one of spinless systems, that we shall call also newtonian systems (NS's), such as, e.g., macroscopic bodies studied in newtonian classical mechanics. Since the works by Compton , Uhlenbeck and Goudsmith , and Frenkel , many classical theories of spinning particles have been investigated for about eighty years . Grassmann variables in classical actions for spinning systems has been employed by Berezin and Marinov , Ikemori and Casalbuoni . In the last twenty years a renewed interest has arisen towards classical theoretical approaches to microsystems, especially in applications to (super)strings and membranes, in view of a possible unification of the elementary forces of Nature. In this section we shall obtain important properties, constraints and equations which rule the kinematics of free classical particles endowed with spin, without any recourse to ad-hoc theories or additional assumptions besides the requirements of the usual spacetime symmetries, and without any recourse to the non-commuting numbers of the Grassmann algebra or to the multivectors of the Clifford “Spacetime” algebra .In the absence of external fields the spacetime isotropy implies the conservation of the total angular momentum: {{formula:07eae9d0-1ab7-445a-aa77-88a332606652}}tensor {{formula:fe20914f-dc47-4937-ac4f-41f3b326e751}} being the orbital angular momentum, and tensor {{formula:9ca826a1-0b2e-4c87-a39a-6d6af6b8f470}} the spin angular momentum. Correspondences between the classical velocity and the quantum
probability current: The most impressive correspondence between the present classical theory and the standard wave-mechanics may be found in the celebrated Gordon decomposition of the conserved current of the Dirac equation , which writes (hereafter we assume {{formula:1e2b3acb-dcea-4ccd-9555-7b19d474270b}} ): {{formula:101083b9-4a0c-4242-8eeb-49d075bfb10e}}where {{formula:953cfec3-1968-47be-9551-a271180db2ff}} is the usual hermitian-adjoint bispinor, {{formula:fe37bc19-d3fb-43d5-b29f-33f794874a32}} is the 4-dimensional momentum operator, and {{formula:515de3e1-8935-4c1d-b7d3-76562b664452}} represents the spin-tensor operator. In fact, the standard interpretation of the above decomposition quite agrees with our zitterbewegung equation (REF ). The first term in the r.h.s. is associated with the translational motion of the CM (the scalar part of the current, corresponding to the Klein–Gordon current). As a matter of fact, for a momentum eigenstate, i.e. for a plane-wave, this term turns out to be proportional to {{formula:463e2d01-b2f2-4ad8-96bc-68b38905a1e7}} . By contrast, the non-newtonian term in the r.h.s. is related to the existence of the spin, and describes the zitterbewegung rotational motion. The correspondences and analogies between classical and quantum laws do not concern only the probability current, but concern also the operators of the basic kinematic quantities. In Dirac theory, indeed, both the 4-velocity operator {{formula:7b763505-b2f0-4e89-913c-a1853d0571b7}} and the 3-velocity operator {{formula:d40e93ef-b9fa-47b9-ad3c-99d1f94f1d98}} do not commute with the Dirac Hamiltonian {{formula:480bc599-2fba-49d1-b6a5-9d08fcd425b9}} . Therefore, such as it happens for CS's, also in quantum mechanics those quantities, differently from the momentum, are not time-constant. Let us recall that the zitterbewegung actually occurs also for non-relativistic particles, in the framework of the Pauli and Schrödinger theories , , . In fact, following Landau , we can write a non-relativistic Gordon-like decomposition of the conserved Pauli current {{formula:4cd3c4f0-c0b2-40a3-9510-4ab42296cf1e}}where {{formula:4f73d2b1-d01c-4b18-bd1d-5ecfa42783e4}} is a Pauli 2-components spinor and {{formula:869bba0c-0ada-4fdf-aa9b-95ab097558b0}} is the usual Pauli vector (2{{formula:090efc75-25d8-44dd-8c2e-fab48d6e4813}} 2) matrix. Also the above current appears as a sum of a newtonian part which, at the classical limit ({{formula:5f3d5667-cb73-4a5d-89fd-1842ac40b445}} ), is parallel to the classical momentum (equal to {{formula:b17a83f0-cf10-4983-bc76-893b4e17ba1c}} times the gradient of the action); and of a non-newtonian part due to the spin, which vanishes only at the classical limit, i.e. for spinless bodies, but not in the non-relativistic limit, i.e. for a small momentum {{formula:75cba6b7-27a0-4bf1-95e7-197d89f939c5}} .Analogous Gordon-like decompositions of the conserved 4-currents can be found also for spin-1 bosons and for spin-{{formula:e1339750-69a0-4fb9-b22d-059072de612c}} fermions in the Proca and Rarita-Schwinger theories, respectively.

Correspondences between the classical velocity and the quantum
probability current: The most impressive correspondence between the present classical theory and the standard wave-mechanics may be found in the celebrated Gordon decomposition of the conserved current of the Dirac equation , which writes (hereafter we assume {{formula:1e2b3acb-dcea-4ccd-9555-7b19d474270b}} ): {{formula:101083b9-4a0c-4242-8eeb-49d075bfb10e}}where {{formula:953cfec3-1968-47be-9551-a271180db2ff}} is the usual hermitian-adjoint bispinor, {{formula:fe37bc19-d3fb-43d5-b29f-33f794874a32}} is the 4-dimensional momentum operator, and {{formula:515de3e1-8935-4c1d-b7d3-76562b664452}} represents the spin-tensor operator. In fact, the standard interpretation of the above decomposition quite agrees with our zitterbewegung equation (REF ). The first term in the r.h.s. is associated with the translational motion of the CM (the scalar part of the current, corresponding to the Klein–Gordon current). As a matter of fact, for a momentum eigenstate, i.e. for a plane-wave, this term turns out to be proportional to {{formula:463e2d01-b2f2-4ad8-96bc-68b38905a1e7}} . By contrast, the non-newtonian term in the r.h.s. is related to the existence of the spin, and describes the zitterbewegung rotational motion. The correspondences and analogies between classical and quantum laws do not concern only the probability current, but concern also the operators of the basic kinematic quantities. In Dirac theory, indeed, both the 4-velocity operator {{formula:7b763505-b2f0-4e89-913c-a1853d0571b7}} and the 3-velocity operator {{formula:d40e93ef-b9fa-47b9-ad3c-99d1f94f1d98}} do not commute with the Dirac Hamiltonian {{formula:480bc599-2fba-49d1-b6a5-9d08fcd425b9}} . Therefore, such as it happens for CS's, also in quantum mechanics those quantities, differently from the momentum, are not time-constant. Let us recall that the zitterbewegung actually occurs also for non-relativistic particles, in the framework of the Pauli and Schrödinger theories , , . In fact, following Landau , we can write a non-relativistic Gordon-like decomposition of the conserved Pauli current {{formula:4cd3c4f0-c0b2-40a3-9510-4ab42296cf1e}}where {{formula:4f73d2b1-d01c-4b18-bd1d-5ecfa42783e4}} is a Pauli 2-components spinor and {{formula:869bba0c-0ada-4fdf-aa9b-95ab097558b0}} is the usual Pauli vector (2{{formula:090efc75-25d8-44dd-8c2e-fab48d6e4813}} 2) matrix. Also the above current appears as a sum of a newtonian part which, at the classical limit ({{formula:5f3d5667-cb73-4a5d-89fd-1842ac40b445}} ), is parallel to the classical momentum (equal to {{formula:b17a83f0-cf10-4983-bc76-893b4e17ba1c}} times the gradient of the action); and of a non-newtonian part due to the spin, which vanishes only at the classical limit, i.e. for spinless bodies, but not in the non-relativistic limit, i.e. for a small momentum {{formula:75cba6b7-27a0-4bf1-95e7-197d89f939c5}} .Analogous Gordon-like decompositions of the conserved 4-currents can be found also for spin-1 bosons and for spin-{{formula:e1339750-69a0-4fb9-b22d-059072de612c}} fermions in the Proca and Rarita-Schwinger theories, respectively.

They also show that the (1/2,1/2) representations can be divided into a triplet and a singlet of opposite relative intrinsic parities, but do not carry a definite spin angular momentum. As a consequence that solution just refers to a helicity-0 spinning particle.
Summary of the results: The theory outlined in this paper appears very general because it is not based on particular models or special approaches. The classical spin is studied simply by generalizing and extending (through the usual tensorial algebra) the newtonian theory, without any recourse to Grassmann variables or special Clifford algebras. The only necessary (for free classical systems) assumptions are spacetime isotropy and homogeneity. Thus, starting from the conservation of the linear and angular momenta, {{formula:3ede6bd1-46ff-456b-b9cf-74e6ddabc8ec}} , in the first section we have obtained a zitterbewegung equation, in which appear besides the timelike newtonian term {{formula:270cebb4-d0d3-478b-b836-763a02661d93}} also a spacelike zitterbewegung-term. Among the consequences of the zitterbewegung we have:a) even in the absence of forces, differently from the momentum, the velocity is not required to be a constant quantity: the Principle of Inertia is not a general law for the classical free motion; or equivalently, the RF is not an inertial reference frame;b) the square of the 4-velocity {{formula:5f3fdf7b-0435-4aac-adc2-cb2878e09abd}} obeys non-ordinary constraints;c) “global” superluminal motions are not forbidden, provided that the energy-momentum, and any related signal or information, move along the worldline of the CM, which travels always with a subluminal speed;d) in general, the zitterbewegung motion of a CS has a component along the momentum;e) the ratio between the time durations measured in a generic frame and in the CMF is not constant and differs from the Lorentz factor (as instead occurs for NS's). In general we can say that a non-linear relation occurs between the time durations measured in different reference frames.Newtonian mechanics and usual relativistic kinematics are of course recovered as a particular case of the present theory: namely the spinless case with no zitterbewegung. We have also analyzed the strict analogy holding between the classical zitterbewegung equation and the quantum Gordon decomposition of the Dirac current.In the second section we have performed the lagrangian formulation of our theory through a direct generalization (satisfying the relativistic covariance and the symmetry under spacetime inversions) of the newtonian Lagrangian to Lagrangians containing time derivatives of the velocity. The results are obtained without any particular choose of the coefficients appearing in the theory and without any ad-hoc assumption. We have derived a constant-coefficients differential equation of the motion (generalization of the Newton law {{formula:7b374d50-0faa-4ce8-ac87-6fcdd0cdcdc7}} ) in which non-newtonian zitterbewegung terms appear. Alternate signs are requested for the coefficients of the terms appearing in the Lagrangian if we want only stationary solutions and finite oscillatory motions. Through the Nöther theorem, by satisfying the rotational symmetry, the classical spin can be defined employing only classical kinematical quantities, without recourse to quantum quantities as the Planck constant {{formula:7a97fa6c-8af6-4f63-92af-e007a9e6f1dd}} , or to Grassmann non-commuting numbers. Imposing the reparametrization invariance the conserved Hamiltonian is also obtained. For the important case of the first-order Lagrangian it can be written a second couple of Hamilton equations for the canonically conjugate variables {{formula:d5fc4822-06dd-479e-9e37-c5ff82ac4d06}} and {{formula:cee555cf-e827-4412-b742-ad4ef0a35985}} , in addition to the usual couple of Hamilton equations referring to the canonical variables {{formula:bba6f01c-4dd9-4320-a25e-f7dd801e480d}} and {{formula:cc78a1a1-e14e-4f3f-a18d-d114baed970b}} .In the third section we have shown that the first-order Lagrangian with {{formula:887a6d9f-7553-49bc-9f8d-6eb9016e1e82}} fully describes classical Dirac particles and derived the classical Dirac spin in the form {{formula:7664ea89-6f08-4a76-a952-87cd2d1c7b11}} . The general solution of the Eulero-Lagrange equation oscillates with the Compton frequency {{formula:717a9995-1d41-4480-a99b-8fab09b7b9b5}} , and the spacetime worldline is a 4-dimensional helix. The particular solutions corresponding to polarized Dirac particles and to constant {{formula:bbad47a2-bf76-4fde-bc4a-1a4ed9e9a266}} have been in detail studied. Finally, we have derived the explicit form of the Pauli-Lubanski 4-vector for classical Dirac particles.In the last section we have studied spinning CS's with zero intrinsic angular momentum and helicity, ispecially in the case of first-order Lagrangians. An interesting quantum analogue has been recently found in a (1/2,1/2) vector representation of the Lorentz group, shown to be a superposition of spin-0 and spin-1 states, with {{formula:d30ffef3-6316-4b1f-9f25-1e8c5358d2af}} only in the CMF.AcknowledgementsThe author is glad to thank E. Recami and the Referee for helpful hints and for having suggested some bibliography. The scientific collaboration of S. Esposito and D. Zappalà is also acknowledged. reasoning.step1: Paper 1704.00029 resolves Wright's conjecture by proving that for all parameter values alpha in (0, pi/2], the zero solution of Wright's equation is globally attractive (Theorem 1.5). It further establishes the equivalence that the zero solution is globally attracting if and only if no slowly oscillating periodic solution (SOPS) exists (Theorem 1.4). Consequently, this paper rigorously demonstrates that there are no SOPS for alpha <= pi/2.
reasoning.step2: Paper 1801.09806 resolves Jones' conjecture for the parameter interval (pi/2, 1.9] by proving that there exists a unique slowly oscillating periodic solution (up to time translation) for every alpha in this range (Theorem 1.1). This provides the existence and uniqueness result immediately above the Hopf bifurcation threshold.
reasoning.connectionExplanation: The final answer requires combining both papers because a complete characterization of slowly oscillating periodic solutions across the full interval (0, 1.9] necessitates knowing both the non-existence below the Hopf bifurcation and the uniqueness above it. Step 2 alone only covers (pi/2, 1.9] and does not rule out the possibility of SOPS for alpha <= pi/2; Step 1 alone only rules out SOPS below the bifurcation but says nothing about existence or uniqueness above it. The Hopf bifurcation at alpha = pi/2 serves as the precise boundary linking the two regimes, and the question is only answerable by synthesizing both results.

question: For Wright's equation with parameter alpha in (0, 1.9], how does the global attractivity of the zero solution for alpha at most pi/2 combine with the uniqueness result for slowly oscillating periodic solutions above pi/2 to characterize the dynamics across the entire interval?
answerWithPaperReferences: For Wright's equation with parameter alpha in (0, 1.9], the dynamics are fully characterized by the Hopf bifurcation at alpha = pi/2. [Paper 1704.00029] proves that for all alpha in (0, pi/2], the zero solution is globally attractive (Theorem 1.5), and establishes that global attractivity of the zero solution is equivalent to the non-existence of slowly oscillating periodic solutions (Theorem 1.4). Thus, no slowly oscillating periodic solutions exist for alpha <= pi/2. [Paper 1801.09806] proves that for alpha in (pi/2, 1.9], there exists a unique slowly oscillating periodic solution up to time translation (Theorem 1.1). Taken together, these results show that across the entire interval (0, 1.9], slowly oscillating periodic solutions exist if and only if alpha > pi/2, and whenever they exist they are unique, making alpha = pi/2 the exact threshold separating the globally attracting zero regime from the regime with a unique periodic orbit.

isNotSingleHop: The question is not single-hop because it requires information from two distinct parameter regimes that are treated in separate papers. One paper establishes the non-existence of slowly oscillating periodic solutions for alpha <= pi/2 through global attractivity of the zero solution, while the other establishes existence and uniqueness for alpha in (pi/2, 1.9]. Neither paper alone covers the full interval (0, 1.9] or provides both the non-existence below the Hopf bifurcation and the uniqueness above it. Removing either paper would leave a gap in the characterization: without the first, one could not rule out slowly oscillating periodic solutions for alpha <= pi/2, and without the second, one could not confirm their existence and uniqueness for alpha > pi/2.
bridgeEvidencePaperText:
First 30099 characters: A proof of Wright's conjecture
abstract: Wright's conjecture states that the origin is the global attractor for the delay differential equation $y'(t) = - \alpha y(t-1) [ 1 + y(t) ] $ for all $\alpha \in (0,\tfrac{\pi}{2}]$. This has been proven to be true for a subset of parameter values $\alpha$. We extend the result to the full parameter range $\alpha \in (0,\tfrac{\pi}{2}]$, and thus prove Wright's conjecture to be true. Our approach relies on a careful investigation of the neighborhood of the Hopf bifurcation occurring at $\alpha =\tfrac{\pi}{2}$. This analysis fills the gap left by complementary work on Wright's conjecture, which covers parameter values further away from the bifurcation point. Furthermore, we show that the branch of (slowly oscillating) periodic orbits originating from this Hopf bifurcation does not have any subsequent bifurcations (and in particular no folds) for $\alpha\in(\tfrac{\pi}{2} , \tfrac{\pi}{2} + 6.830 \times 10^{-3}]$. When combined with other results, this proves that the branch of slowly oscillating solutions that originates from the Hopf bifurcation at $\alpha=\tfrac{\pi}{2}$ is globally parametrized by $\alpha > \tfrac{\pi}{2}$.
Introduction: In many biological and physical systems the dependency of future states relies not only on the present situation, but on a broader history of the system. For simplicity, mathematical models often ignore the causal influence of all but the present state. However, in a wide variety of applications delayed feedback loops play an inextricable role in the qualitative dynamics of a system . These phenomena can be modeled using delay and integro-differential equations, the theory of which has developed significantly over the past 60 years . A canonical and well-studied example of a nonlinear delay differential equation is Wright's equation: {{formula:47e0d6b7-d0ab-4508-9243-10cbb7ce5d88}}Here {{formula:19e74989-5af8-492d-8695-319e4b9de0da}} is considered to be both real and positive. This equation has been a central example considered in the development of much of the theory of functional differential equations. For a short overview of this equation, we refer the reader to . Wright's equation has two equilibria {{formula:152252a7-e75c-490b-ac21-89def6edf75b}} and {{formula:5fd5a8bf-0356-498d-96ce-49371bfed200}} . Moreover, solutions cannot cross {{formula:66c87684-2596-42ba-92be-70b5e7920b79}} . Any solution with {{formula:8ec73eba-f474-4c02-a536-a6f5edf49390}} (for some {{formula:84239604-8e22-4a0f-b27c-3030664b8dae}} ) is identically equal to {{formula:9cbb7ffc-054e-4917-a3ca-adaa0f02262f}} . When {{formula:f958bfb6-a1fe-4806-a029-47c6abb57be8}} then the solution decreases monotonically without bound. When {{formula:f151ccb9-63b8-4055-a188-83b0c875b448}} then {{formula:19094307-0749-4021-b270-c5dfa93ded43}} is globally bounded as {{formula:e2ff6792-464f-4778-b6c7-34ef24d80506}} .Henceforth we restrict our attention to {{formula:c09c1c6a-b835-455d-bd28-dd6d2104f57b}} . In Wright’s seminal 1955 paper , he showed that if {{formula:6a609362-41e2-483b-895f-52e9dfae72cd}} then any solution having {{formula:443093d2-e08e-472e-b09c-2276bd5d534e}} is attracted to 0 as {{formula:df545092-9890-474c-ae51-9e90456edb5c}} . At {{formula:1531814c-88f5-4285-b9f5-7aae36597314}} , the equilibrium {{formula:9f53125b-24d1-4b7f-835e-aca497e05ba3}} changes from asymptotically stable to unstable, and Wright formulated the following conjecture:Conjecture 1.1 (Wright's Conjecture) For every {{formula:9560d1b4-9c66-4557-a3e1-d55f649da30a}} , the zero solution to (REF ) is globally attractive.For {{formula:82196a0c-d0ce-408b-8cd1-9fed8576aacb}} , Wright proved the existence of oscillatory solutions to (REF ) which do not tend towards 0, and whose zeros are spaced at distances greater than the delay. Such a periodic solution is said to be slowly oscillating, and formally defined as follows:Definition 1.2 A slowly oscillating periodic solution (SOPS) is a periodic solution {{formula:07d7c9b1-b733-476c-ab99-8fbe2658939f}} which up to a time translation satisfies the following property: there exists some {{formula:165cc999-bf2d-405d-a29c-99f77aa1f23e}} and {{formula:c21da523-36e7-44ab-a597-3422827f7973}} such that {{formula:bb0e796c-1a0b-494e-9e28-212d90095ee0}} for {{formula:cce4d5dd-6a1a-432b-87c5-24e36b57c4e5}} , {{formula:d726e09e-9f85-412b-adaa-6f6311776653}} for {{formula:3ff44d75-825f-4ac7-b1c8-de18e52be55f}} , and {{formula:dc49c9ab-61dd-493c-b21d-49bda42a57eb}} for all {{formula:47a44f0e-9c29-4661-853d-b9ecdf5532e4}} , so that {{formula:caae334a-6d4d-4371-afb0-792a2f15d900}} is the minimal period of {{formula:0ef4dde6-3d0e-48ad-a3d0-cd921977ce60}} .In Jones' 1962 paper he proved that for {{formula:1dd5186b-156a-4f5d-8a54-152ba2a1ea56}} there exists a slowly oscillating periodic solution to (REF ). Based on numerical calculations Jones made the following conjecture:Conjecture 1.3 (Jones' Conjecture) For every {{formula:bf84769f-ff08-45d4-86e9-dfc83be578cf}} there exists a unique slowly oscillating periodic solution to (REF ).Slowly oscillating periodic solutions play a critical role in the global dynamics of (REF ). The global attractor of (REF ) admits a Morse decomposition , and if there is a unique SOPS and {{formula:dc98414e-521d-47e2-a18e-17b2a6bd99b4}} then it must be asymptotically stable , . A corollary is the following theorem.Theorem 1.4 (Theorem 3.1 in ) The zero solution of (REF ) is globally attracting if and only if (REF ) has no slowly oscillating periodic solution.Despite a considerable amount of work studying Wright's equation, complete resolution of these conjectures has remained elusive (see the survey paper and the references contained therein). To describe a few results, the global bifurcation analysis in proved that for {{formula:3c778767-b814-46a8-b723-64adafd47f6d}} there is a continuum of pairs {{formula:f7e4020f-cb13-4c0d-9d60-374697447c9f}} where {{formula:54d588db-3484-4f88-8784-7b7726b0ebb8}} is a periodic solution to (REF ), and these pairs form a {{formula:33a0db0d-d108-4493-8372-e156801bb825}} dimensional manifold . In it was shown that Wright's equation has a supercritical Hopf bifurcation at {{formula:7794036f-d042-407d-9117-4aaa2df1d5bd}} . By studying the Floquet multipliers of periodic solutions for large {{formula:19d3c797-4872-4a5a-ac58-0c8cbe849e5a}} , Xie showed in that Conjecture 1.2 holds for {{formula:b97a4f12-8c8f-4233-99f3-0fdac34a1fc7}} .Recent results using computer assisted proofs have narrowed the gap to resolving both conjectures. In the work in preparation it is shown that Conjecture REF holds for {{formula:337e81d7-b882-4085-b7d8-09b9334adb4d}} . In , it is shown that the branch of periodic orbits emanating from the Hopf bifurcation does not have any subsequent bifurcations in the interval {{formula:3bb8c027-0405-422c-bd39-1577b697cb44}} where {{formula:a8ec7a1d-a545-4be0-826e-8b15f1ae999b}} . In it was shown that Conjecture REF holds for {{formula:38d74e23-e26b-49aa-8206-b652d36cb6bb}} where {{formula:fdc9c439-e3b8-4198-ae06-b8a306c82a18}} , and the authors remark that “substantial improvement of the theoretical part of the present proof is needed to prove Wright's conjecture fully.”Many normal form techniques for functional differential equations have been developed to transform a given equation into a simpler expression having the same qualitative behavior as the original equation (see and references contained therein). While this transformation is valid in some neighborhood about the bifurcation point, such results usually do not describe the size of this neighborhood explicitly. In this paper we develop an explicit description of a neighborhood wherein the only periodic solutions are those originating from the Hopf bifurcation. The main result of this analysis is the resolution of Wright's conjecture.Theorem 1.5 For every {{formula:2a24c6f4-9303-4922-a7f9-78ebb610f44f}} , the zero solution to (REF ) is globally attractive.This result follows from Theorem REF combined with Theorem REF . Then we show that throughout this entire neighborhood the solution branch behaves as expected from a supercritical bifurcation branch, i.e., it does not bend back into the parameter region {{formula:f32cf054-e591-4be1-a5c1-f4bbea796d95}} .Rather than trying to resolve all small bounded solutions near the bifurcation point through a center manifold analysis, we focus on periodic orbits only.
