bridgeEvidencePaperText:
Large-scale topological and dynamical properties of Internet
abstract: We study the large-scale topological and dynamical properties of real Internet maps at the autonomous system level, collected in a three years time interval. We find that the connectivity structure of the Internet presents average quantities and statistical distributions settled in a well-defined stationary state. The large-scale properties are characterized by a scale-free topology consistent with previous observations. Correlation functions and clustering coefficients exhibit a remarkable structure due to the underlying hierarchical organization of the Internet. The study of the Internet time evolution shows a growth dynamics with aging features typical of recently proposed growing network models. We compare the properties of growing network models with the present real Internet data analysis.
Introduction: The Internet is a capital example of growing complex network , interconnecting millions of computers around the world. Growing networks exhibit a high degree of wiring entanglement which takes place during their dynamical evolution. This feature, at the heart of the new and interesting topological properties recently observed in growing network systems , , has triggered the attention of the research community to the study of the large-scale properties of router-level maps of the Internet , , . The statistical analysis performed so far has focused on several quantities exhibiting non-trivial properties: wiring redundancy and clustering, , , , , the distribution of chemical distances , , and the eigenvalue spectra of the connectivity matrix . Noteworthy, the presence of a power-law connectivity distribution , , , , makes the Internet an example of the recently identified class of scale-free networks , . This evidence implies the absence of any characteristic connectivity—large connectivity fluctuations—and a high heterogeneity of the network structure.As widely pointed out in the literature , , , a deeper empirical understanding of the topological properties of Internet is fundamental in the developing of realistic Internet map generators, that on their turn are used to test and optimize Internet protocols. In fact, the Internet topology has a great influence on the dynamics that data traffic carries out on top of it. Hence, a better understanding of the Internet structure is of primary importance in the design of new routing , and searching algorithms , , and to protect from virus spreading and node failures , , . In this perspective, the direct measurement and statistical characterization of real Internet maps are of crucial importance in the identification of the basic mechanisms that rule the Internet structure and dynamics.In this work, we shall consider the evolution of real Internet maps from 1997 to 2000, collected by the National Laboratory for Applied Network Research (NLANR) , in order to study the underlying dynamical processes leading to the Internet structure and topology. We provide a statistical analysis of several average properties. In particular, we consider the average connectivity, clustering coefficient, chemical distance, and betweenness. These quantities will provide a preliminary test of the stationarity of the network. The scale-free nature of the Internet has been pointed out by inspecting the connectivity probability distribution, and it implies that the fluctuations around the average connectivity are not bounded. In order to provide a full characterization of the scale-free properties of the Internet, we analyze the connectivity and betweenness probability distributions for different time snapshot of the Internet maps. We observe that these distributions exhibit an algebraic behavior and are characterized by scaling exponents which are stationary in time. The chemical distance between pairs of nodes, on the other hand, appears to be sharply peaked around its average value, providing a striking evidence for the presence of well-defined small-world properties . A more detailed picture of the Internet can be achieved by studying higher order correlation functions of the network. In this sense, we show that the Internet hierarchical structure is reflected in non-trivial scale-free betweenness and connectivity correlation functions. Finally, we study several quantities related to the growth dynamics of the network. The analysis points out the presence of two distinct wiring processes: the first concerns newly added nodes, while the second is related to already existing nodes increasing their interconnections. We confirm that newly added nodes establish new links with the linear preferential attachment rule often used in modeling growing networks . In addition, a study of the connectivity evolution of a single node shows a rich dynamical behavior with aging properties. The present study could provide some hints for a more realistic modeling of the Internet evolution, and with this purpose in mind we provide a discussion of some of the existing growing network models in the light of our findings. A short account of these results appeared in Ref. .The paper is organized as follows. In Section we describe the Internet maps used in our study. Sec. is devoted to the study of average quantities as a function of time. In Sec. we provide the analysis of the statistical distributions characterizing the Internet topology. We obtain evidence for the scale-free nature of this network as well as for the stationarity in time of this property. In Sec. we characterize the hierarchical structure of the Internet by the statistical analysis of the betweenness and connectivity correlation functions. Sec. reports the study of dynamical properties such as the preferential attachment and the evolution of the average connectivity of newly added nodes. These properties, which show aging features, are the basis for the developing of Internet dynamical models. Sec. is devoted to a detailed discussion of some Internet models as compared with the presented real data analysis. Finally, in Sec. we draw our conclusions and perspectives.
Mapping the Internet: Several Internet mapping projects are currently devoted to obtain high-quality router-level maps of the Internet. In most cases, the map is constructed by using a hop-limited probe (such as the UNIX traceroute tool) from a single location in the network. In this case the result is a “directed”, map as seen from a specific location on the Internet . This approach does not correspond to a complete map of the Internet because cross-links and other technical problems (such as multiple Internet provider aliases) are not considered. Heuristic methods to take into account these problems have been proposed (see for instance Ref. ). However, it is not clear their reliability and the corresponding completeness of the maps constructed this way.A different representation of Internet is obtained by mapping the autonomous systems (AS) topology. The Internet can be considered as a collection of subnetworks that are connected together. Within each subnetwork the information is routed using an internal algorithm that may differ from one subnetwork to another. Thus, each subnet is an independent unit of the Internet and it is often referred as an AS. These AS communicate between them using a specific routing algorithm, the Border Gateway Protocol. Each AS number approximately maps to an Internet Service Provider (ISP) and their links are inter-ISP connections. In this case it is possible to collect data from several probing stations to obtain complete interconnectivity maps (see Refs. , for a technical description of these projects). In particular, the NLANR project is collecting data since Nov. 1997, and it provides topological as well as dynamical information on a consistent subset of the Internet. The first Nov. 1997 map contains 3180 AS, and it has grown in time until the Dec. 1999 measurement, consisting of 6374 AS. In the following we will consider the graph whose nodes represent the AS and whose links represent the adjacencies (interconnections) between AS. In particular we will focus in three different snapshots corresponding to November 8th 1997, 1998, and 1999, that will be referenced as AS97, AS98, and AS99, respectively.The NLANR connectivity maps are collected with a resolution of one day and are changing from day to day. These changes are due to the addition (birth) and deletion (death) of nodes and links, but also to the flickering of connections, so that a node may appear to be isolated (not mapped) from time to time. A simple test, however, shows that flickering is appreciable just in nodes with low connectivity. We compute the ratio {{formula:58e95c8c-8695-4a82-acac-5a998becc1ab}} between the number of days in which a node is observed in the NLANR maps and the total number of days after the first appearance of the node, averaged over all nodes in the maps. The analysis reveals that {{formula:c5438fef-ebae-4efe-a3d2-696434240d21}} and {{formula:84716988-5c11-4221-98da-cf96863b8798}} for nodes with connectivity {{formula:7c5c38de-05a9-4ae1-9308-cffd150e1694}} , and {{formula:64354446-0a27-4059-bf9d-543ee30a0b36}} , respectively. Hence, nodes with {{formula:ba3d8ecb-9c8c-4011-b0be-6b054a9e76cc}} have fluctuations that must be taken into account. In order to shed light on this point, we inspect the incidence of death events with respect to the creation of new nodes. We consider a death event only if a node is not observed in the map during a one year time interval. In Table REF we show the total number of death events in a year, for 1997, 1998, and 1999, in comparison with the total number of new nodes created. It can be seen that the AS's birth rate appears to be larger by a factor of two than the death rate. More interestingly, if we restrict the analysis to nodes with connectivity {{formula:cc74496b-e2a8-4d26-8952-6aecc923b02d}} , the death rate is reduced to a few percent of the birth rate. This clearly indicates that only poorly connected nodes have an appreciable probability to disappear. This fact is easily understandable in terms of the market competition among ISP's, where small newcomers are the ones which more likely go out of business. {{table:d93f049b-dc46-4f15-9968-7e9718f97660}}
Average properties and stationarity: The growth rate of AS maps reveals that the Internet is a rapidly evolving network. Thus, it is extremely important to know whether or not it has reached a stationary state whose average properties are time-independent. This will imply that, despite the continuous increase of nodes and connections in the system, the network's topological properties are not appreciably changing in time. As a first step, we have analyzed the behavior in time of several average magnitudes: the average connectivity {{formula:d7c66d69-9d6d-4696-9ca4-683566adc04a}} , the clustering coefficient {{formula:356b810d-8f1f-427c-aa7f-e3fab55fad70}} , the average chemical distance {{formula:f031fb8a-56fb-4767-8fdd-056cd895ccbe}} , and the average betweenness {{formula:d03d75b6-6564-49dc-ac27-9080287cc13f}} .The connectivity {{formula:043db4ed-e8d0-47a0-ab19-1b1eda6aca1c}} of a node {{formula:377df35b-4d20-4f54-a625-5a85e024b3d9}} is defined as the number of connections of this node with other nodes in the network, and {{formula:5b167061-fbdd-4a56-9a05-f43162803927}} is the average of {{formula:73a88e2f-088a-4871-9836-50c8d12e4a08}} over all nodes in the network. Since each connection contributes to the connectivity of two nodes, we have that {{formula:2fb4721d-7315-4c10-999e-09728102518f}} , where {{formula:4a9f0e12-2682-4b3f-8c1a-74955d48e9f8}} is the total number of connections and {{formula:74fcc66c-278d-4fce-8519-b7399f506c07}} is the number of nodes. Both {{formula:48d32562-5afd-4eeb-9910-21ef1a3d8401}} and {{formula:eaa38df3-11c4-4397-85bc-fc7b1952c9b3}} are increasing with time but their ratio remains almost constant. The average connectivity for the 1997, 1998, and 1999 years (averaged over all the AS maps available for that year) is shown in Table REF . In average each node has three to four connections, which is a small number compared with that of a fully connected network of the same size ({{formula:ebe36506-db1c-42cd-ba88-e8001b18f271}} ). The average connectivity gives information about the number of connections of any node but not about the overall structure of these connections. More information can be obtained using the clustering coefficient introduced in Ref. . The number of neighbors of a node {{formula:fd6556df-6760-484f-8fd8-38c8f8a08cbb}} is given by its connectivity {{formula:6a8c6d7c-b3fe-4cdc-82ca-ff9f59010fec}} . On their turn, these neighbors can be connected among them forming a triangle with node {{formula:ce05846d-dbed-4548-bce4-401cbe8547b0}} . The clustering coefficient {{formula:3cc0412a-9661-4837-8a9b-db28e1aeeeca}} is then defined as the ratio between the number of connections among the {{formula:32b55034-ec25-4b71-ad87-efe37d86a4f5}} neighbors of a given node {{formula:c4f1548a-6503-407f-8c8d-2f93f5464ef2}} and its maximum possible value, {{formula:5ba3401f-145c-41b2-9c57-173d6a5b7af2}} . The average clustering coefficient {{formula:995ae154-ac55-46f1-bc5b-66b074ceb8ed}} is the average of {{formula:ded465cf-8979-4d63-83c9-74db0b03600d}} over all nodes in the network. The clustering coefficient thus provides a measure of how well locally interconnected are the neighbors of any node. The maximum value of {{formula:dbe42dcc-fc4c-431d-b313-4cca2593f327}} is 1, corresponding to a fully connected network. For random graphs , which are constructed by connecting nodes at random with a fixed probability {{formula:666b6ba1-e8f8-466f-b00a-08251a184395}} , the clustering coefficient decreases with the network size {{formula:7fbfb35c-64c5-4366-a85c-173dd5efa6bb}} as {{formula:db969c54-9aba-446d-9c4d-db9562925677}} . On the contrary, it remains constant for regular lattices. The average clustering coefficient obtained for the 1997, 1998, and 1999 years is shown in Table REF . As it can be seen, the clustering coefficient of the AS maps increases slowly with increasing {{formula:5f7ff1d2-f78f-42fe-b4ca-f696d3137db0}} and takes values {{formula:a6c0625d-6385-49e5-b903-fc59d5e75457}} , two orders of magnitudes larger than {{formula:4199e2e4-d91c-4c1c-a803-0b14dc8e7638}} , corresponding to a random graph with the same number of nodes. Therefore, the AS maps are far from being a random graph, a feature that can be naively understood using the following argument: In AS maps the connections among nodes are equivalent, but they are actually characterized by a real space length corresponding to the actual length of the physical connection between AS. The larger is this length, the higher the costs of installation and maintenance of the line, favoring therefore the connection between nearby nodes. It is thus likely that nodes within the same geographical region will have a large number of connection among them, increasing in this way the local clustering coefficient. {{table:a3c6572d-4da3-4a73-8998-c3c1c0dcbcb6}}With this reasoning one might be lead to the conclusion that the Internet topology is close to a regular two-dimensional lattice. The analysis of the chemical distances between nodes, however, reveals that this is not the case. Two nodes {{formula:f2030cd8-b69a-4291-a2b1-54500f315bf7}} and {{formula:cb26ebc3-c519-4dbb-a960-7316cf20fbfb}} are said to be connected if one can go from node {{formula:1b218181-2ad5-4a3f-aee1-4987ae3083ca}} to {{formula:90cfbba0-647f-40d1-9c88-8c4d9f62b702}} following the connections in the network. The path from {{formula:25b60d2d-b4c0-4a77-839d-86bc2a7dee7a}} to {{formula:556a081d-851b-44b8-8260-d7581bc6b601}} may be not unique and its distance is given by the number of nodes visited. The average chemical distance {{formula:6a0645c1-2259-42d8-a3d6-e00d2f69d71e}} is defined as the shortest path distance between two nodes {{formula:feb62e7b-2991-4fa4-900f-86cc8e03c830}} and {{formula:bca94e35-cfc9-48bc-a41b-9ddb9426dc93}} , {{formula:ac3185bd-705a-4941-bcaf-bb526fc51048}} , averaged over every pair of nodes in the network. For regular lattices, {{formula:03453c1e-a42d-4175-9f65-bc4dc6de7657}} , where {{formula:c7fa7b21-c70d-4b57-ad18-130a65a3dbfa}} is the spatial dimension. Hence, if the Internet could be mapped into a two-dimensional lattice, we should observe {{formula:8ab34bac-c599-4444-a957-84a1db5c63dc}} . However, as it can be seen from Table REF , for the AS maps {{formula:9a5ff7fe-d634-46da-9e8a-158142c3cbe2}} . The Internet strikingly exhibits what is known as the “small-world” effect , : in average one can go from one node to any other in the system passing through a very small number of intermediate nodes. This necessarily implies that besides the short local connections which contribute to the large clustering coefficient, there are some hubs and backbones which connect different regional networks, strongly decreasing the average chemical distance. Another measure of this feature is given by the number of minimal paths that pass by each node. To go from one node in the network to another following the shortest path, a sequence of nodes is visited. If we do this for every pair of nodes in the network, there will be a certain number of key nodes that will be visited more often than others. Such nodes will be of great importance for the transmission of information along the network. This fact can be quantitatively measured by means of the betweenness {{formula:c87b8f40-46d2-43cc-84b1-a64cd1dec833}} , defined by the total number of shortest paths between any two nodes in the network that pass thorough the node {{formula:4da5db0d-658b-4153-880b-e994b6e129a0}} . The average betweenness {{formula:12228062-c357-4751-bd7a-6ada0aa7d489}} is the average value of {{formula:2abf9c48-f81c-4cf9-99be-f14ba2348cb9}} over all nodes in the network. The betweenness has been introduced in the analysis of social network in Ref. and more recently it has been studied in scale-free networks, with the name of load . Moreover, an algorithm to compute the betweenness has been given in Ref. . For a star network the betweenness takes its maximum value {{formula:3ac3c2bd-b81f-4eda-9670-c03de1fe1707}} at the central node and its minimum value {{formula:9824579e-f7de-43a6-8a27-bc76c7881ff6}} at the vertices of the star. The average betweenness of the three AS maps analyzed here is shown in Table REF . Its value is between {{formula:9b04c868-b719-4950-ace8-a14fb340886d}} and {{formula:eed6ff2f-716c-4cfa-8ba4-a408b5c85f93}} , which is quite small in comparison with its maximum possible value {{formula:831cb043-aa7f-4c46-b3c4-63e614241920}} .The present analysis makes clear that the Internet is not dominated by a very few highly connected nodes similarly to star-shaped architectures. As well, simple average measurements rule out the possibility of a random graph structure or a regular grid architecture. This evidence hints towards a peculiar topology that will be fully identified by looking at the detailed probability distributions of several quantities. Finally, it is important to stress that despite the network size is more than doubled in the three years period considered, the average quantities suffer variations of a few percent (see Table REF ). This points out that the system seems to have reached a fairly well-defined stationary state, as we shall confirm in the next Section by analyzing the detailed statistical properties of the Internet.
Fluctuations and scale-free properties: In order to get a deeper understanding of the network topology we look at the probability distributions {{formula:a7f136ae-341f-4a00-a33d-425b9c87321f}} and {{formula:90bb737a-6de5-49bf-95f1-d7a9f252165a}} that any given node in the network has a connectivity {{formula:2e660701-a5b4-4396-8332-683a1c7a7fc1}} and a betweenness {{formula:58801368-ce0a-4b39-9bc6-297dd5dbdc61}} , respectively. The study of these probability distributions will allow us to probe the extent of fluctuations and heterogeneity present in the network. We shall see that the strong scale-free nature of the Internet, previously noted in Refs. , , results in power-law distributions with diverging fluctuations for these quantities. The analysis of the maps reveals, in fact, an algebraic decay for the connectivity distribution, {{formula:ce5c2f5c-f386-411e-a5fd-7f18c131c15b}}extending over three orders of magnitude. In Fig. REF we report the integrated connectivity distribution {{formula:7c0c7bc5-c1e3-4073-9680-3922de0c7276}}corresponding to the AS97, AS98, and AS99 maps. The integrated distribution, which expresses the probability that a node has connectivity larger than or equal to {{formula:c1cc849c-2d0d-4a1e-81ce-9162c8f47a71}} , scales as {{formula:46a028b9-3d3b-471e-b35e-f3e3e122bf36}}and it has the advantage of being considerably less noisy that the original distribution. In all maps we find a clear power-law behavior with slope close to {{formula:c14b2be2-7bfa-487b-9bce-48f8d06d6dd8}} (see Fig. REF ), yielding a connectivity exponent {{formula:3451ab51-21f2-4c84-ad40-d1ff40ad4a2e}} . These large connectivity nodes will be on their turn connected to nodes in different clusters which are not interconnected and, therefore, will have a small local clustering coefficient. Hierarchy and correlations: Due to installation costs, the Internet has been designed with a hierarchical structure. The primary known structural difference between Internet nodes is the distinction between stub and transit domains. Nodes in stub domains have links that go only through the domain itself. Stub domains, on the other hand, are connected via a gateway node to transit domains that, on the contrary, are fairly well interconnected via many paths. This hierarchy can be schematically divided into international connections, national backbones, regional networks, and local area networks. Nodes providing access to international connections or national backbones are of course on top level of this hierarchy, since they make possible the communication between regional and local area networks. Moreover, in this way, a small average chemical distance can be achieved with a small average connectivity.Very likely the hierarchical structure will introduce some correlations in the network topology. We can explore the hierarchical structure of the Internet by means of the conditional probability {{formula:ca04d6db-2acd-4658-bf7a-f76fe217b398}} that a link belonging to node with connectivity {{formula:9b2a21da-2446-4adf-9b6a-b1e89693160a}} points to a node with connectivity {{formula:4a05d47e-2b1f-48bd-aed2-6d1c04924427}} . If this conditional probability is independent of {{formula:e9f39b2d-53ba-4c3f-a57d-1e3031b750aa}} , we are in presence of a topology without any correlation among the nodes' connectivity. In this case, {{formula:90a84de3-e853-42e4-94c9-4b42da75a267}} , in view of the fact that any link points to nodes with a probability proportional to their connectivity. On the contrary, the explicit dependence on {{formula:c5c9d960-0d78-4e79-905a-6e994a09821b}} is a signature of non-trivial correlations among the nodes' connectivity, and the presence of a hierarchical structure in the network topology. A direct measurement of the {{formula:0cd4d186-7e04-4de6-b339-574f255ad11b}} function is a rather complex task due to large statistical fluctuations. More clear indications can be extracted by studying the quantity {{formula:e3cc99df-9bd7-4cb8-be0b-0a179e7c0eb0}}i.e. the nearest neighbors average connectivity of nodes with connectivity {{formula:f31beb51-478b-49ba-87fd-c93d315a6448}} . In Fig. REF (a) we show the results obtained for the AS97, AS98, and AS99 maps, that again exhibit a clear power-law dependence on the connectivity degree, {{formula:3acbd5b1-e612-4ef4-bfb5-1715e3832ea2}}with an exponent {{formula:6015f7e7-454e-4d80-b773-834e99f03ac6}} . This observation clearly implies that the connectivity correlation function has a marked dependence upon {{formula:ed1fd99f-d615-4da8-a6a4-282fa0c3df31}} , suggesting non-trivial correlation properties for the Internet. In practice, this result indicates that highly connected nodes are more likely pointing to less connected nodes, emphasizing the presence of a hierarchy in which smaller providers connect to larger ones and so on, climbing different levels of connectivity.Similarly, it is expected that nodes with high betweenness (that is, carrying a heavy load of transit), and consequently a large connectivity, will be connected to nodes with smaller betweenness, less load and, therefore, small connectivity. A simple way to measure this effect is to compute the average betweenness {{formula:9b29c6d2-2890-4471-8b9d-3d4fae659827}} of the neighbors of the nodes with a given betweenness {{formula:1a0a01b1-91da-4617-9c7a-91f97cfc9e16}} . The plot of {{formula:dd0f09da-5a46-4742-8b93-ad65b39a3cbf}} for the AS97, AS98, and AS99 maps, represented in Fig. REF (b), shows that the average neighbor betweenness exhibits a clear power-law dependence on the node betweenness {{formula:9821b843-2d15-4eab-9b04-b8975b871ce1}} , {{formula:fbf0842e-a5bd-4571-b476-f819baf4616b}}with an exponent {{formula:9b17d59b-3fe1-47dd-bc30-9859f3765d0e}} , evidencing that the more loaded nodes (backbones) are more frequently connected with less loaded nodes (local networks).These hierarchical properties of the Internet are likely driven by several additional factors such as the space locality, economical resources and the market demand. An attempt to relate and study some of these aspects can be found in Ref. , where the geographical distribution of population and Internet access are studied. In Sec. we shall compare a few of the existing models for the generation of scale-free networks with our data analysis, in an attempt to identify some relevant features in the Internet modeling.
Dynamics and growth: In order to inspect the Internet dynamics, we focus our attention on the addition of new nodes and links into the maps. In the three-years range considered, we keep track of the number of links {{formula:50ce949a-b9d5-4ebc-9ed6-3f826a95dc7e}} appearing between a newly introduced node and an already existing node. We also monitor the rate of appearance of links {{formula:a692c232-a1ff-4eba-b011-5f5b38d6148e}} between already existing nodes. In Table REF we can observe that the creation of new links is governed by these two processes at the same time. Specifically, the largest contribution to the growth is given by the appearance of links between already existing nodes. This clearly points out that the Internet growth is strongly driven by the need of redundancy in the wiring and an increased need of available bandwidth for data transmission. {{table:cd360ec7-7a3f-4259-970d-62cebc548ddf}}A customarily measured quantity in the case of growing networks is the average connectivity {{formula:811bd5ea-f01b-4f92-b73d-e1368a7cce39}} of new nodes as a function of their age {{formula:8df03e02-e315-42c4-ba37-3e633089a225}} . In Refs. , , it is shown that {{formula:8e17b729-4652-4ad5-a4ee-886885960aa1}} is a scaling function of both {{formula:03c8f07c-5045-4d2f-8549-a6ec42893875}} and the absolute time of birth of the node {{formula:bb0543fe-be9f-4314-b28f-9ad2c10141aa}} . We thus consider the total number of nodes born within an small observation window {{formula:b9e6a7e4-41a3-428a-9bdc-ca23a427a834}} , such that {{formula:2615f395-ba54-47e8-8e91-35b6f43b0b04}} with respect to the absolute time scale that is the Internet lifetime. For these nodes, we measure the average connectivity as a function of the time {{formula:3f6465e6-da22-4e9d-85f2-24fd95701b98}} elapsed since their birth. The data for two different time windows are reported in Fig. REF , where it is possible to distinguish two different dynamical regimes: At early times, the connectivity is nearly constant with a very slow increase ({{formula:9df41ceb-9c2c-4e38-8abd-aad4f8d43acb}} ). Later on, the behavior approaches a power-law growth {{formula:9b71cd0b-a153-43e5-8fb7-2160a59455df}} . While exponent estimates are affected by noise and limited time window effects, the crossover between two distinct dynamical regimes is compatible with the general aging form obtained in the context of growing networks in Ref. , . {{figure:db789aff-07af-4a14-a6bb-93adab66e3c4}}{{figure:48cd12ab-8628-4fda-ae92-2f86bc6b1adf}}A very important issue in the modeling of growing networks concerns the understanding of the growth mechanisms at the origin of the developing of new links. As we shall see more in detail in the next Section, the basic ingredients in the modeling of scale-free growing networks is the preferential attachment hypothesis . In general, all growing network algorithms define models in which the rate {{formula:65a22607-9bc7-4176-9e29-de99b503a840}} with which a node with {{formula:cb0f8d3a-2a88-4384-a6b2-de8051b84649}} connections receives new links is proportional to {{formula:d53e75dc-bf52-474a-bb45-6b809097064e}} (see Ref. and Sec. ). The inspection of the exact value of {{formula:b66fb082-6eba-4069-bf1c-9864e5f7ea43}} in real networks is an important issue since the connectivity properties strongly depend on this exponent , , . Here we use a simple recipe that allows to extract the value of {{formula:b5e9b007-0b6b-4de7-8eb5-fda59c03fa2f}} by studying the appearance of new links. We focus on links emanating from newly appeared nodes in different time windows ranging from one to three years. We consider the frequency {{formula:c9c8f069-ce6e-4e41-8376-4ffbd69fcafd}} of links that connect to nodes with connectivity {{formula:a166b1a9-b002-48f2-9873-433207220674}} . By using the preferential attachment hypothesis, this effective probability is {{formula:debbd131-ddba-461e-b653-0cbb9757c8a5}} . Since we know that {{formula:aeb868c9-8e88-4dbe-be5f-a9da2d22cca1}} , we expect to find a power-law behavior {{formula:736fbe47-2ed3-4f03-adb1-2d998cc71d39}} for the frequency. In Fig. REF we report the obtained results for the integrated frequency {{formula:48f2e153-2251-4eea-bcb5-0d553aa366d6}} , which shows a behavior compatible with an algebraic dependence {{formula:73f26600-3eec-45db-b9c1-c89717652596}} . By using the independently obtained value {{formula:1b53fedb-4986-418f-a9e0-a9be0e564d08}} we find a preferential attachment exponent {{formula:5d6f80a0-6794-4df0-a224-5ef25a3666b2}} , in good agreement with the result obtained with a different analysis in Ref. . We performed a similar analysis also for links emanated by existing nodes, recovering the same form of preferential attachment (see Fig. REF ). The present analysis confirms the validity of the preferential attachment hypothesis, but leaves open the question of the interplay with several other factors, such as the nodes' hierarchy, space locality, and resource constraints.
Modeling the Internet: In the previous Section we have presented a thorough analysis of the AS maps topology. Apart from providing useful empirical data to understand the behavior of the Internet, our analysis is of great relevance in order to test the validity of models of the Internet topology. The Internet topology has a great influence on the information traffic carried on top of it, including routing algorithms , , searching algorithms , , virus spreading , and resilience to node failure , , . Thus, designing network models which accurately reproduce the Internet topology is of capital importance to carry out simulations on top of these networks.Early works considered the Erdös-Rényi model or hierarchical networks as models of Internet . However, they yield connectivity distributions with a fast (exponential) decay for large connectivities, in disagreement with the power-law decay observed in real data. Only recently the Internet modeling benefited of the major advance provided in the field of growing networks by the introduction of the Barabási-Albert (BA) model , , , which is related to 1955 Simon's model , , . The main ingredients of this model are the growing nature of the network and a preferential attachment rule, in which the probability of establishing new links toward a given node grows linearly with its connectivity. The BA model is constructed using the following algorithm : We start from a small number {{formula:f7dfb5ea-5d35-4766-a377-b4907192c070}} of disconnected nodes; every time step a new node is added, with {{formula:6e46e949-a037-4605-8182-525d958ec113}} links that are connected to an old node {{formula:258cf830-b7b4-43a2-9326-b77c56281dad}} with probability {{formula:0c75b74e-87b0-4d5f-a7a6-b80c8e0daaf6}}where {{formula:32b139d0-4697-4cf2-8394-4094f840e316}} is the connectivity of the {{formula:c66d8b74-107f-420d-9bda-0c5acf2ce095}} -th node. After iterating this procedure {{formula:aa061812-67ca-4f1e-91b5-a528a2d07534}} times, we obtain a network with a connectivity distribution {{formula:e43156c4-3113-443a-9bb2-55f05c5c1426}} and average connectivity {{formula:e40a4b9c-31b8-412d-89a5-c8c5bbc78529}} . In this model, heavily connected nodes will increase their connectivity at a larger rate than less connected nodes, a phenomenon that is known as the “rich-get-richer” effect . It is worth remarking, however, that more general studies , , have revealed that nonlinear attachment rates of the form {{formula:c33b6e0a-35ca-4727-be07-90fa34338df3}} with {{formula:469c27c6-b3c8-41f4-9c41-3ce0d8c2b2dd}} have as an outcome connectivity distributions that depart form the power-law behavior. The BA model has been successively modified with the introduction of several ingredients in order to account for connectivity distribution with {{formula:87d9f45d-b14a-47f7-a81b-b5efe77797c1}} , , , local geographical factors , wiring among existing nodes , and age effects .In the previous Section we have analyzed different measures that characterize the structure of AS maps. Since several models are able to reproduce the right power law behavior for the connectivity distribution, the analysis obtained in the previous sections can provide the effective tools to scrutinize the different models at a deeper level. In particular, we perform a data comparison for three different models that generate networks with power-law connectivity distributions. First we have considered a random graph constructed with a power-law connectivity distribution, using the Molloy and Reed (MR) algorithm , . Secondly, we have studied two variations of the BA model, that yield connectivity exponents compatible with the one measured in Internet: the generalized Barabási-Albert (GBA) model , which includes the possibility of connection rewiring, and the fitness model , that implements a weighting of the nodes in the preferential attachment probability. {{figure:ab2afeee-d6a0-4f63-a4a8-25e8c3750cad}}The models are defined as follows:MR model: In the construction of this model , , , we start assigning to each node {{formula:25f61300-7c46-4ab9-96f9-95f276e9c9ca}} in a set of {{formula:13b727eb-8263-4530-ada5-8579ff94a5be}} nodes a random connectivity {{formula:393cf7f6-ed40-4e9c-80de-cac8ab000713}} drawn from the probability distribution {{formula:efc8f7a8-2bdf-4afe-8784-1a676b5863c3}} , with {{formula:62486c26-5a53-437f-a26a-ad9efdddecce}} , and imposing the constraint that the sum {{formula:782481c0-b5ba-40fa-8004-77645649154f}} must be even. The graph is completed by randomly connecting the nodes with {{formula:d4c05110-b8a9-41d0-8be4-20f1d664b46d}} links, respecting the assigned connectivities. The results presented here are obtained using {{formula:af0a9989-0320-4d58-9f84-4e9dd1bb86d8}} and a connectivity exponent {{formula:11d315bb-ba3c-4448-92e3-12623126f7fb}} , equal to that found in the AS maps. Clearly this construction algorithm does not take into account any correlations or dynamical feature of the Internet and it can be considered as a first order approximations that focuses only in the connectivity properties.GBA model: It is defined by starting with {{formula:22bab695-61ff-4f95-a88e-8184073cd298}} nodes connected in a ring : At each time step one of the following operations is performed:(i) With probability {{formula:2eb5e538-4b9c-478f-a0a8-e016a8aebe08}} we rewire {{formula:5cd2f0de-384f-4b65-9c4b-73700fda0aa6}} links. For each of them, we randomly select a node {{formula:57d380b8-7d0d-40f3-af1a-0b88f8460f85}} and a link {{formula:0ad6e233-00fb-4009-8f54-bb66e0b369f0}} connected to it. The fitness model adds to the growing dynamics with preferential attachment a stochastic parameter, the fitness, that embeds all the properties, other than the connectivity, that may influence the probability of gaining new links. {{table:f1fe1969-21bb-4d38-ab22-639c574656ab}}We have performed simulations of these three models using the parameters mentioned above and using sizes of {{formula:920d5a10-6f1e-425a-9856-d57dda8663b6}} nodes, in analogy with the size of the AS map analyzed. In each case we perform averages over 1000 different realizations of the networks. It is worth remarking that while the fitness model generates a connected network, both the GBA and the MR model yield disconnected networks. This is due to the rewiring process in the GBA model, while the disconnect nature of the graph in the MR model is an inherent consequence of the connectivity exponent being larger that 2 . For the GBA model we obtain numerically {{formula:1c7f7b1b-a989-4a38-b1a1-6ae275a9bf0a}} for the giant component, in excellent agreement with the value predicted by Eq. (REF ) for the asymptotic network. For the fitness model, on the other hand, a numerical regression of the integrated connectivity distribution yields an effective exponent {{formula:63d1abaf-07fc-45f2-bccb-c612e92cb6eb}} . This value is larger than the theoretical prediction {{formula:44051ec2-9bd2-4141-a046-583a746d5edb}} obtained for the model . The discrepancy is mainly due to the logarithmic corrections present in the connectivity distribution of this model. These corrections are more evident in the relatively small-sized networks used in this work and become progressively smaller for larger network sizes. {{figure:301240ad-8e31-40f4-a384-08c270ab363b}}In Table REF we report the average values of the connectivity, clustering coefficient, chemical distance, and betweenness for the three models, compared with the respective values computed for Internet during 1998. From the examination of this Table, one could surprisingly conclude that the MR model, which neglects by constructions any correlation among nodes, yields the average values in better agreement with the Internet data. As we can observe, the fitness model provides a too small value for the average clustering coefficient, while the GBA model clearly fails for the average chemical distance and the betweenness. A more crucial test about the models is however provided by the analysis of the full distribution of the various quantities, that should reproduce the scale-free features of the real Internet.The betweenness distribution {{formula:bdf378a8-7cd4-451f-842a-9cd6c77db1b0}} of the three models give qualitatively similar results. The integrated betweenness distribution {{formula:aba4975a-29ea-4161-bc17-c7973eedab64}} obtained is plotted in Fig. REF (a). Both the MR and the fitness models follow a power-law decay {{formula:7394403c-30a0-4789-ba66-86d2466aded3}} with an exponent {{formula:6135a673-c4f7-4968-a686-51f5c11757c3}} , in agreement with the value obtained from the AS maps. The GBA model shows an appreciable bending which, nevertheless, is compatible with the experimental Internet behavior. These results are in agreement with the numerical prediction in Ref. and support the conjecture that the exponent {{formula:9c3823d3-0394-4d99-b7b1-c28d669bee20}} is a universal quantity in all scale-free networks with {{formula:d5eac3c8-8ce4-4a60-9eb2-e1fd16b97d10}} . In order to further inspect the betweenness properties, we plot in Fig. REF (b) the average betweenness {{formula:afcbfceb-f3f9-441f-adcf-85d04e39fdb3}} as a function of the connectivity. In this case, the MR and GBA models yield an exponent {{formula:01486b96-acb2-4b71-8e91-9fad001b6e9f}} , compatible with the AS maps, while the fitness model exhibits a somewhat larger exponent, close to {{formula:2aeab2ba-b7ff-4974-9978-d1006605c193}} . Also in this case, we have that the finite size logarithmic corrections present in the fitness model could play a determinant role in this discrepancy. {{figure:41a0e635-331d-46d9-9d8a-9aa1351b951d}}{{figure:76bc4c07-d9c7-4102-b6e0-8f70fe92fb13}}While properties related to the betweenness do not appear to pinpoint a major difference among the models, the most striking test is provided by analyzing the correlation properties of the models. In Figs. REF and REF , we report the average clustering coefficient as a function of the connectivity, {{formula:25098aba-6077-4358-9501-d8aa8c4a3981}} , and the average connectivity of the neighbors, {{formula:8476b3d7-67a1-40c2-90e7-2e0cac35bc11}} , respectively. The data from Internet maps show a nontrivial {{formula:4e689b18-3069-4653-a6b0-e40dee44a136}} structure that, as discussed in previous Sections, is due to scale-free correlation properties among nodes. These properties depend on their turn upon the underlying hierarchy of the Internet structure. The only model that renders results in qualitative agreement with the Internet maps is the fitness model. On the contrary, the MR and GBA models completely fail, producing quantities which are almost independent on {{formula:7d0b09cd-472b-4edd-b9b1-f44e85855be8}} . The reason of this striking difference can be traced back to the lack of correlations among nodes, which in the MR model is imposed by construction (the model is a random network with fixed connectivity distribution), and in the GBA model it is due to the destruction of correlations by the random rewiring mechanism implemented. The general analytic study of connectivity correlations in growing networks models can be found in Ref. , and it is worth noticing that a {{formula:ceb31f15-fae4-4594-bfaf-2a5886eba7f3}} -structure in correlation functions, as probed by the quantity {{formula:64eda8d1-b89f-4646-8d6a-dc2e7da972d9}} , does not arise in all growing network models. In this perspective we can use correlation properties as one of the discriminating feature among various models that show the same scale-free connectivity exponent.The fitness model is able to reproduce the non trivial correlation properties because of the fitness parameter of each node that mimics the different hierarchical, economical, and geographical constraints of the Internet growth. Since the model is embedding many features in one single parameter, we have to consider it just as a very first step towards a more realistic modeling of the Internet. In this perspective, models in which the attachment rate depends on both the connectivity and the real space distance between two nodes has been studied in , . These models seem to give a better description of the Internet topology. In particular, the model of Ref. , includes geographical constraints, obtaining that, on average, the probability to connect to a given node scales linearly with its connectivity and it is inversely proportional to the distance to that node. A comparison with real data is, in this case, more difficult because Internet maps generally lack geographical and economical information.
Summary and conclusions: In summary, we have shown that the Internet maps exhibit a stationary scale-free topology, characterized by non-trivial connectivity correlations. An investigation of the Internet dynamics confirms the presence of a preferential attachment behaving linearly with the nodes' connectivity and identifies two different dynamical regimes during the nodes' evolution. We have compared several models of scale-free networks to the experimental data obtained from the AS maps. While all the models seem to capture the scale-free connectivity distribution, correlation and clustering properties are captured only in models that take into account several other ingredients, such as the nodes' hierarchy, resource constraints and geographical location. Other ingredients that should be included in the Internet modeling concern the possibility of including the wiring among existing nodes and age effects that our analysis show to be an appreciable feature of the Internet evolution. The results presented in this work show that the understanding and modeling of Internet is an interesting and stimulating problem that need the cooperative efforts of data analysis and theoretical modeling.This work has been partially supported by the European Network Contract No. ERBFMRXCT980183. R.P.-S. acknowledges financial support from the Ministerio de Ciencia y Tecnología (Spain) and from the Abdus Salam International Centre for Theoretical Physics (ICTP), where part of this work was done.

First 53869 characters: Compressibility of complex networks
abstract: Many complex networks depend upon biological entities for their preservation. Such entities, from human cognition to evolution, must first encode and then replicate those networks under marked resource constraints. Networks that survive are those that are amenable to constrained encoding, or, in other words, are compressible. But how compressible is a network? And what features make one network more compressible than another? Here we answer these questions by modeling networks as information sources before compressing them using rate-distortion theory. Each network yields a unique rate-distortion curve, which specifies the minimal amount of information that remains at a given scale of description. A natural definition then emerges for the compressibility of a network: the amount of information that can be removed via compression, averaged across all scales. Analyzing an array of real and model networks, we demonstrate that compressibility increases with two common network properties: transitivity (or clustering) and degree heterogeneity. These results indicate that hierarchical organization -- which is characterized by modular structure and heterogeneous degrees -- facilitates compression in complex networks. Generally, our framework sheds light on the interplay between a network's structure and its capacity to be compressed, enabling investigations into the role of compression in shaping real-world networks.
Rate-distortion theory of network clustering: In compression , one begins with an information source, a sequence of items that defines the object of interest. In the context of networks, the details of information flow often vary from one setting to another. Therefore, a logical choice for the information source is a random walk, which encodes only the information contained in a network's structure and nothing more . One then seeks to reduce the amount of information in the sequence by constructing a coarse-grained representation of the network. We remark that the lossless compression of random walks has provided important information-theoretic perspectives on the problem of community detection . By contrast, rather than choosing a specific number of communities, here we are interested in analyzing the compressibility of networks across all scales. To do so, we employ rate-distortion theory, the foundation of lossy compression. Importantly, rate-distortion theory will enable tractable strategies for compressing networks across all scales and, in doing so, will allow us to develop an intuitive definition for compressibility.
Compressing random walks: To see how compression unfolds in practice, consider the network in Fig. REFA. A random walk on the network defines a sequence of nodes {{formula:01c4f0f6-8a5a-4fe9-8864-b2548b61cfca}} , with each node transitioning to one of its four neighbors uniformly at random. The rate at which this sequence generates information is given by the entropy {{formula:5c40bb6a-4eff-4ba4-b031-eef414740536}} , which (because there are four possible nodes at each step) equals 2 bits (see Materials and Methods for a definition of {{formula:2f4396f7-622d-49f1-9736-f461818d50f7}} ). To reduce the amount of information in the sequence, we can construct a coarse-grained representation by clustering nodes together , , . This clustering yields a new sequence {{formula:de1b01e1-83f3-47a8-beaf-f9fbd23e544f}} , where {{formula:c6090d2f-b400-4cb2-af38-a6317b6581bf}} is the cluster containing node {{formula:baaaa93b-943d-40d1-83c9-9b53428eaee3}} (Fig. REFB), which communicates information at a rate equal to the mutual information {{formula:da4195d4-7c45-448c-89a3-d307df198cd4}} , , , . If the clusters are chosen deterministically, as is common , , , then the conditional entropy {{formula:7910451e-72c7-4d16-a92b-631bc27b26a6}} vanishes, and the information rate simplifies to the entropy of the clustered sequence, {{formula:71c602cc-49e0-432d-8f6b-7b68d4d7a0e2}} .[][t] {{figure:799c0706-7e41-4b0f-b732-9ee02083b451}}Rate-distortion theory of random walks on networks. (A) A simple network with {{formula:c7160159-7a44-4639-8ca8-1f79497a16fe}} nodes, each with constant degree {{formula:318410d7-7ebc-4b9b-be12-8e4ac97f6a02}} . A random walk {{formula:720f647d-5b7f-447e-bdc0-7322918c110e}} generates information at a rate {{formula:9f3e5cc7-6311-4c50-9908-7e1b7abaf620}} bits. (B) Network clusterings across various scales of description. For {{formula:2e2a6d22-251b-4f1e-9473-9ca799eb9762}} clusters, each containing its own node, the sequence communicates {{formula:367f0ed8-a03e-4818-97e7-09159de14298}} bits of information (Top). For {{formula:c0821278-afd7-4a1d-b3b8-8c4796b5f712}} clusters, each corresponding to one of the three modules in the original network, the information rate is {{formula:dbf5c1a3-cd9a-4ff2-9e27-022e4bd622b9}} bits (Middle). For {{formula:df4a8930-d719-4514-8bd1-5a4899e31c42}} cluster containing the entire network, the sequence no longer communicates information (Bottom). (C) Schematic of the optimal information rate {{formula:599ba45a-dedf-4450-9d7c-68b1415a505b}} as a function of the scale of description {{formula:2faa20cf-5ad3-4e2a-ba80-929f3341d0e7}} for networks that are either more compressible (black) or less compressible (grey). For more compressible networks, one can achieve a lower information rate at a given scale of description (vertical line), and one can achieve a more fine-grained description for a given information rate (horizontal line).Consider, for example, a trivial clustering in which each node belongs to its own cluster (Fig. REFB, top). In this case, we maintain a complete description of the network, but we have not reduced the information rate, since {{formula:77dda99f-272c-44ae-a254-a5a2cc4feefe}} bits. By contrast, consider the opposite setting in which all nodes belong to the same large cluster (Fig. REFB, bottom). Now we have reduced the information rate to zero ({{formula:df4ebc38-53aa-429a-95bc-a1182412660c}} bits), but all details about the network structure have been lost. Between these two extremes lies a range of clusterings (such as that in Fig. REFB, middle), each inducing its own information rate and yielding a unique distortion of the network structure.
Scale as a measure of distortion: Building representations that strike an optimal balance between minimizing information rate while also minimizing distortion is precisely the purview of rate-distortion theory , . As in any rate-distortion problem, one must choose a specific definition for the distortion of the object of interest. When clustering a network, a natural choice for the distortion presents itself: the scale of description. Specifically, for a network with {{formula:8211e550-3a7e-4c1c-8c32-e58215309365}} nodes and a clustering with {{formula:63af5c84-6e4c-49ce-ac34-a793426bad65}} clusters, we define the scale to be {{formula:33d6d855-0c72-414f-931f-bdca691133df}} . For example, if {{formula:94acd805-d626-4302-be61-2a8a158285f2}} , then we have an exact fine-grained description of the network at a scale {{formula:8dc0c318-f44d-40ca-b734-cad7d721b285}} (Fig. REFB, top); whereas if {{formula:f48023a2-5b7c-447d-a281-70c74f17e0b5}} , then one cluster encloses the entire network and {{formula:e1a9b7f5-3db9-4914-9d1d-e06ed9190915}} (Fig. REFB, bottom).At each scale {{formula:d4509541-e767-41de-9a34-fa036cedd2e4}} (equivalently, for each number of clusters {{formula:d4c51e17-fb26-482d-88c1-42e4cef7306a}} ), we seek to identify the clustering that minimizes the information rate {{formula:b030ab7d-4914-4f81-aec1-87a9ab33a821}} . This optimal information rate, denoted {{formula:99c3b6cb-9ed9-41a2-9c6c-d5f6d7e233a6}} , defines a unique rate-distortion curve for each network (Fig. REFC). If a network is easier to compress, then at each scale {{formula:14cff52f-48aa-433b-8939-3f58206b0a80}} one should be able to find a clustering that is more efficient, reducing the information rate {{formula:81615c67-5573-4d06-b4b6-bfe05a553ac1}} (Fig. REFC, vertical line); similarly, for a given information rate {{formula:066d686a-b69e-40db-8bc1-f672403edcb9}} one should be able to construct a more fine-grained clustering, decreasing the scale {{formula:6a75512d-7de3-467c-bcf5-6e6542147bc4}} (Fig. REFC, horizontal line). Thus, in order to quantify the compressibility of a network, we must first be able to compute its rate-distortion curve.
Computing the rate-distortion curve of a network: Computing the rate-distortion curve {{formula:0c63e30d-8888-45ad-8f1b-5950c9d24979}} of a network – in particular, doing so efficiently to enable applications to large systems – poses two distinct challenges. First, we must estimate the mutual information {{formula:192301a5-d25d-49b9-a0b1-11a66c68cd15}} for different clusterings; and second, we must identify the clusterings that minimize this information rate across all scales.Although estimating mutual information is generally difficult , the simplicity of our setup allows for tractable upper and lower bounds (see Materials and Methods). Of particular interest is the upper bound {{formula:fd44e394-c763-4ca4-8604-7a79e8dc3b57}} , which follows by approximating the clustered sequence {{formula:52e551a5-2c95-4a9f-8727-67e5a36a4da9}} as Markovian (a property that we note is not guaranteed, even though the original random walk {{formula:6f22d548-a21f-4b74-8188-dbbbb53f0466}} is Markovian ). Rather than minimizing the information rate {{formula:24cd4d7d-63e2-4ca7-a76a-a9ed9b5d29da}} directly, we instead minimize the upper bound {{formula:08a0e7aa-7e63-4837-bd4b-21bf9cb275ab}} , yielding an upper bound {{formula:1896195f-7da1-49ff-878f-1cac8f2b3979}} on the rate-distortion curve. For simplicity, in what follows we often refer to {{formula:a72aa04f-4eff-4911-8323-41d6b2f88f3f}} as the information rate and {{formula:83097380-9895-44a2-b032-142ae41aa849}} as the rate-distortion curve.To compute {{formula:7208350c-7793-49c7-b80a-37fad0325140}} – that is, to find clusterings that minimize the information rate {{formula:de49e430-d569-428a-949c-50223c99878a}} – we employ a greedy clustering algorithm. Beginning with {{formula:e5ad923e-0711-4e01-8266-f56a12ecc1e1}} clusters, each containing its own node, we combine the pair of clusters that yields the largest reduction in the information rate {{formula:fc5be6bb-0f02-4de3-9e58-eff7d24810d6}} . Repeating this agglomerative process across all scales {{formula:ad91910f-d326-4040-930e-668f841c7507}} (until only one cluster remains), we arrive at an estimate for the rate-distortion curve {{formula:2c76f23a-8dc3-4865-86bc-1491dd818529}} . To speed up the calculation, rather than searching through all {{formula:236639e7-762e-493d-95b1-6462ae9fc24a}} pairs of clusters at each step, we only consider a limited number of pairs chosen via principled heuristics (see Materials and Methods). Importantly, these heuristics do not affect the definitions of information-theoretic quantities, such as the rate {{formula:52123a8a-51a6-44e8-8c0e-946a58cec02c}} and upper bound {{formula:c3480878-bd42-4fe7-94c2-8bb4e33db84b}} . In practice, not only do these heuristics enable applications to networks of approximately {{formula:de40616a-9c0f-4d82-be3e-25ca92bb0b2f}} nodes, they also improve the accuracy of the rate-distortion estimates themselves (see Supporting Fig. 1). {{figure:e85948ec-841f-41e6-be8a-d227baddab40}}We are now prepared to compute the rate-distortion curve for a specific system. In Fig. REFA, we plot the upper and lower bounds on the rate-distortion curve {{formula:f23c34cd-0334-4a57-9ffd-dc307e6b0495}} for Zachary's karate club network . As is true for all networks (see Materials and Methods), the two bounds are exact at both the minimum scale {{formula:b705917f-a6b2-4905-8ad2-31e999cf55fe}} (when the information rate simply equals the entropy of random walks {{formula:1f4967c8-dfab-4817-8dfa-02b4045fedbd}} ) and the maximum scale {{formula:1a143b42-bc6f-46ef-87e0-c1c0253a851a}} (when the information rate is zero). Moreover, the two bounds remain close across all intermediate scales (Fig. REFA), demonstrating that the upper bound {{formula:925c356f-55e4-4274-ba36-ace9d6392396}} provides a good approximation to the true rate-distortion curve {{formula:c365d1ca-a588-4747-b414-2a00eb9acb4f}} . To understand how the rate-distortion curve depends on the structure of a network, however, it helps to examine the properties of optimal compressions themselves.
Properties of optimal compressions: Using the framework developed above, we are ultimately interested in studying compression in real systems. The networks chosen for analysis span from communication networks (including semantic, language, and music networks) and information networks (including hyperlinks on the web and citations in science) to social networks, animal and protein interactions, transportation networks, and structural and functional connections in the brain (see Materials and Methods; Supporting Table 1). Although these networks encompass a wide range of systems bridging several orders of magnitude in size, they are all encoded biologically, either in genetic material or in the neural code.
Emergence of one large cluster: To begin, we compute the rate-distortion curve {{formula:5ca8c237-26f9-4041-b7e4-f7dd41f1f249}} for each of the above networks, and we confirm that these upper bounds provide good approximations to the true rate-distortion curves {{formula:4f36eada-894e-4b6a-af77-21be7b43fdb9}} (see Supporting Fig. 2). In the process of computing {{formula:bf78ca81-01f6-4d78-b021-d4842f4c121f}} , our compression algorithm also provides estimates for the optimal clusterings over all scales. Examining the structure of these compressions, we find a striking consistency across different networks. As can be observed in Zachary's karate club (Fig. REFA, Right), rather than dividing the network into multiple clusters of moderate size, optimal compressions tend to comprise one large cluster containing {{formula:8ac8c88b-ff44-4d78-8793-b09fe016bc02}} nodes and {{formula:8b6e6f88-e306-477e-be49-0fc8fa247710}} minimal clusters each containing one node. In fact, among the networks studied, this tendency to form one large cluster is a nearly ubiquitous feature of optimal compressions (Fig. REFB).We remark that the clustering that minimizes the information rate need not (and indeed, does not) provide a faithful characterization of a network's community structure, as is the goal in community detection , , . Instead, we find that optimal compressions seek to identify the group of nodes that can be combined to maximally reduce the information rate. By dividing the network into two parts – one inside the large cluster and the other outside – the challenge of compressing random walks thus resembles the graph partitioning problem , which has generated key insights about the modular structure of networks across scales . This simplification, in turn, allows us to develop analytic predictions about the properties of optimal compressions and the structures of compressible networks.
Information rate of optimal compressions: Although our framework is general, applying to any weighted, directed network (see Materials and Methods), in order to make analytic progress, here we focus on the special case of an unweighted, undirected network with adjacency matrix {{formula:1252c45f-8cd9-440e-bc0f-3339ac5af962}} . Information content of different edges: Using Eq. REF , can we predict the properties of the optimal cluster {{formula:88e79960-1c21-4a55-8860-b18c1ed9462d}} ? More broadly, can we anticipate the types of network topologies that facilitate compression? To answer these questions, it helps to group the edges in a network into three distinct categories (Fig. REFC): those connecting nodes within {{formula:02abd66d-0ca1-465b-8969-3fa401747d82}} , those connecting nodes outside of {{formula:fc117ad9-583f-4408-86f2-af1f5b2f81e2}} , and those on the boundary of {{formula:2d6bc4a1-f646-431b-85c6-15b48809dcfa}} (connecting nodes within {{formula:366a86d4-a804-406f-936e-0eac73a347ac}} to nodes outside of {{formula:183b6ccc-cd9a-45e7-8039-5e24b621a650}} ). This proportion of edges leaving the cluster is a well-studied quantity, known as the conductance or Cheeger constant of a network . Thus, networks with low conductance – such as those with modular structure and strong transitivity (the tendency for nodes to form triangles, also known as clustering) – should be highly compressible , . This is our first hypothesis about the impact of network structure on compressibility.We now consider an edge connecting two nodes {{formula:464d0273-20f6-4b3b-873f-047bd16309f8}} and {{formula:b47cc588-b12c-499b-8657-475e4aafeeb1}} outside of {{formula:d7f592c9-a306-49ed-aaf7-1195250ef74d}} , which increases the information rate by approximately {{formula:943f806d-bd13-4382-a062-d06fe83f5086}} . As before, one can show that {{formula:8d29ab5d-300a-4599-8282-7b91a7e36656}} (see Supporting Information), demonstrating that edges within the large cluster are informationally preferred to those outside the cluster. In turn, this preference for the large cluster to include as many edges as possible suggests that {{formula:58e1b765-ad13-401d-ab4e-9aaf112b94ce}} will favor high-degree nodes over low-degree nodes, which we confirm in real networks (Fig. REFE). This result leads to our second hypothesis: networks should be more compressible if they have heterogeneous degrees (or heavy-tailed degree distributions), containing “rich-clubs” of high-degree hub nodes , . Given the predictions that modular and heterogeneous topologies facilitate compression, we now propose a quantitative definition for the compressibility of a network.When analyzing optimal clusterings (that is, clusterings that minimize the information rate {{formula:f0414f07-3bb4-4921-8831-54b92197bbc8}} , Eq. 9 in the main text), we find that they tend to consist of one large cluster containing {{formula:de450c76-4310-45aa-a5bf-8a50e1e5f8f0}} nodes and {{formula:b2bc8557-92cd-4ee5-8ec4-cd4d5cfb4132}} clusters containing one node each (see Fig. 2A, B in the main text). Quantifying network compressibility: Intuitively, a network should be compressible if one can achieve a large reduction in the information rate at a given scale (Fig. REFC). However, rather than choosing a specific scale {{formula:faa2aead-bc92-48c1-b47a-cd07f15e3114}} (equivalently, a specific number of clusters {{formula:e7de99f5-43f2-453b-80af-6c08584c5009}} ), we would like our definition of compressibility to be a property of the network itself. We therefore define the compressibility of a network to be the amount of information that can be removed via compression, averaged across all scales, {{formula:1cb4b55b-3e6f-469f-a776-cce906460c78}}Visually, the compressibility represents the area above a network's rate-distortion curve (Fig. REFA). In practice, plugging our tractable upper bound on the rate-distortion curve {{formula:a98ba221-f755-492e-b900-43bb14718bf8}} into Eq. REF yields a lower bound {{formula:013dd5a3-d5dd-4c31-933e-e9d794fa5bf5}} , which (for simplicity) we will refer to as compressibility. {{figure:f11a5e32-203d-449c-adbf-9186b963b54e}}To make the notion of compressibility concrete, consider the class of random {{formula:bc7c0b97-28be-4876-b4d9-0743ae8e1a90}} -regular networks (Fig. REFB). On average, these networks have no structure (besides the requirement that nodes have uniform degree {{formula:794d97d2-421e-4286-9502-7aa45d4c34a0}} ), which allows us to derive an analytic approximation for the rate-distortion curve (see Supporting Information), {{formula:a2004155-5fc3-41fc-984c-6b89f0bcf053}}Each individual network, however, contains small structural variations, such as groups of nodes that are more tightly connected than expected. Generating random {{formula:e7b76543-afa3-4abc-aed5-05c4844e195f}} -regular networks and computing their rate-distortion curves directly, we find that optimal compressions are able to capitalize on these structural variations (see Supporting Fig. 3), thereby achieving lower information rates than the approximation in Eq. REF (Fig. REFC). By contrast, as the degree {{formula:e15995ed-abab-4fad-9dd6-309a429fb967}} increases, the networks become uniform in structure, and the analytic approximation becomes exact (Fig. REFC).Using Eq. REF , one can predict the compressibility of {{formula:dda47bf6-36fc-42ea-b38a-d07a4e6f2d5d}} -regular networks. Specifically, noting that the entropy of {{formula:4452caa9-777b-417f-8df1-e4e1445acb2e}} -regular networks is {{formula:260daaae-5d71-450a-95d6-049b0bb03d28}} (see Materials and Methods), and approximating the average in Eq. REF by an integral over {{formula:ec1502a1-3741-42eb-a5d8-e5310d33cdc7}} , we arrive at the analytic form {{formula:136b693f-ef90-4e1e-b17a-95b6767d0634}}which we verify numerically (Fig. REFD). We note that the compressibility grows logarithmically with the degree {{formula:b62a85f3-8de5-4adb-ae1a-2868a69f392b}} , reflecting the fact that networks with larger degrees have more information to be removed via compression (see Materials and Methods). Indeed, computing the compressibility of the real networks in Supporting Table 1, we find precisely the same logarithmic dependence on the average degree (Fig. REFE). Furthermore, we verify that this logarithmic dependence generalizes to directed versions of the networks (Supporting Fig. 5) and is not simply due to our clustering heuristics (Supporting Fig. 6). These results demonstrate that the compressibility of a network increases predictably with average degree. But how does compressibility depend on the topology of a complex network?
Impact of network structure on compressibility: Based on the properties of optimal compressions (Fig. REF ), we hypothesized that the compressibility of a network should increase with both (i) transitivity and (ii) degree heterogeneity. These two features are frequently observed across an array of real-world networks, from social, scientific, and biological interactions , , to the Internet , language , music , and the brain . Moreover, the combination of transitivity (with tightly-connected modules) and heterogeneous degrees (with well-connected hubs) defines hierarchical organization , which has been shown to support multi-scale representations of complex networks , and enable efficient information processing in neural and communication systems , . In fact, when encoding information about the world, the brain itself often employs hierarchical representations , , . If correct, our hypotheses will lend to these perspectives a new outlook on the role of hierarchical structure: that it supports the efficient compression of complex networks.To investigate the impact of transitivity and modular structure on compressibility, we consider a class of stochastic block networks (Fig. REFA), wherein nodes are grouped into modules of equal size and a specified fraction {{formula:483d4cb9-2b0d-4147-8ef4-82522b0746c6}} of the edges in the network connect nodes within the same module. We find that optimal compressions take advantage of this modular structure by clustering together nodes within the same module (see Supporting Fig. 3). Indeed, strengthening the modular structure – that is, increasing the fraction {{formula:4616dea5-9454-4344-a958-c2331076afeb}} of within-module edges – decreases the rate-distortion curve {{formula:b8490cbb-3498-4182-9e6b-1dc7bb5bea18}} (Fig. REFB). We therefore find that compressibility increases with both modularity (Fig. REFC) and transitivity (Fig. REFD). Importantly, these results on stochastic block networks generalize to real networks, with increases in transitivity yielding significant improvements in network compressibility (Fig. REFE).To examine the dependence of compressibility on degree heterogeneity, we study scale-free networks (Fig. REFF), which have heavy-tailed degree distributions {{formula:e74143e4-b960-42d4-9a84-c52046bbbcdb}} characterized by a power-law exponent {{formula:07871484-b502-48af-b59a-16d8ec7ceac3}} . Optimal compressions exploit this heterogeneous structure by clustering together high-degree hub nodes (see Supporting Fig. 3). As {{formula:258583db-560a-477e-ae02-19113d92c6f5}} decreases, accentuating the heterogeneity in node degrees, the rate-distortion curve {{formula:58025ea3-6816-41e4-ac76-74e454f643e1}} increases at small scales and decreases at intermediate and large scales (Fig. REFG). Both of these rate-distortion effects serve to improve the compressibility of scale-free networks (Fig. REFH). Moreover, rather than indirectly investigating the impact of heavy-tailed structure via the scale-free exponent {{formula:4da834a8-d2ba-444d-89f7-0a04ce946898}} , we can directly quantify the degree heterogeneity of a given network {{formula:5bbbf65e-6879-4847-9b5b-16e14a096eb8}} , where {{formula:fdd20293-04ae-41c1-ad07-45d964eef666}} is the absolute difference in degrees averaged over all pairs of nodes and {{formula:45e6999c-d495-4832-8341-6505a60b90bd}} is the average degree. We find that the compressibility of scale-free networks grows linearly with degree heterogeneity (Fig. REFI), a result that generalizes to real networks (Fig. REFJ). Furthermore, we confirm that the dependencies of compressibility on both transitivity and degree heterogeneity extend to directed networks (Supporting Fig. 5) and are robust to our choice of clustering heuristics (Supporting Fig. 6).Together, the above results demonstrate that transitivity and degree heterogeneity – the two defining features of hierarchical organization – increase the compressibility of complex networks. Indeed, in networks with explicit hierarchical organization (such as those examined in Ref. ), we verify that optimal compressions capitalize on both modular structure and heterogeneous degrees in order to reduce the information rate (see Supporting Fig. 3). By contrast, for networks with uniform structure (such as Erdös-Rényi or {{formula:9d72578b-4942-43fd-8fc1-ed28506115ec}} -regular networks), natural groupings of nodes do not exist (see Supporting Fig. 3), and therefore such networks are highly incompressible (Fig. REFD,I).Interestingly, by focusing on specific families of networks, we discover variations in compressibility that reflect a network's specific function. Road networks, for example, exhibit the lowest transitivity and degree heterogeneity, and therefore the lowest compressibility, among the networks studied. This low compressibility is likely due to the fact that, unlike the other networks, road networks are confined to exist in two dimensions, severely constraining their topology . Besides road networks, we find that protein interactions have the lowest transitivity and brain networks have the lowest degree heterogeneity, leading both classes of networks to be relatively incompressible. Interestingly, these two families are unique among the networks studied in that they are only encoded genetically and need not be represented cognitively by a human or animal. By contrast, language networks are highly compressible, perhaps reflecting the primary function of language as a means for encoding and communicating information. Thus, although many networks are encoded biologically, the pressure for these encodings to be efficient manifests to varying degrees in different families of networks, yielding a spectrum of compressibilities.We are now prepared to study the compressibility of directed networks. In the main text, we demonstrated that the compressibility of undirected networks increases with the logarithm of the average degree (Fig. 3E in the main text). Moreover, based on the structure of optimal clusterings (Fig. 2 in the main text), we hypothesized (and confirmed) that the compressibility of undirected networks increases with both transitivity and degree heterogeneity (Fig. 4 in the main text). Here, we demonstrate that each of these results about the impact of network structure on compressibility generalizes to directed networks.We begin by analyzing the dependence of network compressibility on average degree. For a directed network with adjacency matrix {{formula:3fcf9706-9b29-4067-bf03-1c73c1647de1}} , where {{formula:3c385e30-6019-4dee-8c81-b09b8071f325}} if there is a directed edge from node {{formula:f7f77c06-6df0-40be-9ce6-9995e5f87218}} to node {{formula:50c54dfb-b8b7-4374-b434-4b2b6b20c8a1}} , the out-(in-)degree of node {{formula:aba9ec18-9f9b-468a-9cc2-ed69cb2697da}} is given by {{formula:e45227e6-f2ac-424a-b262-a687559100ee}} ({{formula:2ca334dd-0c68-43e7-af17-c69ce9976c53}} ). Despite each node possibly having different out- and in-degrees, the average out- and in-degrees in a network are equal, since {{formula:3b4b3b9e-8c16-4fd3-b4ab-b9e3a1eb6b7b}}Therefore, even for directed networks, we can simply discuss the average degree. In Supporting Fig. REFA, we demonstrate that the compressibility {{formula:44db6245-6c57-45b0-a420-bb6f970b5451}} (Eq. REF ) of real directed networks grows logarithmically with the average degree, confirming that our prediction for undirected networks (Fig. 3D-E in the main text) extends to directed networks. {{figure:e5390d32-5c46-4c18-8645-2117dfa84223}}We now consider the impact of transitivity on the compressibility of directed networks. As in the main text, we quantify transitivity using the average clustering coefficient. For undirected networks, the clustering coefficient of a node {{formula:52a76db1-2e1d-4f4c-8768-b1e0a84c6b44}} is the number of edges connecting the neighbors of {{formula:8febde0d-2c3d-4515-8e2e-cd2321363591}} divided by the {{formula:6c67dd17-0bae-45fd-a84c-f67be5416100}} possible connections, and the average clustering coefficient is given by averaging over the nodes in a network. Although the clustering coefficient was originally defined for undirected networks, this definition has since been extended to directed networks . In a directed network, the clustering coefficient of a node {{formula:6554f485-b577-4f38-a971-febd65fdd525}} is the number of connected pairs among its {{formula:c518635d-642c-4726-a879-d21e7c9a35c4}} out- and in-neighbors divided by the {{formula:42c576fc-a62c-4541-b1af-fdb884ec4dbc}} possible connections. Just as we found for undirected networks (Fig. 4A-E in the main text), the compressibility of directed networks is significantly correlated with the average clustering coefficient (Supporting Fig. REFB), thereby indicating that transitivity and the presence of tightly-knit communities serve to make networks more compressible.Finally, we study the impact of heterogeneous (or heavy-tailed) degrees on the compressibility of directed networks. For directed networks, there are two definitions of degree heterogeneity: that of out-degrees {{formula:026514fd-57e0-4ffc-bb99-f89893e16e31}} and that of in-degrees {{formula:81434329-0de4-4d5d-acf5-a93c833d0f3f}} . We find that the compressibility of directed networks is significantly correlated with both the out-degree (Supporting Fig. REFC) and in-degree (Supporting Fig. REFD) heterogeneities. Thus, even in directed networks, heavy-tailed degree distributions with well-connected hubs serve to increase network compressibility. Together, these results demonstrate that the central conclusions from the main text generalize to directed networks; namely, that strong transitivity and degree heterogeneity – the two defining features of hierarchical organization – increase the compressibility of complex networks.
Discussion: Complex networks perform an astonishing array of functions, which are supported by a multitude of topological structures. Many networks, however, are unified by a common constraint: that they rely on biological entities to encode them and pass them on. Encoding a network efficiently – that is, striking an optimal balance between simplicity and accuracy – requires compression, an insight that has provided information-theoretic perspectives on network structure , , . Naturally, some networks should be more compressible than others, with structural regularities enabling efficient representations across multiple scales. To investigate this hypothesis, here we introduce a rate-distortion theory of network compression (Fig. REF ) and propose a quantitative definition for the compressibility of a network (Eq. REF ; Fig. REFA). Applying our framework to a number of real and model networks, we demonstrate that network compressibility increases with both transitivity and degree heterogeneity (Fig. REF ), two features that together characterize hierarchical organization .The interplay between network structure and compressibility hints at one possible factor contributing to the hierarchical organization observed in many real networks , , , , , , , , , , : that it enables efficient representations across scales. But do the actual encodings themselves – from representations in the minds of humans and animals to the information stored in the genetic code – take advantage of this hierarchical organization? Moreover, do the encodings employed in nature approach the limit of optimal efficiency specified by rate-distortion theory? Answering these questions will require new exciting investigations into the information-theoretic forces that shape complex networks.
