Clustering algorithm: To compute the rate-distortion curve {{formula:6d4daa78-7195-44bc-b032-071f20ce6264}} , we use an agglomerative clustering algorithm. Beginning with {{formula:3152b04d-5a72-431c-a62f-41ad00cc5f7e}} clusters (corresponding to the minimum scale {{formula:956afa5d-9f29-4f80-bb17-73746d422157}} ), each containing an individual node, we iteratively combine pairs of clusters until we eventually arrive at one large cluster containing the entire network (corresponding to the maximum scale {{formula:9b295650-1247-4d50-90ca-dd5f84dc4a0c}} ). At each step, we greedily select the pair of clusters to combine that minimizes the information rate {{formula:a4b0035e-bf04-476f-96be-9f7ac1c170a0}} (Eq. REF ). However, rather than searching through all {{formula:c9f879b3-af6a-48d5-b02a-97fea6c70b93}} pairs of clusters at each iteration (which would limit applications to small networks), we instead focus on a subset of {{formula:efa36b43-b2f0-4180-a571-c58d4fdc4daf}} pairs chosen through one of two heuristics.The first heuristic, motivated by the observation that optimal clusterings tend to combine clusters with large degrees (Fig. REFE), selects the {{formula:ded29028-ca77-444e-ab37-9a5b99e5229e}} pairs of clusters {{formula:784ffef3-7996-4f83-8b61-aabc58a5a431}} and {{formula:2819b59d-3e1e-48db-9ad4-db299891fb9e}} with the largest combined stationary probabilities {{formula:1990c3d8-839f-4ae3-87ae-73523d883c80}} . For unweighted, undirected networks, we note that this choice is equivalent to selecting the pairs of clusters with the largest combined degrees, since {{formula:92ce767e-6ec4-42c2-9223-b0946478ffaa}} . The second heuristic, motivated by the fact that optimal compressions tend to form clusters with tight intra-cluster connectivity (Fig. REFD), selects the pairs of clusters {{formula:05bfd24f-ff43-4b56-8171-8b6880591dd5}} and {{formula:3c90f4d3-b3fa-454a-90da-49c7bc8c8100}} with the largest combined joint transition probabilities {{formula:d97787f8-168a-4aaf-8214-d98ecaf5e1d5}} . For unweighted, undirected networks, we remark that this second heuristic is equivalent to selecting the pairs of clusters with the largest number of connecting edges, since {{formula:ca1f112a-6e2e-465d-8075-69d22c756b24}} . In practice, we consider {{formula:c374cda1-ec34-488b-9cb3-ba4da7bb44aa}} pairs of clusters at each iteration. In Supporting Fig. 1, we compare these two heuristics to the brute-force approach that searches through all pairs of clusters at each iteration of the clustering algorithm. In addition to significantly speeding up the algorithm, we find that these two heuristics often yield more accurate estimates of the rate-distortion curve {{formula:c0e169aa-eb64-4186-b3c4-d3a4ce255927}} than the brute-force implementation.

Here we sought to proactively consider choosing references that reflect the diversity of the field in thought, form of contribution, gender, and other factors. We obtained predicted gender of the first and last author of each reference by using databases that store the probability of a name being carried by a woman , . By this measure (and excluding self-citations to the first and last authors of our current paper), our references contain {{formula:703adc9b-5c29-471c-bd22-048643a9fbf2}} woman(first)/woman(last), {{formula:a5b9cff1-5489-487b-873e-52af2ffc301f}} man/woman, {{formula:7bfbb8a6-0992-4342-a376-14df0d5be15e}} woman/man, and {{formula:1f768e89-d716-4cb1-9204-33889dcb6180}} man/man. Second, we obtained predicted racial/ethnic category of the first and last author of each reference by databases that store the probability of a first and last name being carried by an author of color , . By this measure (and excluding self-citations), our references contain {{formula:ea27621e-0ddc-4758-a334-13725b92057e}} author of color(first)/author of color(last), {{formula:677d4298-60a7-4ecd-b3c2-cc242fedbd69}} white author/author of color, {{formula:ea3274ac-70a4-4259-97b0-ed034551cdfa}} author of color/white author, and {{formula:5b7a0123-67a4-468f-82e8-24567773d019}} white author/white author. Introduction: In this Supporting Information, we provide extended analysis and discussion to support the results presented in the main text. In Sec. , we discuss the information costs of the different edge types in Fig. 2C in the main text. In Sec. , we derive an analytic approximation of the rate-distortion curve for {{formula:2ef2fdf2-41aa-40ef-bee8-22540d772bfa}} -regular networks (Eq. 3 and Fig. 3C in the main text). In Sec. , we discuss the different heuristics used to speed up the clustering algorithm and compare their estimates of optimal information rates with those of a brute-force implementation. In Sec. , we demonstrate that the tractable upper bound on the rate-distortion curve {{formula:09c6cf40-716f-4ad8-9be5-8928828c0586}} used throughout the main text provides a reasonable approximation to the true rate-distortion curve. In Sec. , we study the structure of optimal compressions for the model networks analyzed in the main text. In Sec. , we demonstrate that the central results from the main text generalize to directed networks. In Sec. , we show that the dependencies of compressibility on average degree, transitivity, and degree heterogeneity do not depend on the heuristics used to speed up the clustering algorithm. Finally, in Sec. , we list the real networks analyzed in this work and describe how we sample large networks.

In the main text, we demonstrated that the compressibility of undirected networks increases with the logarithm of the average degree (Fig. 3E in the main text). Moreover, based on the structure of optimal clusterings (Fig. 2 in the main text), we hypothesized (and confirmed) that the compressibility of undirected networks increases with both transitivity and degree heterogeneity (Fig. 4 in the main text). Here, we demonstrate that each of these results about the impact of network structure on compressibility generalizes to directed networks.We begin by analyzing the dependence of network compressibility on average degree. For a directed network with adjacency matrix {{formula:3fcf9706-9b29-4067-bf03-1c73c1647de1}} , where {{formula:3c385e30-6019-4dee-8c81-b09b8071f325}} if there is a directed edge from node {{formula:f7f77c06-6df0-40be-9ce6-9995e5f87218}} to node {{formula:50c54dfb-b8b7-4374-b434-4b2b6b20c8a1}} , the out-(in-)degree of node {{formula:aba9ec18-9f9b-468a-9cc2-ed69cb2697da}} is given by {{formula:e45227e6-f2ac-424a-b262-a687559100ee}} ({{formula:2ca334dd-0c68-43e7-af17-c69ce9976c53}} ). In Supporting Fig. REFA, we demonstrate that the compressibility {{formula:44db6245-6c57-45b0-a420-bb6f970b5451}} (Eq. REF ) of real directed networks grows logarithmically with the average degree, confirming that our prediction for undirected networks (Fig. 3D-E in the main text) extends to directed networks. {{figure:e5390d32-5c46-4c18-8645-2117dfa84223}}We now consider the impact of transitivity on the compressibility of directed networks. As in the main text, we quantify transitivity using the average clustering coefficient. For undirected networks, the clustering coefficient of a node {{formula:52a76db1-2e1d-4f4c-8768-b1e0a84c6b44}} is the number of edges connecting the neighbors of {{formula:8febde0d-2c3d-4515-8e2e-cd2321363591}} divided by the {{formula:6c67dd17-0bae-45fd-a84c-f67be5416100}} possible connections, and the average clustering coefficient is given by averaging over the nodes in a network. Although the clustering coefficient was originally defined for undirected networks, this definition has since been extended to directed networks . In a directed network, the clustering coefficient of a node {{formula:6554f485-b577-4f38-a971-febd65fdd525}} is the number of connected pairs among its {{formula:c518635d-642c-4726-a879-d21e7c9a35c4}} out- and in-neighbors divided by the {{formula:42c576fc-a62c-4541-b1af-fdb884ec4dbc}} possible connections. Just as we found for undirected networks (Fig. 4A-E in the main text), the compressibility of directed networks is significantly correlated with the average clustering coefficient (Supporting Fig. REFB), thereby indicating that transitivity and the presence of tightly-knit communities serve to make networks more compressible.Finally, we study the impact of heterogeneous (or heavy-tailed) degrees on the compressibility of directed networks. For directed networks, there are two definitions of degree heterogeneity: that of out-degrees {{formula:026514fd-57e0-4ffc-bb99-f89893e16e31}} and that of in-degrees {{formula:81434329-0de4-4d5d-acf5-a93c833d0f3f}} . We find that the compressibility of directed networks is significantly correlated with both the out-degree (Supporting Fig. REFC) and in-degree (Supporting Fig. REFD) heterogeneities. Thus, even in directed networks, heavy-tailed degree distributions with well-connected hubs serve to increase network compressibility. Together, these results demonstrate that the central conclusions from the main text generalize to directed networks; namely, that strong transitivity and degree heterogeneity – the two defining features of hierarchical organization – increase the compressibility of complex networks.
Discussion: Complex networks perform an astonishing array of functions, which are supported by a multitude of topological structures. Many networks, however, are unified by a common constraint: that they rely on biological entities to encode them and pass them on. Encoding a network efficiently – that is, striking an optimal balance between simplicity and accuracy – requires compression, an insight that has provided information-theoretic perspectives on network structure , , . Naturally, some networks should be more compressible than others, with structural regularities enabling efficient representations across multiple scales. To investigate this hypothesis, here we introduce a rate-distortion theory of network compression (Fig. REF ) and propose a quantitative definition for the compressibility of a network (Eq. REF ; Fig. REFA). Applying our framework to a number of real and model networks, we demonstrate that network compressibility increases with both transitivity and degree heterogeneity (Fig. REF ), two features that together characterize hierarchical organization .The interplay between network structure and compressibility hints at one possible factor contributing to the hierarchical organization observed in many real networks , , , , , , , , , , : that it enables efficient representations across scales. But do the actual encodings themselves – from representations in the minds of humans and animals to the information stored in the genetic code – take advantage of this hierarchical organization? Moreover, do the encodings employed in nature approach the limit of optimal efficiency specified by rate-distortion theory? Answering these questions will require new exciting investigations into the information-theoretic forces that shape complex networks.

Clustering algorithm: To compute the rate-distortion curve {{formula:6d4daa78-7195-44bc-b032-071f20ce6264}} , we use an agglomerative clustering algorithm. Beginning with {{formula:3152b04d-5a72-431c-a62f-41ad00cc5f7e}} clusters (corresponding to the minimum scale {{formula:956afa5d-9f29-4f80-bb17-73746d422157}} ), each containing an individual node, we iteratively combine pairs of clusters until we eventually arrive at one large cluster containing the entire network (corresponding to the maximum scale {{formula:9b295650-1247-4d50-90ca-dd5f84dc4a0c}} ). At each step, we greedily select the pair of clusters to combine that minimizes the information rate {{formula:a4b0035e-bf04-476f-96be-9f7ac1c170a0}} (Eq. REF ). However, rather than searching through all {{formula:c9f879b3-af6a-48d5-b02a-97fea6c70b93}} pairs of clusters at each iteration (which would limit applications to small networks), we instead focus on a subset of {{formula:efa36b43-b2f0-4180-a571-c58d4fdc4daf}} pairs chosen through one of two heuristics.The first heuristic, motivated by the observation that optimal clusterings tend to combine clusters with large degrees (Fig. REFE), selects the {{formula:ded29028-ca77-444e-ab37-9a5b99e5229e}} pairs of clusters {{formula:784ffef3-7996-4f83-8b61-aabc58a5a431}} and {{formula:2819b59d-3e1e-48db-9ad4-db299891fb9e}} with the largest combined stationary probabilities {{formula:1990c3d8-839f-4ae3-87ae-73523d883c80}} . For unweighted, undirected networks, we note that this choice is equivalent to selecting the pairs of clusters with the largest combined degrees, since {{formula:92ce767e-6ec4-42c2-9223-b0946478ffaa}} . The second heuristic, motivated by the fact that optimal compressions tend to form clusters with tight intra-cluster connectivity (Fig. REFD), selects the pairs of clusters {{formula:05bfd24f-ff43-4b56-8171-8b6880591dd5}} and {{formula:3c90f4d3-b3fa-454a-90da-49c7bc8c8100}} with the largest combined joint transition probabilities {{formula:d97787f8-168a-4aaf-8214-d98ecaf5e1d5}} . For unweighted, undirected networks, we remark that this second heuristic is equivalent to selecting the pairs of clusters with the largest number of connecting edges, since {{formula:ca1f112a-6e2e-465d-8075-69d22c756b24}} . In practice, we consider {{formula:c374cda1-ec34-488b-9cb3-ba4da7bb44aa}} pairs of clusters at each iteration. In Supporting Fig. 1, we compare these two heuristics to the brute-force approach that searches through all pairs of clusters at each iteration of the clustering algorithm. In addition to significantly speeding up the algorithm, we find that these two heuristics often yield more accurate estimates of the rate-distortion curve {{formula:c0e169aa-eb64-4186-b3c4-d3a4ce255927}} than the brute-force implementation.

For networks of size {{formula:306fd1af-68ad-4b03-9c54-04c114342202}} , we perform analyses directly. For larger networks with {{formula:c525646d-5c15-4f16-aa14-462eed6c962a}} , we analyze 50 subnetworks of {{formula:35ef09cd-364b-44e1-b95a-d358c132a5e1}} nodes each. CITATION DIVERSITY STATEMENT: Recent work in several fields of science has identified a bias in citation practices such that papers from women and other minorities are under-cited relative to the number of such papers in the field , , , , , . Here we sought to proactively consider choosing references that reflect the diversity of the field in thought, form of contribution, gender, and other factors. We obtained predicted gender of the first and last author of each reference by using databases that store the probability of a name being carried by a woman , . By this measure (and excluding self-citations to the first and last authors of our current paper), our references contain {{formula:703adc9b-5c29-471c-bd22-048643a9fbf2}} woman(first)/woman(last), {{formula:a5b9cff1-5489-487b-873e-52af2ffc301f}} man/woman, {{formula:7bfbb8a6-0992-4342-a376-14df0d5be15e}} woman/man, and {{formula:1f768e89-d716-4cb1-9204-33889dcb6180}} man/man. This method is limited in that a) names, pronouns, and social media profiles used to construct the databases may not, in every case, be indicative of gender identity, and b) it cannot account for intersex, non-binary, or transgender people. Second, we obtained predicted racial/ethnic category of the first and last author of each reference by databases that store the probability of a first and last name being carried by an author of color , . By this measure (and excluding self-citations), our references contain {{formula:ea27621e-0ddc-4758-a334-13725b92057e}} author of color(first)/author of color(last), {{formula:677d4298-60a7-4ecd-b3c2-cc242fedbd69}} white author/author of color, {{formula:ea3274ac-70a4-4259-97b0-ed034551cdfa}} author of color/white author, and {{formula:5b7a0123-67a4-468f-82e8-24567773d019}} white author/white author. This method is limited in that a) names, Census entries, and Wikipedia profiles used to make the predictions may not be indicative of racial/ethnic identity, and b) it cannot account for Indigenous and mixed-race authors, or those who may face differential biases due to the ambiguous racialization or ethnicization of their names. We look forward to future work that could help us to better understand how to support equitable practices in science.
Introduction: In this Supporting Information, we provide extended analysis and discussion to support the results presented in the main text. In Sec. , we discuss the information costs of the different edge types in Fig. 2C in the main text. In Sec. , we derive an analytic approximation of the rate-distortion curve for {{formula:2ef2fdf2-41aa-40ef-bee8-22540d772bfa}} -regular networks (Eq. 3 and Fig. 3C in the main text). In Sec. , we discuss the different heuristics used to speed up the clustering algorithm and compare their estimates of optimal information rates with those of a brute-force implementation. In Sec. , we demonstrate that the tractable upper bound on the rate-distortion curve {{formula:09c6cf40-716f-4ad8-9be5-8928828c0586}} used throughout the main text provides a reasonable approximation to the true rate-distortion curve. In Sec. , we study the structure of optimal compressions for the model networks analyzed in the main text. In Sec. , we demonstrate that the central results from the main text generalize to directed networks. In Sec. , we show that the dependencies of compressibility on average degree, transitivity, and degree heterogeneity do not depend on the heuristics used to speed up the clustering algorithm. Finally, in Sec. , we list the real networks analyzed in this work and describe how we sample large networks.

Speeding up the clustering algorithm: To compute the rate-distortion curve {{formula:40e9ed44-57b2-48c7-8d39-b760873ff7b8}} for a given network, one must identify clusterings that minimize the information rate {{formula:e18676de-6f8f-4392-89c6-b9d03d17ed8e}} across all scales {{formula:fb86e870-79f0-4e5f-a3b2-3239f5dbf8bd}} (equivalently, for all numbers of clusters {{formula:b067ab44-6e7a-4441-b4a7-13f078fc13b6}} ). Here, we employ a greedy clustering algorithm that iteratively combines pairs of clusters so as to minimize the information rate (see Materials and Methods in the main text). Specifically, beginning with {{formula:d55048f4-7f8a-40f5-97bb-27d21df88d36}} clusters (one for each node in the network), we attempt to combine different pairs of clusters and compute the resulting changes to the information rate {{formula:7cb8a03e-6865-4cf0-ab95-2e9c2a6592a7}} . Combining the pair of clusters that yields the largest reduction in information rate, we arrive at a new clustering with {{formula:2c32d29f-cf3e-43aa-920c-233e6769d1bc}} clusters. Repeating this process for all numbers of clusters {{formula:b09c53d9-bbf3-4213-afdd-829de4279b5c}} , we arrive at estimates of the optimal clusterings and information rates across all scales {{formula:b914d8e0-541a-48ab-945c-f76269347714}} .A brute force implementation of this algorithm would attempt to combine all {{formula:5b74aeee-f160-4203-b0b9-3a139a1367d2}} pairs of clusters at each iteration. For each pair of clusters, one would then compute the new information rate {{formula:edc3de50-80dd-40dd-a5ea-c52eb202ddfd}}where {{formula:f45cda0b-4320-48f2-a853-372bebef5fa4}} is the stationary distribution over clusters, and {{formula:d80141c3-0ba4-4000-ac59-31ded3a5ae50}}is the conditional probability of transitioning from cluster {{formula:2e2ce9a9-505c-4c8f-be01-33bd7fbaf0bd}} to cluster {{formula:51242f67-0f39-42d2-a954-75aae9c8e35b}} . Since Eq. REF involves summing over all pairs of clusters {{formula:84678d27-0e0c-457e-b548-f421a2a48cca}} and {{formula:306234f6-e82d-419e-8f26-403745f8ebad}} , computing the information rate requires {{formula:45437ce7-bb07-4b06-a675-457ae7a7ba17}} computations. Finally, the algorithm repeats this process for all numbers of clusters {{formula:f4e15449-8ef4-49f2-b7da-62de3e66cff5}} , requiring a total of {{formula:93189435-2a29-4e9f-be7d-9dd37a5772fe}} computations. This {{formula:a79d0b76-c48b-4d1f-a0fb-077b723b6c45}} dependence limits a naïve implementation of our clustering algorithm to small networks. In what follows, we will show how to reduce this size dependence to {{formula:2f6954a3-7a5f-4b82-ada3-f5049ff698df}} , significantly improving the efficiency of the algorithm and enabling applications to networks of reasonable size.

Heuristics for cluster selection: In the naïve implementation of the clustering algorithm, one searches through all {{formula:af5f9d3d-32f5-4c51-9a2d-e303b93ebc04}} pairs of clusters at each iteration to find the pair whose combination yields the largest decrease in the information rate. Here, we instead propose two heuristics for selecting a subset of {{formula:218fd6aa-9bb5-44df-b546-0e1e0ba88fc5}} pairs of clusters at each iteration, thereby reducing the number of pairs from {{formula:9875dc31-d867-4351-8110-0848b68d515b}} to {{formula:d9bc1250-f2df-4ff7-8e56-fc14540722a0}} . For all results here and in the main text, we consider {{formula:88dde003-13f3-430c-9cda-3d3c5fb5cada}} pairs of clusters at each iteration of the clustering algorithm.The first heuristic is motivated by the observation that optimal clusterings tend to include one large cluster with high-degree nodes (Fig. 2E in the main text). In undirected networks, the stationary distribution over clusters is proportional to the cluster degrees, such that {{formula:645c7282-1660-48bc-8727-a2bc83455e7d}} , where {{formula:b27836a5-c66b-4a90-aacb-8678546607d2}} is the degree of cluster {{formula:2dc59f4b-f301-4940-b377-47d74a27b1be}} and {{formula:433a84b5-995a-4d62-ac3f-602f8c11f014}} is the number of edges in the network. We therefore select the {{formula:6a0d8de5-dd10-42eb-8c70-f017aac99ebc}} pairs of clusters {{formula:0da22c6b-7ea4-4e50-8ee2-3d58cf8db41c}} and {{formula:e319afc2-d6db-4329-9608-ebee5229f46a}} with the largest combined stationary probabilities {{formula:975b2ec6-00b1-42c8-9adc-7862d68c9a15}} ; for undirected networks, this process is equivalent to selecting the pairs of clusters with the largest combined degrees {{formula:64ff4448-39c9-451b-b326-51e9c4d0989f}} .The second heuristic is motivated by the observation that the one large cluster tends to include nodes that are tightly connected to one another (Fig. 2D in the main text). In undirected networks, the joint transition probability from one cluster {{formula:eb542e81-8a79-4c23-8d77-3084d17cc2f9}} to another {{formula:d227fbb6-e4d4-4f6e-a5da-4f1a9f9ddcca}} is proportional to the number of edges between the clusters, such that {{formula:317421ee-cf4a-4542-a469-ccc61723fe1b}} , where {{formula:e4ff07e9-c7cf-4d34-bd6f-86e7415c86e1}} is the number of edges connecting nodes in {{formula:971cb724-0483-4547-ab2f-2a4f0e64f258}} to nodes in {{formula:3cd86a4b-3572-4bd0-b4f0-fd23dc1cfcf4}} . We therefore select the {{formula:df6c7a7d-ef80-4a7d-bd23-4986946a2989}} pairs of clusters {{formula:7d2df727-9e7e-4c62-a719-d68ff3b8e5f4}} and {{formula:faaf8bc1-7051-4f3d-a3f1-af9e77500739}} with the largest joint transition probabilities {{formula:0699ddcf-5782-400f-a6ce-45f84908b4dd}} ; for undirected networks, this process is equivalent to selecting the pairs of clusters with the largest number of connecting edges {{formula:1db927d3-36a4-4fc1-b185-94c5aea35752}} .To evaluate the performance of these two heuristics, we compare the rate-distortion curves for the real networks in Supporting Table 1 computed using (i) the brute-force approach that attempts to combine all pairs of clusters, (ii) the stationary distribution heuristic, and (iii) the joint transition probability heuristic. Since each algorithm computes an upper bound on the rate-distortion curve {{formula:f2365c63-1468-48ab-b9d7-4bb1fe26398c}} for a given network, whichever algorithm returns a smaller upper bound will have achieved a more accurate estimate of the true rate-distortion curve {{formula:d3068f9b-4c79-466c-bcc8-2b8e1e69d8cb}} . Consider, for example, the social network of bottlenose dolphins . For scales {{formula:64bea84a-df77-4498-9a6c-0488e48fc0cc}} , we find that the stationary distribution heuristic provides a lower (and thus more accurate) upper bound on the rate-distortion curve {{formula:814d5a61-c71b-4072-b0b6-d0b91525245a}} than both the brute-force algorithm and the joint transition probability heuristic (Supporting Fig. REFA). By contrast, for scales {{formula:04807ace-a404-4710-bd93-0cc0f171fbc1}} , the joint transition probability heuristic provides the most accurate estimate of the rate-distortion curve (Supporting Fig. REFA). Notably, even though both heuristics only consider a limited set of cluster pairs, they both produce rate-distortion estimates that are comparable in accuracy to, if not more accurate than, the brute-force approach that searches through all pairs at each iteration. {{figure:bc5b82fd-c7c8-4bc3-92e9-bcd888313bb4}}To compare the accuracy of the different algorithms (that is, to determine which algorithm provides a lower upper bound {{formula:19ae4b6c-9d51-414e-a474-2934a16dbb5d}} across all scales) we can compare their compressibility estimates, {{formula:ee8f1f3a-0447-4092-ac96-34b6e8a7986f}}If one algorithm produces a lower (that is, more accurate) rate-distortion estimate {{formula:b57b3eb9-9236-4052-ac93-27538ebc63f4}} on average across all scales {{formula:7aa105ce-3610-4abd-8d46-c01cc23539ed}} , then one will arrive at a larger lower bound on the compressibility {{formula:89538c7d-a829-4c90-b224-174b7f124a78}} . In Supporting Fig. REFB, we see that the compressibility computed using the stationary distribution heuristic {{formula:d5b7bd55-fd9c-4185-87dd-a4426e75b935}} is almost always as large as (if not larger than) that computed using all pairs of clusters {{formula:a8651de4-940f-4129-b425-987078d7cfdb}} for the real networks in Supporting Table 1. Similarly, in Supporting Fig. REFC we see the joint transition probability heuristic provides compressibility estimates {{formula:f15c274d-98a6-4645-a016-c99921d64646}} that are nearly as accurate as {{formula:d0f91085-47e1-467b-be40-4619e194a21e}} across most of the real networks. In fact, the brute-force compressibility estimates {{formula:e996d60a-3a22-4f79-8721-321fa378d1d8}} are significantly larger (that is, more accurate) than both of the heuristic estimates {{formula:cbc7567a-78bf-4fee-a9da-d415825154fb}} and {{formula:f97ad882-5576-42a5-a9f2-8bfce17d4748}} for only 10 of the 69 real networks.Together, these results demonstrate that the two cluster-selection heuristics provide rate-distortion estimates that are comparable, if not more accurate, than the brute-force clustering algorithm. Moreover, these heuristics reduce the search for an optimal pair of clusters at each iteration from {{formula:baf54633-efac-4a6e-bf72-5df96879f492}} pairs to {{formula:4cefe4cc-1e00-4f8a-94cf-a8421d67d51d}} pairs. In combination with the speed-up in Sec. , this reduces the total run-time of the clustering algorithm from {{formula:09d2b1b4-4dff-4973-9e61-e0f50e14d8f4}} to {{formula:fcfd553e-18c2-4889-b87d-7ce1705c89d0}} , thereby allowing applications to networks of reasonable size.
Errors in information bounds: In the main text, rather than computing the information rate {{formula:bb4c553d-44f4-42ba-b5ee-88c97f48720f}} of a given clustering directly, we instead consider a tractable upper bound {{formula:c7d1e8a1-df25-4cf5-bcbe-0794ba9a590e}} (see Materials and Methods in the main text). For a given network, we minimize {{formula:9b976c73-2ceb-4a4b-b324-1d179cb45a4d}} across all scales to arrive at an upper bound on the rate-distortion curve {{formula:1e8e060c-440f-4ffa-8ca4-9ac4e8c6d9b8}} , which we then use to compute a lower bound {{formula:30079e28-bd2c-4b02-9e20-89f95c500937}} on the compressibility (Eq. REF ). The upper bound {{formula:f215e2d4-df7c-4497-a679-221fad4635b2}} on the rate-distortion curve and the corresponding lower bound {{formula:9c686a90-78b9-47a3-afb8-3a9f6f6726a0}} on the compressibility together form the basis of our main results (Figs. 3 and 4 in the main text). Therefore, it is important to verify that these bounds provide reasonable approximations to the true rate-distortion curves {{formula:acc94487-fb98-4678-b8e0-3d30e53fa91d}} and compressibilities {{formula:f97b0ed5-eb49-4160-ad47-47da8fef5f9c}} of the networks analyzed in the main text.To investigate the accuracy of the upper bound on the rate-distortion curve {{formula:4f48a2a1-3c96-4526-a963-93d50744d3ce}} , we consider a tractable lower bound {{formula:8aaa65f5-0ea0-4e5a-a5c8-7b05b5d2c387}} (see Materials and Methods in the main text). Importantly, the true rate-distortion curve {{formula:12028f9e-87a6-451d-9a1b-98085eeeb467}} lies between the upper and lower bounds, such that {{formula:4a70026b-b2e0-4cf5-8683-7f80b4fa72a6}} . Thus, the error in the upper bound ({{formula:2e8cecfd-ca0e-442f-b68f-341d2b0cfdb2}} ) is no larger than the difference between the upper and lower bounds ({{formula:b4f60c31-0b6b-48d5-81a3-30dbf065b967}} ). Put simply, if the difference {{formula:7fffa9da-fbeb-4b9b-9468-0153ac49d87b}} between the bounds is small, then we know that the error {{formula:5456b5a4-6713-41b6-8099-c99c2256a45e}} is even smaller. {{figure:2c913870-6036-4226-bbcf-45da99e9c831}}For all networks, one can show that the upper and lower bounds are equal (and therefore exact) at both the minimum scale {{formula:bc7dc970-de89-4a6a-94e5-5111c4ffbdf1}} and the maximum scale {{formula:9d683202-7b60-4934-96a2-850193c6c78f}} (see Materials and Methods in the main text). Moreover, in the main text, we demonstrated for Zachary's karate club that the upper bound {{formula:a731511d-ad4d-4231-98d5-b2d745e991f9}} remains close to the lower bound {{formula:7fa7845b-a2d0-43b9-8581-04e40946bb1a}} across all intermediate scales (Fig. 2A in the main text). In order to compare the rate-distortion bounds across different networks, here we normalize {{formula:7e4a6480-b3f1-41c9-b3ad-5cc2c9264d24}} and {{formula:6506b038-4426-4283-a636-bff9b35121f4}} by the entropy {{formula:3c1ea15d-794e-4045-a2fc-24e70210c173}} of each network. Notably, we find that a tight correspondence between the upper and lower bounds is not unique to Zachary's karate club, but instead is a general feature of the real networks in Supporting Table 1 (Supporting Fig. REFA). Indeed, the maximum difference {{formula:03aac421-0bad-4d0e-ada6-16501d696e2d}} between the upper and lower bounds tends to only reach about 10% of the entropy of a network (Supporting Fig. REFB). For comparison, the difference between bounds is actually larger in Zachary's karate club (reaching 15% of the entropy) than the typical network in Supporting Table 1 (Supporting Fig. REFB). These results establish that the upper bound {{formula:2db69fc0-c848-46cd-8da2-a63efec9665b}} provides a good approximation to the true rate-distortion curve {{formula:937045ec-d67b-4b94-be84-e49fcb8f97a9}} .We now investigate the accuracy of the lower bound {{formula:27fc20f5-b762-4841-9ece-5bf704e64e5d}} on the compressibility (Eq. REF ). To do so, we consider the upper bound {{formula:5a6619d3-c819-4322-a6e3-22dd25e7d0d5}} on the compressibility induced by the lower bound {{formula:ae50e803-eaac-4ebe-86e5-47b4a335f1de}} on the rate-distortion curve. We find that the lower bound {{formula:c458343c-823b-46f7-86e7-018b02e0783c}} remains close to the upper bound {{formula:31c21b01-3262-4175-9364-d765c0dec217}} across almost all networks in Supporting Table 1 (Supporting Fig. REFC). For comparison, Zachary's karate club exhibits a difference {{formula:6ff9a581-fe6d-4139-ac21-63f3836573d1}} that is typical for the networks in Supporting Table 1 (Supporting Fig. REFC, right). Interestingly, among the five outliers with an abnormally large difference {{formula:21f4f071-201a-4b10-aff7-c7398403050f}} , four are the road networks in Supporting Table 1 (Supporting Fig. REFC, right). As discussed in the main text, the abnormal compression properties of road networks likely reflects the unique physical constraints on their structure. Together, the results of this section verify that the upper bound {{formula:919d8781-46d9-4938-beb2-75d04f256c4a}} on the rate-distortion curve and the corresponding lower bound {{formula:1dfb8929-afe9-4c11-8716-df9157a4ff42}} on the compressibility provide reasonable estimates of the true information properties of the real networks analyzed in the main text.
Compressing model networks: In our investigations of network compressibility, we analyzed a number of model networks, including Erdös-Rényi, {{formula:5390847a-70c3-4432-a63a-b118dee41147}} -regular (Fig. 3B in the main text), stochastic block (Fig. 4A in the main text), and scale-free (Fig. 4F in the main text) networks. Here, we study the structure of optimal compressions in these model networks, as well as networks with hierarchical structure, wherein small tightly-connected groups of nodes connect to form larger, but looser groups .To recall, based on the information content of different edges (see Sec. ), we predicted that optimal compressions would tend to maximize the number of edges within the one large cluster and minimize the number of edges on the boundary and outside of the cluster. In the main text, we confirmed these predictions for the real networks in Supporting Table 1 (see Fig. 2 in the main text). In Supporting Fig. REF , we verify that these results extend to all of the model networks listed above.First, across all model networks considered, we find that the edges emanating from the one large cluster tend to connect to nodes within the cluster (Supporting Fig. REFA) and avoid crossing over to nodes outside of the cluster (Supporting Fig. REFB). Interestingly, we observe stark differences in the properties of optimal compressions between different network models. For example, although Erdös-Rényi and {{formula:2b859367-a118-4b99-971a-90c6f1846796}} -regular networks do not contain large-scale structure, optimal compressions are still able to identify groups of nodes that are slightly more strongly connected to each other than to the rest of the network. Meanwhile, optimal compressions in stochastic block, scale-free, and hierarchical networks identify groups of nodes with much stronger within-group connectivity. In fact, for stochastic block networks, it is clear that optimal compressions identify the built-in modules, with the one large cluster iteratively enveloping each module one by one as the scale increases (Supporting Fig. REFA-B). {{figure:dac415ef-f36c-47f4-a889-799b55bf02a0}}Second, for Erdös-Rényi, scale-free, and hierarchical networks, we confirm that optimal compressions select groups of nodes with higher degrees than average (Supporting Fig. REFC) while omitting low-degree nodes (Supporting Fig. REFD). As expected, this effect is much stronger in scale-free and hierarchical networks (which exhibit large heterogeneities in node degree) than in Erdös-Rényi networks (which do not contain large-scale structure). We remark that in {{formula:b191ffe5-deed-4c90-870e-fafcae1a34a4}} -regular networks, there are no differences in node degrees by definition. Similarly, for stochastic block networks, we find a negligible difference between the degrees of nodes inside versus outside the large cluster. This final result once again suggests that optimal compressions in stochastic block networks focus on their modular, rather than heterogeneous, structure. Together, the results of this section demonstrate that the structure of optimal compressions observed in real networks (Fig. 2 in the main text) extends to a range of model networks. Moreover, for hierarchical networks, we establish that optimal compressions cluster together groups of nodes that are more tightly connected than scale-free networks (Supporting Fig. REFA), yet higher in degree than stochastic block networks (Supporting Fig. REFC), thereby capitalizing on both the modular and heterogeneous properties of hierarchical organization.
Directed networks: In the main text, in order to develop analytic predictions for the structure of optimal clusterings and the impact of network structure on compressibility, we focused on the special case of undirected networks. Specifically, we predicted (and confirmed) that optimal compressions would tend to maximize the number of edges within the one large cluster and minimize the number of edges on the boundary and outside of the cluster (Fig. 2D-E in the main text). In turn, these findings led to the predictions that network compressibility (Eq. REF ) should increase with both modular structure and heavy-tailed degrees, which we confirmed in undirected real and model networks (Fig. 4 in the main text). Here we demonstrate that these central results from the main text are not limited to undirected networks, but in fact generalize to directed networks.
Structure of optimal compressions: Our clustering algorithm described in the main text is general, applying to any weighted, directed network. We can therefore use the algorithm to compute optimal compressions and rate-distortion curves {{formula:b245faf7-6953-4173-96c6-3cd2dd2c6c00}} for the directed real networks listed in Supporting Table 1. We remark that among the 69 real networks studied in the main text, 38 have directed versions (see Supporting Table 1), which we analyze here.As was the case for undirected networks (Fig. 2B in the main text), we find that optimal compressions in directed networks tend to form one large cluster with the maximum possible size {{formula:1c45171c-a917-4d59-8677-b4e4e50b707c}} , where {{formula:a8da06f0-08c5-40d3-b156-02b003425883}} is the scale of description, and {{formula:2959d96a-7217-4437-b1b1-916c04966708}} minimal clusters containing one node each (Supporting Fig. REFA). To analyze the structure of the large cluster, in the main text we divided the edges in an undirected network into three categories (Fig. 2C in the main text): those within the cluster, those outside of the cluster, and those on the cluster boundary. For directed networks, we can further divide boundary edges into two categories – those connecting from inside to outside the cluster and those connecting from outside to inside the cluster – thereby resulting in a total of four edge types (Supporting Fig. REFB). {{figure:ed5f089f-fab7-43ae-b2ac-dbb0e336ccb0}}For undirected networks, in the main text we demonstrated that the one large cluster had tight within-cluster connectivity (maximizing the number of edges inside the cluster) and sparse connectivity to the rest of the network (minimizing the number of boundary edges; Fig. 2D in the main text). Indeed, this result generalizes to directed networks, with the one large cluster favoring within-cluster edges over both outgoing (Supporting Fig. REFC) and incoming (Supporting Fig. REFD) boundary edges. In the main text, we also demonstrated that the one large cluster sought to include high-degree nodes and exclude low-degree nodes in undirected networks (Fig. 2E in the main text). Here, we confirm that this result also applies to directed networks, with the one large cluster containing nodes with both larger out-degrees (Supporting Fig. REFE) and in-degrees (Supporting Fig. REFF) than the rest of the network. Together, these results establish that our predictions about the structure of optimal compressions (see Sec. ) generalize to directed networks.
Robustness to clustering heuristics: In the main text, we computed rate-distortion curves {{formula:10a7ea9c-d9cd-446e-bd29-cc25e6661d6d}} using our clustering algorithm with the pair-selection heuristics described in Sec. . We found that network compressibility increased with average degree (Fig. 3D-E in the main text), transitivity (quantified by average clustering coefficient; Fig. 4D-E in the main text), and degree heterogeneity (Fig. 4I-J in the main text). Here, we confirm that these results are not simply due to our choices of clustering heuristics. To do so, we recompute the compressibilities {{formula:fbd981e0-2dd4-4997-8c55-9c9e06617b26}} of the networks in Supporting Table 1 using the brute-force implementation of our clustering algorithm that searches through all pairs of clusters at each iteration (see Sec. ). We remark that, in order to employ the brute-force implementation, for each network of size {{formula:44b64790-a419-41ab-ae3f-54434a01c266}} we analyze 50 randomly-sampled subnetworks of 100 nodes each. Using the brute-force algorithm, we confirm that the compressibility increases with average degree (Supporting Fig. REFA), transitivity (Supporting Fig. REFB), and degree heterogeneity (Supporting Fig. REFC). These observations demonstrate that the central results from the main text are robust to our choice of pair-selection heuristic in the clustering algorithm. {{figure:5768c0ce-777e-4063-b875-ea4d37994475}}
Network datasets and processing: The real-world networks analyzed in the main text are listed and briefly described in Supporting Table 1. The web, citation, animal, semantic, social, protein, flight, and road networks are gathered from online network repositories. The language and music networks were generated by the authors previously (see below) . The brain networks are generated from structural and functional data gathered and analyzed previously (see below) , .For the language networks, we developed code to (i) remove punctuation and white space, (ii) filter words by their part of speech, and (iii) record the transitions between the filtered words . Here we focus on networks of transitions between nouns, noting that the same methods can be used to record transitions between other parts of speech. The raw text was gathered from Project Gutenberg (gutenberg.org/wiki/Main_Page). {{figure:a01df40e-e765-4309-b673-75add2b1015e}}{{figure:26877179-e1ea-4bf5-8b67-e9fda54d2d9b}}For the music networks, we read in audio files in MIDI format using the readmidi function in MATLAB (R2018a). For each song, we split the notes by their channel, which represents the different instruments. For each channel, we created a network of note transitions. We then create a transition network representing the entire song by aggregating the transitions between notes across the different channels. The MIDI files were gathered from midiworld.com and from kunstderfuge.com. Our code and data are available upon request from the corresponding author.For the brain networks, we study the structural and functional connectivity of five randomly-selected subjects from the Human Connectome Project . For all subjects, the brain is divided into 100 predefined cortical regions . The structural connectivity networks reflect physical white-matter tracts between brain regions measured using diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). We threshold the structural networks to only include connections between regions that are stronger than the mean. The functional connectivity networks reflect Pearson correlations between regional brain activity. Specifically, the activity is defined by blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) functional magnetic resonance imagining (fMRI) signals. To ensure that the functional networks have approximately the same edge density as the structural networks, we threshold the functional networks to only include connections stronger than the mean plus one standard deviation.

questionDraft: How do the structural properties of recently quenched cluster galaxies at z~1 explain the morphological transition from disk-dominated to early-type galaxies in the post-starburst evolutionary sequence without requiring major mergers?
question: How do the structural properties of recently quenched cluster galaxies at z~1 explain the morphological transition from disk-dominated to early-type galaxies in the post-starburst evolutionary sequence without requiring major mergers?
answerWithPaperReferences: [Paper A] identifies an evolutionary sequence in which post-starburst galaxies progress from blue, disk-dominated Hδ-strong systems to green-valley E+A galaxies and finally to red-sequence, early-type pure E+A galaxies. A central puzzle raised by [Paper A] is that this transition occurs despite a lack of disturbed morphologies or merger signatures, implying that the change from disk-dominated to elliptical cannot be driven by stellar redistribution from major mergers. [Paper B] provides a resolution by studying recently quenched cluster galaxies at z~1, which are found to have symmetric, undisturbed stellar continua but lie on a distinct stellar mass–size relation with high Sersic indices indicative of bulge-dominated light profiles. Through disc-fading toy models, [Paper B] demonstrates that outside-in fading of a star-forming disk—caused by quenching processes such as ram-pressure stripping or strangulation—can produce the observed contraction in galaxy size and the increase in bulge dominance without altering the underlying stellar distribution. This supports the hypothesis that the post-starburst morphological transition is driven by the rapid fading of the disk, making the bulge appear relatively brighter and the galaxy resemble an early-type system, without invoking major mergers.
answerWithoutPaperReferences: Post-starburst galaxies follow an evolutionary sequence from blue, disk-dominated systems with residual star formation to fully quenched, red-sequence early-type galaxies. A key puzzle in this sequence is that the morphological transition from disk to elliptical occurs despite a lack of disturbed morphologies or merger signatures, suggesting that stellar redistribution is not the cause. Studies of recently quenched cluster galaxies at z~1 provide a solution: these galaxies have symmetric, undisturbed stellar distributions but lie on a distinct mass–size relation with high Sersic indices indicative of bulge-dominated light profiles. Disc-fading toy models demonstrate that outside-in fading of the disk—where quenching processes such as ram-pressure stripping or strangulation remove gas and halt star formation in the disk preferentially—can cause the disk to fade rapidly while the bulge remains bright. This makes the galaxy appear smaller and more bulge-dominated, effectively mimicking an early-type morphology without altering the underlying stellar distribution, thereby explaining the morphological transition in the post-starburst phase without invoking major mergers.
isNotSingleHop: The question is not single-hop because answering it requires first knowing from Paper A that a morphological transition from disk-dominated to early-type galaxies exists in the post-starburst evolutionary sequence and that it lacks merger signatures. It then requires the specific observational evidence and disc-fading models from recently quenched cluster galaxies in Paper B to explain how this transition occurs. Paper A alone only speculates about disk fading without providing observational support or quantitative modeling, while Paper B alone discusses disc fading in cluster post-starburst galaxies but does not frame it as the resolution to the specific low-redshift evolutionary sequence puzzle. Both papers are necessary to connect the puzzle to its explanation.
bridgeAnswerPaperText:
First 31153 characters: HST/WFC3 grism observations of $z\sim1$ clusters: evidence for evolution in the mass-size relation of quiescent galaxies from poststarburst galaxies
abstract: Minor mergers have been proposed as the driving mechanism for the size growth of quiescent galaxies with decreasing redshift. The process whereby large star-forming galaxies quench and join the quiescent population at the large size end has also been suggested as an explanation for this size growth. Given the clear association of quenching with clusters, we explore this mechanism by studying the structural properties of 23 spectroscopically identified recently quenched (or "poststarburst" (PSB)) cluster galaxies at $z\sim1$. Despite clear PSB spectral signatures implying rapid and violent quenching, 87\% of these galaxies have symmetric, undisturbed morphologies in the stellar continuum. Remarkably, they follow a mass-size relation lying midway between the star-forming and quiescent field relations, with sizes $0.1$ dex smaller than $z\sim1$ star-forming galaxies at log$(M_{*}/M_{\odot})=10.5$. This implies a rapid change in the light profile without directly effecting the stellar distribution, suggesting changes in the mass-to-light ratio gradients across the galaxy are responsible. We develop fading toy models to explore how star-forming galaxies move across the mass-size plane as their stellar populations fade to match those of the PSBs. "Outside-in" fading has the potential to reproduce the contraction in size and increase in bulge-dominance observed between star-forming and PSB cluster galaxies. Since cluster PSBs lie on the large size end of the quiescent mass-size relation, and our previous work shows cluster galaxies are smaller than field galaxies, the sizes of quiescent galaxies must grow both from the quenching of star-forming galaxies and dry minor mergers.
Introduction: Quiescent galaxies have been observed to grow disproportionately more in size than stellar mass with decreasing redshift (e.g. , , , , , , , , , , ). This has been a topic of debate for many studies, with a variety of physical processes suggested for the cause. So far, it has been found that major mergers (equal-mass mergers) lead to a proportionate increase in the stellar mass and size of a galaxy. If this were the mechanism driving galaxy size growth, it would lead to a larger number of high mass galaxies than have been observed , , , .Two processes have emerged that can successfully explain the growth trend of quiescent galaxies with decreasing redshift. The first is the minor mergers (mergers between two galaxies that have a mass ratio of {{formula:a8f4227e-ce92-4122-a4ee-050fd059475a}} 10:1 or in some cases {{formula:7ec20b11-4985-4f26-a899-016247e225e8}} 3:1) hypothesis of size growth , , , , , . In this scenario, quiescent galaxies can grow disproportionately more in size than stellar mass, approximately of the form {{formula:9b9e9bb8-2020-4cdf-b82c-46c3cc16b45e}} , , . The second process is the addition of recently quenched galaxies to the quiescent population with decreasing redshift , . Star-forming galaxies on average have larger sizes than quiescent galaxies at fixed stellar mass and redshift. Furthermore, their sizes at fixed stellar mass increase with decreasing redshift (e.g. ). Hence when star-forming galaxies quench, they join the quiescent population of galaxies at the large size end of the distribution. This process predicts that age gradients as a function of size should exist for quiescent galaxies, whereby larger quiescent galaxies are younger than smaller quiescent galaxies at fixed stellar mass. Several studies have found evidence both for (e.g. , ) and against (e.g. , , ) this age gradient existing.Recently, used the cluster environment as a laboratory to test whether minor mergers can explain the majority of the size growth observed in quiescent galaxies residing in the field environment. Galaxies in high density environments such as clusters have higher peculiar velocities compared to galaxies residing in low density environments. Consequently, satellite galaxies in clusters rarely collide with one another and merge , . This merger suppression ( and references therein) makes growth via minor mergers in clusters a rarity. By measuring the average difference in size between cluster and field galaxies at {{formula:40365284-3575-43fa-b8aa-ffa2c91defeb}} in , it was found that cluster galaxies are on average smaller than field galaxies at fixed stellar mass. Other works similar to have found a wide range of results. Early-type galaxies at low redshift ({{formula:75466a38-a5ef-48a3-8d54-374b2dd6e1c6}} ) are often found to exhibit no significant difference in size at fixed stellar mass with environment (e.g. , , , , , ). However, some studies have found evidence for early-type galaxies being smaller in clusters compared to the field at low redshift (e.g. , ). At intermediate to high redshifts ({{formula:120e9e82-c6a5-466b-a883-280017f5b7d1}} ), early-type galaxies are more often found to be larger in clusters at fixed stellar mass (e.g. , , , , , , ). A summary of results from these studies and many others that have been conducted since 2009 are collated in Appendix A of . The magnitude of the size difference measured in was found to be consistent with the size growth cluster galaxies would have undergone if they had remained in the field rather than accreted on to their clusters at the time most of the mass in their clusters was assembled. This result suggested that minor mergers could indeed be responsible for the dramatic size growth observed in the quiescent field population of galaxies. However, what is now required is evidence for whether or not recently quenched galaxies contribute to this observed size growth.In this study, we investigate whether the addition of recently quenched cluster galaxies – also known as “poststarburst" (PSB) galaxies in the literature – can lead to an increase in the average size of quiescent cluster galaxies with decreasing redshift. We do this by comparing the position of 23 spectroscopically confirmed recently quenched cluster galaxies on the stellar mass–size relation to the position of the star-forming and quiescent cluster members. Our size measurements for the cluster sample come from Hubble Space Telescope (HST), Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3) F140W imaging of ten clusters at {{formula:0e2fde1e-5a26-48bd-b1d3-9462fde7cf84}} drawn from the GCLASS survey. This sample represents the largest sample of spectroscopically confirmed cluster galaxies at {{formula:b3bb5cc3-874a-4770-8240-58ced7f99fb1}} to-date.This paper is organised as follows. In Section we describe our data and the sample of recently quenched cluster galaxies. Section discusses the F140W direct images of the recently quenched galaxies and what clues this provides for the quenching mechanism(s) responsible. The position of the recently quenched cluster galaxies on the stellar mass–size relation is presented and studied in Section . A more thorough analysis of their morphology with respect to other cluster members is then studied in Section . In Section , we investigate if the distinct properties of the recently quenched galaxies in GCLASS can aid in explaining their evolutionary path on the mass–size plane. We discuss the implications of our findings in Section and summarise in Section .All magnitudes quoted are in the AB system and we assume a {{formula:56659b72-a995-4453-bf62-89110afcff04}} CDM cosmology with {{formula:dd321439-e025-4230-a317-c3c003eede62}} , {{formula:d5f10cda-307d-4239-b689-af6cbde9125e}} and {{formula:5256f177-f411-4b60-bf38-d90de183844c}} kms{{formula:8da52600-a653-4bde-8bf6-7f3d373c77ea}} Mpc{{formula:f5adca5d-a0c3-44aa-8408-2df805e70af5}} .

PSB sample: The PSBs form part of the sample of cluster galaxies that were spectroscopically confirmed as part of the GCLASS survey (see Section REF ). As part of a study into the effects of environment and stellar mass on galaxy properties, the PSBs were identified as recently quenched star-forming galaxies based on features in their GMOS spectra. These were identified from 9 of the 10 clusters, since the rest-frame wavelength coverage of the spectra for the 10th cluster were limited to {{formula:e3dc33f7-d778-40e1-9b40-fe4e53709c86}} Å due to its high redshift. The spectra were taken with the R150 grating, giving a spectral resolution of {{formula:5fde540b-e3c8-44b5-b60a-ce412dc4ad92}} . In the rest-frame, this corresponds to a spectral resolution of {{formula:1f7a124b-c3a1-463e-a0b1-4fac7f578267}} Å, and is sufficient for identifying absorption lines. The wavelength coverage of the spectra are {{formula:21a2c5d3-99d9-4798-ae77-f48a6654294b}} Å {{formula:6c87f4f6-e71b-4d94-82d7-7fc22695cca9}}, corresponding to {{formula:0c9bcfe6-850f-4141-a250-26f19fb18924}} Å{{formula:94ecb1fb-8511-40b7-b5de-15e825143b3c}} in the rest-frame. For full details on the GMOS spectra, we refer the reader to .The criteria for the poststarburst classification was chosen to select galaxies similar to K+A galaxies which are identified from rest-frame optical spectra in the literature , , , , . Despite there being no strict definition for these galaxies, they are usually defined by their spectral properties, as having an absence of emission lines, but strong Balmer line absorption (EW(H{{formula:93abeb94-d63f-4fed-8feb-2cd2a6fb7002}} ){{formula:13a6fc00-eccc-43a8-b8d7-84a6b6a7c6fd}} Å). The H{{formula:4426e3bc-d682-40fa-a100-335b58fe1274}} absorption feature that is required in the K+A classification has weak equivalent widths of 2-7Å. The signal-to-noise ratio of most galaxies in GCLASS at {{formula:82ca0e29-518d-4f11-afc6-bfe24d723f1c}} make it difficult to detect reliably. This line is also further weakened by the contamination of many sky lines. Consequently for GCLASS, {{formula:ec919205-f681-4a3c-af28-3456615b8cea}} was used since it is correlated with EW(H{{formula:1a42485d-d09f-411c-9abb-536e9e77d886}} ) . {{formula:a3488ce6-5344-445c-8a69-f1083136f89e}} is defined as the strength of the 4000Å break in spectra. For the GMOS PSB spectra, it is measured by taking the ratio of the flux in the red continuum at 4000-4100Å to that in the blue continuum at 3850-3950Å , . The GCLASS PSBs were therefore defined as those galaxies with an absence of [OII] emission and {{formula:0c505896-b383-4288-846b-76e293ece800}} in their GMOS spectra. A stacked spectrum of the cluster galaxies that met this criteria revealed a spectrum very similar to that of a K+A galaxy, suggesting that the average galaxy selected by this criteria is a K+A galaxy. For more details on the PSB classification process, we refer the reader to .The stacked spectrum from GMOS, along with the stacked spectrum obtained from the G141 grism for the PSBs is shown in Figure REF . The grism spectra were taken with the WFC3 G141 grism on board the HST. These spectra have a resolution of {{formula:d17e03e1-5538-4509-aff6-2e1f546c8351}} and a wavelength coverage of {{formula:44e3395b-2f0e-4c55-92a5-98ed656cb5a6}} Å {{formula:8b4ba25d-e728-4202-9140-163f6b8c7a19}}. Raw grism spectra are two-dimensional, providing a spatially-resolved spectrum of each object in the field-of-view (see Figure 1 of for example). One-dimensional spectra can be obtained from these and stacked. 13 of the 23 PSBs presented in this study had grism spectra with good enough quality (no contamination from neighbouring objects and more than half the grism spectrum available) such that they could be stacked. 28 PSBs were used for the stacked spectrum in the optical, of which 5 are not in the HST fields-of-view and therefore not part of the study presented in this paper. It is clear from Figure REF that the optical spectra (shown in green) fit the model (shown in black) well. Despite the much lower signal-to-noise ratio of the grism spectra (shown in red), they remain consistent with the optical template. There is also evidence for very weak H{{formula:7236a963-98b7-4d55-868b-dcb85d888b0c}} emission, since H{{formula:31cc38d8-a7fe-4f8a-a599-c0320571eb42}} emission is clearly seen in the grism spectrum of one of the PSBs. Nevertheless, the absence of H{{formula:a8e7d9b8-6528-4c5f-b259-c72efd2148cb}} emission for most of the PSBs confirms that these galaxies have strongly suppressed star formation.Since the classification of the GCLASS PSBs was based on a spectroscopic criteria that was designed to apply to {{formula:503e1d37-8bb7-40a5-95e1-dea3fce7531b}} galaxies, a clarification is required as to what galaxies this selection criteria leads to at {{formula:39e831e0-53df-491b-8da3-6e1d2efcb5c1}} , the redshift of GCLASS. In general, galaxies in the nearby universe have much lower star formation rates (SFRs) than those at higher redshifts. To explain a PSB spectrum at low redshifts, the galaxy in question must have experienced a starburst before it quenched. i.e, it must have had high levels of star formation, which are uncommon for {{formula:ec9f8a74-8923-4fff-b6fd-ee38d7ba0df5}} star-forming galaxies. A galaxy undergoing a starburst usually lies systematically above the star-forming main sequence at fixed redshift, with SFRs {{formula:51c616be-e150-4eaa-bcb4-bad102544db1}} (e.g. , , ). Towards higher redshifts, the intercept of the star-forming main sequence (SFR–stellar mass relation for star-forming galaxies) increases , . Therefore, a galaxy that is considered a starburst galaxy at {{formula:2d846233-a72b-47e5-9a32-de67906c81a2}} will be considered a normal star-forming galaxy at higher redshifts. The GCLASS PSBs reside at {{formula:42cdf47e-25a0-4483-b649-1a312a0a81c3}} , where SFRs were {{formula:42d5c05e-0ab0-44af-b895-d07013afebf3}} times higherAt a fixed stellar mass of Log{{formula:046a9461-d077-4341-ae10-4e0b73ecaf31}} . than at {{formula:c1a63333-f051-4b60-a2e3-cc22ef73ced9}} , . Employing the term “poststarburst" is somewhat misleading in connection with this sample of galaxies because these are normal star-forming galaxies at {{formula:9ab43d9a-2d4f-4e6a-bc5d-c59b2c0e4997}} that have had their regular levels of star formation suddenly terminated, rather than true PSB galaxies akin to those found locally. There is no requirement to invoke a starburst as the explanation for their spectral properties. At this redshift, they can therefore be considered as “post star-forming" galaxies. Despite the term “poststarburst” being misleading for this sample of galaxies, we choose to continue using it to maintain consistency with previous analyses on this sample , and with the K+A notation used throughout the literature.
HST imaging of the PSBs: In Figure REF we show the F140W direct images of the PSBs in square cutouts. The dimensions of each cutout in kiloparsecs is shown in the top right-hand corner of each cutout. The spectroscopic redshift of each galaxy is shown in the bottom left-hand corner of each cutout. The images are ordered by increasing stellar mass. Cutouts with solid line (dashed line) borders are those PSBs with reliable (low-confidence) spectroscopic redshifts.The majority of the PSBs show no signs of disturbances or interactions and are symmetric in shape. This is somewhat puzzling, since the abrupt end in these galaxies' star formation suggests that a severe violent process (e.g. a merger or a high-speed close-proximity flyby, both of which would likely leave tidal signatures or some sort of asymmetry) would likely be responsible. The fact that most of the PSBs are symmetric and undisturbed effectively rules out violent quenching mechanisms that are capable of altering the stellar distribution of galaxies. These include harassment, mergers and tidal-stripping.These quenching mechanisms were already ruled out in more detailed previous work done on the PSBs. A detailed study using the large sample of spectroscopically confirmed cluster galaxies in GCLASS unveiled that the PSBs reside in a distinct location of clustercentric velocity versus position phase space . Using several zoom-in dark-matter-only simulations, the coherent “ring" traced by the PSBs in this phase space could be reproduced by quenching galaxies rapidly (within 0.1 - 0.5 Gyr) after they made their first passage of {{formula:043cb97b-3971-42e6-85f0-188ba563a969}} . In it was also found that the GMOS spectra of the PSBs could only be fit well with high resolution stellar population models if a rapid quenching timescale of {{formula:ea4429c3-8953-4e1f-9a69-d7aa3eeed062}} Gyr is assumed. The rapidity of the quenching, suggested both by this phase space analysis and the Spectral Energy Distribution (SED) fitting of the PSBs, ruled out quenching mechanisms that operate on long timescales such as mergers, harassment and tidal-stripping. The short quenching timescale is consistent with gas stripping processes such as ram-pressure stripping and/or strangulation .Some of the PSBs however do show evidence of processes involving the possible stripping of stars or mergers. The most striking example is the second PSB on the penultimate row, which seems to have a tail of stripped stars as well as asymmetry in the overall galaxy. The last PSB on the second row shows evidence of a bridge between itself and a close companion. A close companion is also seen near the second PSB on the fifth row, which may be tidally interacting with the PSB. Whilst some of the PSBs have clear neighbouring galaxies, none have identifiable tidal features. Additionally, it is reasonable to expect close companions in projection when observing high density environments such as clusters. Furthermore, the PSBs quenched {{formula:55e0bedd-7bfc-461b-b48f-ce08994b3139}} Gyr prior to observation . If a merger, harassment or tidal interaction was responsible for triggering the PSB phase, {{formula:c924a8d6-7a26-4d2e-911b-6c949f942258}} Gyr is not enough time for the stars to settle into a symmetric, undisturbed disc. Therefore, it seems unlikely that mergers or tidal stripping are the dominant processes responsible for the emergence of the GCLASS PSBs.

Disc-like, intermediate-type and bulge-like galaxies are defined as those galaxies with {{formula:1b131cdf-e677-4ddf-9ab6-996e5c9c2878}} , {{formula:1eabcb7b-6e1b-4f7e-a93b-2e8755bfe7c3}} and {{formula:8d46616b-0604-4dfd-8fd9-f4bfe18cbc5f}} respectively. In general, lower Sérsic indices are a proxy for more disc-like morphologies and vice versa. PSBs with reliable (low-confidence) spectroscopic redshifts are shown as large squares (diamonds). The smaller circular points in the background show the rest of the cluster galaxies. BCGs are circled in grey. The lines are the same as in Figure REF . The top right panel shows the percentage of each morphological type within the star-forming, quiescent and PSB (offset for clarity) populations within the mass completeness limits. The quiescent mass completeness limit is used for the PSBs and the error bars show Poisson errors. The bottom right panel shows the mean Sérsic index for each of the three populations within the mass completeness limits. The errors bars show the standard error in the mean.Since Sérsic index has been found to be well-correlated with quiescence (e.g. , ), it is not surprising that we find the quiescent (star-forming) population with the highest percentage of bulge-like (disc-like) galaxies. This can be seen both in the main panel – where most of the blue (red) circular points lie on the star-forming (quiescent) mass–size relation – and in the top right panel. Also evident from the top right panel is that the PSBs have the highest percentage ({{formula:a3c615e5-d4a9-4954-905e-f76b532c3ca9}} ) of intermediate-type galaxies out of the three populations. They also have a percentage of bulge-like galaxies that falls almost exactly between the percentages of bulge-like galaxies found for the star-forming and quiescent populations. Interestingly, they have the lowest percentage of disc-like galaxies among the three populations. Due to poor sample statistics (stated in the legend of this panel), the uncertainties on the PSB morphology fractions are large ({{formula:9c5bd0bc-7d4d-4c87-8e92-4e8c8b311e1d}} ). We therefore appreciate that these results need to be verified with better statistics in future work. Since the PSB population is dominated by intermediate-types and bulge-like galaxies, it is therefore not surprising that the PSBs have a mean Sérsic index that is closer to the mean Sérsic index of the quiescent population, yet still intermediary between the mean Sérsic indices of the star-forming and quiescent populations (bottom right-hand panel).Since the PSBs have only recently quenched, we would have expected them to have a similar percentage of disc-like galaxies to the star-forming population and therefore a mean Sérsic index much closer to that of the star-forming population. Instead, these results suggest that the PSBs are galaxies which morphologically transformed both recently and rapidly.The PSBs do not exhibit disturbed morphologies in the stellar continuum (see Section ), but do have Sérsic indices more reminiscent of bulge-like morphologies. Since the PSBs are recently quenched galaxies, it is surprising how quickly their morphology has become bulge-dominated. One hypothesis is that before these galaxies quenched, they had both a disc and bulge component, but the disc is likely to have been brighter than the bulge. The rapid quenching could have caused a rapid fading of the disc, such that the bulge became relatively brighter than the disc. Quenching processes that are capable of causing a rapid fading of galactic discs without affecting the stellar distribution are processes which solely affect the gas content of galaxies. Candidate processes for this are ram-pressure stripping and strangulation/starvation . The gas – which is required for star formation – is more loosely bound in galactic discs. Therefore, these processes remove gas more efficiently from the discs of galaxies rather than their bulges .In the next section, we investigate whether a simple disc-fading model of galaxy quenching can explain the formation of most of the GCLASS PSB population.
Are PSBs faded discs?: As mentioned at the end of the previous section, the quenching processes that are likely to be responsible for the emergence of the PSBs can cause the fading of galactic discs. To build a better understanding of how disc-fading affects the structural properties of typical star-forming galaxies at {{formula:7061271e-470f-4542-bae0-d55a10aa599d}} , we will be presenting a variety of disc-fading toy models in this Section. For each model, we will track how typical star-forming galaxies move across the mass–size plane as their discs fade, and how their morphology (as dictated by the Sérsic index) changes.The star-forming, PSB and quiescent cluster galaxies in GCLASS have very well defined stellar populations as dictated by their spectral properties (e.g. see Section REF for a discussion on the spectral properties of the PSBs). Therefore, there are tight constraints on the allowed amount of disc-fading in each model, such that the final galaxy exhibits stellar populations reminiscent of the average PSB.The aim of this Section is therefore twofold: we will be exploring whether disc-fading can simultaneously create a population of galaxies with similar stellar populations to the PSBs and similar structural properties to the PSBs, as dictated by their distinct mass–size relation.
