Whilst this fall in size is larger than that seen in the disc and bulge disc-fading model (20% compared to 15% in the disc and bulge disc-fading model, measured at the median stellar mass of the PSBs within the quiescent mass completeness limit (Log{{formula:15181639-15f4-43e2-a2e1-b2b3bca9a4b0}} M{{formula:f5888914-73ed-4e37-8c56-5c2e9094a4ff}} )), it is not enough to explain the stellar mass–size relation of the PSBs.In the top right-hand panel of Figure REF , we show the average sizes of starting and faded galaxies which have identical stellar masses to the GCLASS star-forming cluster galaxies and PSBs beyond the star-forming and quiescent mass completeness limits, respectivelyThe errors on these measurements come from monte carlo sampling, which is described in Section REF .. We also show the average sizes of the star-forming and PSB galaxies in GCLASS within the star-forming and quiescent mass completeness limits, respectively, for comparison. It is evident that just as there is a drop in average size between the star-forming and PSB cluster galaxies, there is also a drop in average size as a result of outside-in fading in the models. The magnitude of this drop is similar to that observed in the disc and bulge disc-fading model.
The average Sérsic index of outside-in faded galaxies: In the bottom right-hand panel of Figure REF , we compare the average Sérsic indices of the starting and faded galaxy modelsFor the starting galaxy models, these are calculated from model galaxies that have exactly the same stellar masses as the star-forming cluster galaxies in GCLASS beyond the star-forming mass completeness limit. For faded galaxy models, these are calculated from model galaxies that have exactly the same stellar masses as the PSBs beyond the quiescent mass completeness limit. to the average Sérsic indices of the GCLASS star-forming cluster members and the PSBswithin the star-forming and quiescent mass completeness limits, respectively..We can straight away see that outside-in fading has led to a bulgier morphology on average for the faded galaxy models. However similar to the bulge + disc-fading model, the difference in the average Sérsic index is much smaller than the difference observed in the observations.
Disc-fading toy model (bulge and outside-in faded disc): In Section REF , we presented a more representative model of disc-fading, based on recent observations of how ram-pressure stripping operates in low redshift cluster galaxies. However, we did not model our galaxies with a bulge and disc component, as was done in the uniform disc-fading model presented in Section REF . The natural question therefore arises, whether modelling a galaxy with a bulge and disc component, and fading the disc with the more representative outside-in fading, can produce galaxies with structural and stellar population properties similar to the PSBs.In this Section, we therefore present a disc-fading model that attempts to combine representative modelling of a galaxy's structure and the fading process. The bulge and disc models are constructed in exactly the same way as those in the bulge and disc disc-fading model (Section REF ). The difference between the model presented in this Section and the previous two models is how the fading is implemented. The allowed amount of fading in this model remains constrained by the {{formula:fcbf0dc6-3810-40d6-9618-6407dd1a5fb4}} measurements of the star-forming, PSB and quiescent cluster galaxies in GCLASS.
Outside-in disc fading in the bulge+disc case: As was highlighted in Section REF , there are strict boundaries set on how much the disc can be faded in a bulge+disc model. These boundaries are dictated by the spectroscopic properties of the cluster galaxies. In the case of uniform disc-fading, the disc was faded by a factor of 2 such that the resulting composite bulge+disc model would represent a galaxy that had similar stellar populations to the PSBs. In the model presented in this Section, we want to fade the disc “outside-in", yet still produce a galaxy with similar stellar populations to the PSBs. To do this, we need to ensure that the outside-in fading we implement on the disc components results in the same total brightness as when we fade the same discs uniformly by a factor of 2.The outside-in fading is implemented using the same method described in Section REF with a few modifications. For each model disc, we first check what the total brightness of the disc is when it is uniformly faded by a factor of 2. We do not fade the central pixel of the disc model. We check how much the disc model needs to be faded at {{formula:913a17b9-165e-42d8-87ec-a4fbe02bb9ba}} (see Section REF for reasoning) from the centre, such that the entire model has the same brightness as when it is uniformly faded by a factor of 2. We then adjust the slope of our linearly interpolated fading accordingly. Examples of galaxy models for three stellar masses within the mass completeness limits of GCLASS are shown in Figure REF . Alongside the faded galaxy models, we show select PSBs that have similar stellar masses to the model galaxies.
The stellar mass–size relation of bulges + outside-in faded discs: In the largest panel of Figure REF , we show the median size measurements for the starting (open green squares) and faded (filled green squares) galaxy models for multiple stellar mass bins, as well as the disc (small blue circles) and bulge (large red circles) components. The lines are the same as in Figure REF . The most striking aspect of these measurements is that this model of disc-fading leads to a dramatic drop in the size of galaxies. So much so, that the half-light radii are smaller than those of the bulge models. At the median stellar mass of the PSBs within the quiescent mass completeness limit (Log{{formula:c52f835c-a38c-476e-9d79-e7a9efd07b7a}} M{{formula:1e7d0af0-e588-4e32-a776-308b8b334051}} ), the half-light radius shrinks by 85%. This large size reduction is likely due to the fact that the central pixels of the disc models have not been faded. As a result, the outside-in fading implemented has a particularly steep gradient. Consequently, there is far more light in the central regions of the faded galaxies compared to the corresponding bulge model. This is also evident in the first row of Figure REF . This leads to a galaxy with a particularly steep light profile, and therefore a smaller half-light radius.In the top right-hand panel of Figure REF , we show the average sizes of the starting and faded galaxy models for models that have stellar masses identical to the GCLASS star-forming cluster galaxies and PSBs beyond the star-forming and quiescent mass completeness limits, respectively. We also show the average sizes of the star-forming and PSB cluster galaxies in GCLASS within the star-forming and quiescent mass completeness limits, respectively. Errors are calculated in the same way as for the previous disc-fading modelsIf error bars are not visible, it is because the error bar is smaller than the size of the marker.. The dramatic reduction in the average size of a galaxy is evident in this model, with the faded models reaching an average size that is almost half that of the average PSB.
The average Sérsic index of bulges + outside-in faded discs: In the bottom right-hand panel of Figure REF , we compare the average Sérsic indices of the starting and faded galaxy models to the average Sérsic indices of the star-forming and PSB cluster galaxiesThese, as well as their errors are calculated in the same way as in the first two disc-fading toy models.. It is immediately noticeable that this disc-fading model – unlike the previous two models – can reproduce the dramatic rise in Sérsic index that is seen in the observations.
Caveats: It should be emphasised that while considerable effort has been made to model disc-fading realistically, the three toy models presented in Sections REF , REF and REF are still very simplistic. For the models that consider bulge and disc components, only the case where the two components have the same stellar mass has been considered. In all three of the models presented, we only consider models with specific Sérsic indices, axis ratios, F140W magnitudes and position angles. Realistically, galaxies will have a range of disc-to-bulge stellar mass ratios, Sérsic indices, axis ratios, F140W magnitudes and position angles. The fading of galactic discs would also occur in varying amounts and the stellar populations would vary. These variances would cause a scattering in the positions of the starting and faded galaxies on the mass–size plane.Furthermore, our understanding of outside-in fading, and its implementation in Sections REF and REF , is based on a single – albeit well-studied – example of a cluster galaxy undergoing ram-pressure stripping at low redshift (see Section REF ). Ram-pressure stripping may operate very differently at high redshift, where gas fractions are higher than at low redshift. There may also be a stellar mass dependency on how ram-pressure stripping operates, which we will discuss in more detail in Section .Particularly in the last disc-fading model (Section REF ), the outside-in fading seems to be too aggressive. The way in which the fading is implemented leads to a large contraction in the half-light radius of a galaxy. Certainly, if the gradient of the outside-in fading was shallower, the magnitude of this contraction could be reduced (as is evident in Figure REF for example), and faded galaxies that approximately follow the PSB mass–size relation could be achieved.Nevertheless, it is clear that the combination of modelling a galaxy with a bulge and disc component, as well as implementing outside-in disc-fading (Section REF ) can lead to the required contraction in size and the required increase in bulge-dominance that is observed between the star-forming and PSB cluster galaxies.
Evidence for the PSBs being transition galaxies: The PSBs are cluster galaxies that were selected as being recently quenched – and therefore intermediary to star-forming and quiescent galaxies – based solely on their spectroscopic properties in the optical (Section REF ). In Sections and , we presented two pieces of evidence that suggest the PSBs also have structural properties intermediary to those exhibited by typical star-forming and quiescent cluster galaxies: 1) The PSBs lie on a distinct stellar mass–size relation that almost perfectly bisects the region between the star-forming and quiescent mass–size relations, and 2) Morphologically, out of the three populations (Star-forming, PSB and Quiescent), the PSB population contains the largest fraction of intermediate-type galaxies. The fraction of bulge-like galaxies in the PSB population is also intermediary to the fraction of bulge-like galaxies found in the star-forming and quiescent populations. The fact that the PSBs all lie on the same mass–size relation suggests that most, if not all of them formed via the same physical process. After inspecting the HST WFC3 F140W imaging of the PSBs (Section ), we find most (20 out of 23) of them have symmetrical, undisturbed morphologies in the stellar continuum. This observation rules out physical quenching mechanisms such as mergers, harassment , or tidal stripping which lead to the redistribution of stars. Instead, it supports a scenario where the PSBs are formed via a quenching process that only effects the gas reservoir of the galaxy.Quenching mechanisms prevalent in the cluster environment which solely affect the gas content of a galaxy include ram-pressure stripping and strangulation . Spectacular examples of on-going ram-pressure stripping quenching galaxies rapidly have been observed in low redshift clusters (e.g. , , , , , , ). Both the rapidity of this process and its potential to indirectly reduce the half-light radius of a galaxy support the short quenching timescales found for the PSBs from our previous work and the location of the PSB mass–size relation relative to the star-forming one in this study.It must be noted that there is no definitive way to identify galaxies that are transitioning from star-forming to quiescent. Therefore, results on galaxies that are similarly selected to the GCLASS PSBs tend to vary, making comparison with the literature challenging. In general, PSBs have strong Balmer absorption and no emission lines which are induced by star formation. However, by altering the exact spectroscopic selection criteria, very different samples of transition galaxies can be selected which exhibit a range of physical properties (e.g. , ). Some of these selection criteria can lead to significant contamination by dusty star-forming galaxies . Particularly strong Balmer absorption can be indicative of a starburst occurring in the galaxy prior to quenching (Section REF ). Such starbursts are likely to be the result of violent interactions such as galaxy-galaxy mergers or harassment, not gas-related processes such as ram-pressure stripping or starvation (e.g. ).Nevertheless, many other similar works to ours have also concluded that PSB galaxies in clusters are most likely the product of ram-pressure stripping , , , . In most cases, this is usually associated with the higher occurence of PSBs in clusters compared to other environments such as the field and groups , , , , , , , suggesting cluster-specific quenching mechanisms are more efficient in transforming star-forming galaxies into PSBs. More detailed studies of the spatial distribution of PSBs in clusters have uncovered more convincing evidence for ram-pressure stripping being responsible for their emergence. found that their E+A cluster galaxies were evenly distributed within the projected ram-pressure stripping radius of the cluster MACS J0717.5+3745. Going a step further, found that their PSBs were radially distributed in a shell-like structure, congregating in between where most of the star-forming and quiescent cluster galaxies were found. This seemed to suggest a transition region in clusters, where there is a change in the physical properties, perhaps in the density of the intracluster medium, triggering efficient ram-pressure stripping. Similarly, found that most of the GCLASS PSBs with spectroscopic redshifts from GMOS followed a coherent “ring" in clustercentric velocity versus position phase space. Most of the GCLASS PSBs are situated at small clustercentric radii ({{formula:103c613c-7b68-4ae6-9f98-ae136d875619}} ) with high clustercentric velocities. Such conditions were found to be consistent with the radii at which ram-pressure stripping and starvation are most effective in clusters , , .Since ram-pressure stripping is capable of removing the cold gas reservoir of a galaxy, it can remove the fuel for star formation. With no younger stars actively forming, the average age of the stellar populations in the galaxy increases, eventually leading to a fall in the brightness of the galaxy. Ram-pressure stripping is more effective at removing gas from galactic discs . With a strong body of evidence suggesting the GCLASS PSBs are a product of ram-pressure stripping, we decided to test whether the fading of a star-forming galaxy's disc could lead to a population of galaxies that would lie along the PSB mass–size relation.
Outside-in disc-fading qualitatively explains the structural properties of the PSBs: Initially, we modelled star-forming galaxies as having both a disc and bulge component of equal stellar mass. The disc would then uniformly fade such that the galaxy's stellar populations matched those of the PSBs (Section REF ). In this scenario, we found that the fading did not produce model galaxies with similar sizes and Sérsic indices to the average PSB (Figure REF ). Far more fading was required to explain the small sizes and high Sérsic indices of most of the PSBs. This is perhaps unsurprising, since observational evidence suggests quenching in clusters does not operate in this way.Given that numerous previous results suggest that outside-in quenching occurs in low redshift clusters, we therefore proceeded to model outside-in fading on the mass–size plane (Section REF ), finding that it also fails to produce model galaxies with similar structural properties to the PSBs. Furthermore, this model fails to reproduce the steep slope of the PSB stellar mass–size relation. A possible reason for this could be due to a difference in the fading rate for low- and high-mass galaxies. Outside-in fading may operate at a faster rate for low-mass galaxies, but much slower for high-mass galaxies. This may also allow for the average Sérsic index to rise, since at fixed stellar mass, all the galaxies with Log{{formula:3b89a1eb-7160-4c86-9850-232de6fcbc1d}} –which are in the majority – will have smaller sizes at fixed stellar mass, more similar to quiescent galaxies.Nevertheless, we decided to combine our first and second attempts at modelling disc-fading into a third model (Section REF ). From the first model (Section REF ), we took the more realistic modelling of galactic structure, modelling our galaxies with a disc and bulge component. From the second model (Section REF ), we took the more realistic modelling of “outside-in" fading. The result is a model that can explain the high Sérsic indices of the PSBs and has the potential to produce disc-faded galaxies that approximately follow the PSB mass–size relation. The results of these three disc-fading toy models have shown that the PSBs are plausibly the product of star-forming galaxies which have experienced disc-fading. This disc-fading is likely to have been brought on by quenching processes such as ram-pressure stripping. To better reproduce the structural properties of the PSBs with disc-fading, various fading gradients with more sophisticated modelling need to be explored. The gradient of outside-in fading could very much rely upon the stellar mass of the galaxy, which in turn dictates the slope of the relation the faded galaxies lie on.Many recent works have found that disc fading could explain the formation of transition galaxies in clusters. Using a bulge and disc decomposition of quiescent galaxies in the Coma cluster, find that S0 (intermediate-type) galaxies have systematically bluer bulges and discs further away from the cluster centre. This observation favoured environmentally-induced disc fading as the dominant route for S0 formation. Going further, were able to show that most S0 galaxies in the Fornax cluster have quenched “outside-in", with the latest star formation in the central regions being capable of enhancing the brightness of the bulge. Similarly, find that kinematically-disturbed emission-line cluster galaxies out to {{formula:27894d04-16f9-4887-abc9-8aca3690bd83}} have truncated gas discs and that their star formation is more centrally concentrated than analogous galaxies in low density environments. They suggest that gas is either more efficiently removed from the outskirts of galaxies and/or is driven towards the centre. Driving gas towards the centre of the galaxy would further fuel the centrally-concentrated star formation and contribute to the build-up of a significant bulge. Perhaps this may be an attribute of gas-stripping processes which was not considered in our toy models. If ram-pressure stripping could also contribute to enhancing the stellar mass build-up of the bulge, a scenario could emerge where there is bulge brightening as well as disc fading. This could most certainly explain the more bulgier morphologies of the PSBs compared to the faded galaxies in our fading models. Enhanced star formation in the core of a ram-pressure stripped galaxy in the Coma cluster was seen in for example. Furthermore, found that the bulges of low mass ({{formula:11d3a4d0-d3d1-47f5-b851-469dbc637e84}} M{{formula:b8744314-4f5b-4ce5-a8e6-4715fee03453}} ) S0 galaxies in the MaNGA survey hosted younger stellar populations than their discs, supporting an outside-in fading scenario where the bulge may end up brighter than the disc.Nonetheless, other works have stated that outside-in quenching may not be the only explanation for how cluster galaxies quench. Using a bulge-disc decomposition of late- and early-type galaxies in six low redshift clusters, found that the bright end of the disc luminosity function does not vary much with bulge fraction, but the bright end of the bulge luminosity function increases with bulge fraction. Quenching in clusters seems to favour the bulge becoming brighter rather than the disc fading as a galaxy moves from spiral to elliptical morphology. This seems to suggest that environmental quenching processes are not enough to explain the structural properties of recently quenched cluster galaxies. For example, to explain how low mass (Log{{formula:230a6368-7027-4e28-b717-f4e3fee03698}} ) PSBs evolved from compact star-forming galaxies in {{formula:b107d134-dec4-4296-86f7-a720c0135dec}} clusters, found that a combination of gas stripping and strong outflows from stellar or AGN feedback were needed to explain their structural properties.
Recently quenched galaxies & evolution in the quiescent mass–size relation with redshift: The distinct location of the PSBs on the mass–size plane has important implications for the growth in the average size of quiescent cluster galaxies with decreasing redshift. The majority of the PSBs lie on the large size end of the quiescent distribution at fixed stellar mass (see Figure REF ). Their location in Figure REF provides direct evidence showing that galaxies which quench later are on average larger in size than galaxies that quenched earlier. Therefore, the addition of recently quenched galaxies to the quiescent population can induce an increase in the average size of quiescent galaxies with decreasing redshift.In , we found that minor mergers could explain the size growth observed in quiescent field galaxies with decreasing redshift at fixed stellar mass. Now, with the study presented in this paper, we confirm that the addition of recently quenched galaxies to the quiescent population will also induce a rise in the average size of quiescent galaxies with decreasing redshift. The relative importance of these two size growth mechanisms however still needs to be determined. For example, a higher occurence of PSBs in clusters have been found by a number of other studies , , , , . Since minor mergers are rare between satellite cluster galaxies, these findings may suggest that the addition of recently quenched galaxies to the quiescent population is more important for the size growth observed in the quiescent cluster population than for the size growth observed in the quiescent field population with decreasing redshift.On the other hand, claim that the addition of recently quenched galaxies to the quiescent population can explain the majority of the size growth observed in the median size of quiescent field galaxies between {{formula:9d3d5c9b-817e-4bfb-bdcd-804293c1aeb1}} . This conclusion was motivated by the fact that these authors do not observe a decrease in the number density of compact quiescent galaxies in this redshift range (which, if observed, would have suggested they have grown physically in size). Since this result, many other studies have also found that progenitor bias plays an important role in the size growth of quiescent galaxies at fixed stellar mass , , , , , , , . In further support of this conclusion, found that large quiescent field galaxies with {{formula:3e1f3c47-3947-412f-b689-132547a515cf}} Log{{formula:1c377c26-5d92-4109-ba79-f894a6f6d931}} at {{formula:233effd0-9329-4952-ab8d-2dbdc951f819}} were composed of younger stellar populations than smaller quiescent field galaxies within the same stellar mass range. Similar results to this one have also been found by , , , , and . however did observe a decrease in the number density of compact quiescent galaxies with a much larger sample of field galaxies between {{formula:ee55453d-ea7c-470e-9e57-4ff625509787}} , concluding that minor mergers drive the observed growth in the average size of quiescent galaxies with decreasing redshift. Many other works have also concluded that minor mergers are the main drivers of size growth at fixed stellar mass for the quiescent population , , , , , , . Regardless, there remains disagreement in which of the two processes dominates the observed size growth , , , .Using the results in and this work, we confirm that both minor mergers and recently quenched galaxies are responsible for the observed growth in the average size of quiescent galaxies at fixed stellar mass with decreasing redshift. However, better sample statistics spread over a large range in redshift and environments will be required to quantify which of the two processes dominates.
Summary: In this paper, we have studied the structural properties of 23 spectroscopically identified recently quenched (or “poststarburst" (PSB)) cluster galaxies residing in nine clusters at {{formula:b70e3666-bd4c-4f99-bdcf-2cc50980eb71}} , to better understand the physical process responsible for their quenching. Our main conclusions are as follows:In most cases, the F140W direct images of the recently quenched galaxies show no disturbances to their stellar light profiles that could be the result of violent interactions such as mergers, harassment or tidal stripping. This suggests the quenching mechanism responsible effects solely the gas content of these galaxies. By fitting the F140W direct images of the recently quenched galaxies with single component Sérsic profiles, we find that most of the recently quenched galaxies lie on a distinct mass–size relation that almost perfectly bisects the region lying in between the star-forming and quiescent field stellar mass–size relations. This suggests the quenching mechanism responsible is capable of altering the light profile of these galaxies in a very specific way, with the likelihood that most of the recently quenched galaxies underwent the same quenching process. Using Sérsic index as a proxy for morphology, we compare the Sérsic profiles of the recently quenched, star-forming and quiescent cluster galaxies. The highest fraction of intermediate-type galaxies is found in the recently quenched population. Recently quenched galaxies also exhibit a higher fraction of bulge-dominated galaxies than the star-forming population, but a lower fraction compared to the quiescent population. Therefore, recently quenched galaxies have morphologies that are intermediary to those of the star-forming and quiescent populations. However, on average, their morphologies are more similar to those exhibited by the quiescent population. By modelling a star-forming cluster galaxy with a bulge and disc component of equal stellar mass, we explored how star-forming galaxies move across the mass–size plane as their discs fade uniformly, resulting in galaxies with similar stellar populations to the recently quenched galaxies. Although a reduction in half-light radius and a rise in Sérsic index is found, the magnitude of these changes in physical properties are too small to explain the structural properties of the PSBs. We then used a more realistic model of outside-in fading based on recent observations of quenching in clusters. We found that this model still failed to produce galaxies with similar structural properties to the PSBs. A significant drop in average size is achieved, but the high Sérsic indices of the PSBs and the steep slope of the PSB mass–size relation was not achieved. This suggests longer fading timescales with increasing stellar mass are required and/or bulge brightening also occurs as part of quenching processes like ram-pressure stripping which could drive gas towards the centre. By combining the more realistic modelling of a galaxy with a disc and bulge component, and the more realistic outside-in disc-fading, we showed that disc-fading can explain the high Sérsic indices of the PSBs and has the potential to produce galaxies that follow the PSB mass–size relation. Further exploration of outside-in fading gradients combined with more sophisticated modelling is required to fully reproduce the structural properties of the PSBs. The fact that the PSB mass–size relation runs through the large size end of the quiescent distribution of galaxies provides direct evidence for recently quenched galaxies contributing to the size growth of quiescent galaxies with decreasing redshift.In tandem with the results presented in , we confirm both minor mergers and the addition of recently quenched galaxies to the quiescent population are responsible for the rapid size growth at fixed stellar mass observed in the quiescent population of galaxies with decreasing redshift. However, it remains unclear which of these two processes dominate. Determining this will require better sample statistics over a broad redshift range in a variety of environments.

4. Toy disc‑fading models (uniform fading, outside‑in fading, and a combined bulge+outside‑in fading) demonstrate that rapid fading of the disc – without altering the stellar mass distribution – can reproduce both the observed size reduction and the increase in Sérsic index. The preferred physical mechanism for such disc fading is gas‑only quenching (ram‑pressure stripping or strangulation) that removes gas from the disc while leaving the stellar component intact (Section ‘Evidence for the PSBs being transition galaxies’ and ‘Outside‑in disc‑fading qualitatively explains the structural properties of the PSBs’). 
5. Because the observed structural changes can be explained by disc fading driven by gas‑stripping processes, the morphological transition from disk‑dominated to early‑type galaxies in the post‑starburst sequence does not require major mergers.

questionDraft: How does the Rfit frequentist statistical treatment of theoretical uncertainties as non-random fixed parameters shape the derivation of confidence level bounds on the axion-like particle coupling to top quarks in top-antitop production analyses?
question: In a frequentist statistical analysis of top-antitop production, how does treating theoretical uncertainties as fixed, non-random quantities with allowed ranges—rather than as Gaussian-distributed random variables—shape the procedure for deriving confidence level bounds on the coupling of an axion-like particle to top quarks?
answerWithPaperReferences: The analysis relies on the Rfit scheme introduced in [Paper A], which treats theoretical uncertainties as non-random, fixed parameters that are uniformly distributed within their allowed ranges rather than as Gaussian random variables. In this framework, confidence levels are derived by profiling over the theoretical parameters, minimizing the chi-squared within their allowed intervals, which avoids the peaking effects and coverage issues that can arise in Bayesian treatments. In [Paper B], this Rfit framework is applied to bound the ALP-top coupling c_tt from LHC top-antitop data. For each fixed value of c_tt, the overall theory uncertainty delta_th is profiled by minimizing the log-likelihood over the interval between the central prediction minus and plus delta_th, yielding chi^2_min(c_tt). The 95% confidence level bound is then set where the difference Delta chi^2(c_tt) = chi^2_min(c_tt) - chi^2_bf^2 equals 3.84. This treatment properly accounts for the non-Gaussian nature of theory uncertainties in the Standard Model and ALP cross section predictions and reduces the dependence of the bound on potential mismatches between SM predictions and data.
answerWithoutPaperReferences: In this frequentist framework, theoretical uncertainties are regarded as fixed but unknown quantities that are uniformly distributed within their allowed ranges, rather than as Gaussian random variables. Confidence levels are derived by profiling over these theoretical parameters, minimizing the chi-squared within their allowed intervals, which avoids the peaking effects and coverage issues that can arise in Bayesian treatments. When applied to bound the axion-like particle coupling to top quarks from LHC top-antitop data, the analysis proceeds by fixing the coupling and profiling over the overall theory uncertainty by minimizing the log-likelihood over the interval between the central prediction minus and plus that uncertainty. The 95% confidence level bound is set where the difference between this minimum chi-squared and the best-fit chi-squared equals 3.84. This procedure properly accounts for the non-Gaussian nature of theory uncertainties in the Standard Model and new-physics cross section predictions and reduces the dependence of the bound on potential mismatches between Standard Model predictions and experimental data.
isNotSingleHop: The question is not single-hop because answering it requires both the general statistical framework—specifically, why and how theoretical uncertainties are treated as non-random fixed parameters with uniform likelihoods, and the concept of profiling by minimization within allowed ranges—and the specific application to ALP-top coupling bounds, including how this profiling is implemented with the overall theory uncertainty and how the Delta chi^2 bound is computed. Neither paper alone contains both the general Rfit philosophy and the ALP-specific fit procedure.

First 31806 characters: A New Approach to a Global Fit of the CKM Matrix
abstract: We report on a global CKM matrix analysis taking into account most recent experimental and theoretical results. The statistical framework (Rfit) developed in this paper advocates formal frequentist statistics. Other approaches, such as Bayesian statistics or the 95% CL scan method are also discussed. We emphasize the distinction of a model testing and a model dependent, metrological phase in which the various parameters of the theory are determined. Measurements and theoretical parameters entering the global fit are thoroughly discussed, in particular with respect to their theoretical uncertainties. Graphical results for confidence levels are drawn in various one and two-dimensional parameter spaces. Numerical results are provided for all relevant CKM parameterizations, the CKM elements and theoretical input parameters. Predictions for branching ratios of rare K and B meson decays are obtained. A simple, predictive SUSY extension of the Standard Model is discussed.
Introduction: Within the Standard Model (SM), CP violation is generated by a single non-vanishing phase in the unitary Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) quark mixing matrix {{formula:fe1b8b3d-f630-4212-9d33-2123bf167a2c}} , . A useful parameterization , follows from the observation that the elements of {{formula:61f14d15-b129-4c04-98f5-abe06f08f063}} exhibit a hierarchy in terms of the parameter {{formula:3da64440-0426-43c5-bde8-e33653eace47}} . Other parameters of this representation are {{formula:6a9c783d-dc48-4428-b36a-bf069e02acc9}} , {{formula:8555b7a5-eb70-4824-a5c0-9f3aa717f1af}} and {{formula:2ac6818a-b188-4bb9-aff4-4ac0df2d86eb}} , where CP violation necessarily requires {{formula:68eb8dc6-2294-4599-b55c-c969711ad704}} . The parameters {{formula:4b74cb31-140c-420f-b1a1-5ddccab94ded}} and {{formula:c953f243-749f-4628-9390-ce5d20308439}} are obtained from measurements of semileptonic decay rates of {{formula:1a964c90-0785-42a5-83a9-b82796394cd6}} mesons and {{formula:0b75ae5c-1305-4bd6-a2e2-4d7bda47d948}} meson decays involving {{formula:ba46a506-f65b-4ade-84c5-001c76641697}} transitions, respectively. Constraints on {{formula:79ad3eaa-5ebc-4c75-ad41-8004f09978c5}} and {{formula:d79d47e6-c58e-40bc-a4a5-518d09b06f3f}} are obtained from measurements of semileptonic {{formula:c1054e37-980c-4bf5-9745-6929f058dd53}} decays yielding {{formula:02346c11-d3e6-4312-b9f4-e418b3ccdd0d}} and the ratio {{formula:2b383c1c-9c2c-4514-b19d-180d498a35a8}} . Standard Model predictions of {{formula:3aaf40bb-ab2b-498d-b180-7a67c4a5d31a}} and {{formula:9c11076b-eb76-4490-be62-ebc5825f9cfe}} oscillations, and of indirect CP violation in the neutral kaon sector, depend on CKM parameters; therefore measurements of these observables provide constraints in the {{formula:88b54862-f2c0-47e1-a2b2-42057ed9808a}} plane, albeit being limited by theoretical uncertainties coming mainly from long distance QCD effects. Finally, in the era of the B-factories, it will be possible, for the first time, to assess the CP-violating angles {{formula:a5841037-b24f-4f73-810d-322198c34482}} , {{formula:187a13ce-0493-4eb5-a7b3-1a1ff9435f47}} and {{formula:a9e4cd61-b5fe-4e76-8f80-9a3bdc6ebbf7}} of the Unitarity Triangle (UT) expressing the unitarity relation between the first and the third column of {{formula:cc45ed86-d062-441c-a37f-f6b51d6946ed}} .The first goal of a global CKM fit is to probe the validity of the SM, that is to quantify the agreement between the SM and the experimental information. Furthermore, one intends to perform a detailed Metrology, that is to find allowed ranges for CKM matrix elements and related quantities, assuming the SM to be correct. Finally, within an extended theoretical framework, one may search for specific signals of new physics, by estimating the additional theoretical parameters.Analyzing data in a well defined theoretical framework ceases to be a straightforward task when one moves away from Gaussian statistics. This is the case for the theoretically limited precision on the SM predictions of the neutral {{formula:1b56bab3-d02d-4eef-9f32-c7029ce92fcd}} and {{formula:4a67be87-c045-4b33-862c-288b17eed0b0}} mixing observables and, to a lesser extent, for the semileptonic decay rates of {{formula:367f8d8d-8210-4ab1-b85a-6434fa0d09b2}} decays to charmed and charmless final states. The statistical approach (Rfit) developed in this analysis allows a non-Bayesian treatment of the, a priori unknown (i.e., not statistically distributed), theoretical parameters and theoretical systematics of measurements. The ensemble of the statistical analysis is realized in the program package CkmFitterCkmFitter is a framework package that hosts several statistical approaches to a global CKM fit, such as Rfit, Bayesian techniques and the 95% CL Scan method. It is available as public share ware. Please, contact the authors for more information.. A detailed description of the methods it uses, with emphasis on the new method denoted Rfit which is proposed here, and the presentation of state-of-the-art results are the subject of this paperVisit the CkmFitter web page to find plots, reference links, detailed descriptions and more: http://www.slac.stanford.edu/{{formula:e8463aec-6332-45d1-8fa8-ebb6505e882a}} laplace/ckmfitter.html .The paper is organized as follows: after recalling the most common CKM parameterizations, we comprehensively discuss the statistical framework of the analysis, starting with the introduction of the relevant likelihoods in Section REF , followed by a definition of the three analysis steps: metrology, model testing and probing for new physics. We then recall the principles of the 95% CL Scan scheme and of the Bayesian approach , in Section (see also Refs. and references therein for a tentative collection of publications on the CKM matrix and related topics). We work out their limitations and motivate further going ideas, while never leaving non-Bayesian grounds. This is followed by a discussion of the treatment of experimental and theoretical systematics in Section . In Section we present a compendium of the input measurements, their predictions in the framework of the SM, and discuss the theoretical parameters and their uncertainties used in the analysis. We display our fit results as confidence levels in various parameter spaces in Section and produce tables of constraints on all relevant CKM parameters, constraining measurements and theoretical inputs, and predictions of rare {{formula:72eddf49-2800-46db-a6f8-db90b242a7cf}} and {{formula:d41d8589-18ff-4fa8-900f-0dc99c264cb1}} decays. Within our statistical approach, we perform a test of the goodness of the theory and discuss the effect of a simple, predictive Minimal Supersymmetric extension of the SM. Deepening statistical discussions on some crucial issues of the analysis are given in the appendix.
The CKM Matrix: Invariance under local gauge transformation prevents the bare masses of the leptons and quarks to appear in the {{formula:3382f161-97cf-43a0-a877-f075d1bb7440}} Lagrange density of the SM. Instead, the spontaneous breakdown of electroweak symmetry dynamically generates masses for the fermions due to the Yukawa coupling of the fermion fields to the Higgs doublet. Since the latter has a non-vanishing vacuum expectation value, the Yukawa couplings {{formula:2c686483-7c36-4545-959e-e33cf6db5710}} give rise to the {{formula:5863b275-585b-47d2-b8a9-135b19201150}} mass matrices {{formula:e7a862f9-f630-40aa-8435-71f10673dc3e}}with {{formula:7151a430-a327-41d1-9a77-ff5d443778a5}} for up(down)-type quarks and {{formula:9e3dee04-76a3-4bfb-a505-72e06b9360ef}} for the massive leptons. The transformation of the {{formula:a363a47d-4970-48af-8043-906e74e5da18}} from the basis of the flavor eigenstates to the basis of the mass eigenstates is realized by unitary rotation matrices {{formula:3ab15844-b5b9-4624-83fb-6980004ae12d}} , where {{formula:5b023666-19d4-4a97-8cc5-1af2ca78c972}}For the Lagrange density in the basis of the mass-eigenstates the neutral-current part remains unchanged (i.e., there are no flavor changing neutral currents present at tree level), whereas the charged current part of the quark sector is modified by the product of the up-type and down-type quark mass matrices, {{formula:bb9dba4b-76a5-4c3e-b388-e0968a9030af}}which is the CKM mixing matrix. By convention, {{formula:6af25cf8-4ab7-4eed-ba1f-91e796116821}} operates on the {{formula:e2a1fe9e-f41b-4717-94c4-ceec52a618b4}} charged down-type quark mass eigenstates {{formula:519f2455-62e0-42a1-969c-40a50cb0d999}}and, being the product of unitary matrices, {{formula:eedeb988-e2dc-4a1c-b317-4d9a42a85874}} itself is unitary: {{formula:6d588924-4783-4461-a7ed-b2b9d58e13d9}}There exists a hierarchy between the elements of {{formula:00b3078c-904e-4409-b248-b03e5f846064}} both for their value (the diagonal elements dominate) and their errors (since they dominate, they are better known). Unitarity and the phase arbitrariness of fields reduce the initially nine complex parameters of {{formula:ca2bce64-4df3-4263-b785-7f3311a0856b}} to three real numbers and one phase, where the latter accounts for CP violation. It is therefore interesting to over-constrain {{formula:e2ddbf79-20c2-4091-843a-4eb225ccf49e}} since deviations from unitarity would reveal the existence of new generation(s) or new couplings.The charged current couplings among left-handed quark fields are proportional to the elements of {{formula:39238ce4-6704-4e36-8cbe-92adfcf2b69a}} . For right-handed quarks there exist no {{formula:d17cd4b4-8f68-43c6-82e4-709421720578}} boson interaction in the SM and the {{formula:362f0e11-63ce-4b64-95c3-9d8dd41c8ecb}} , photon and gluon couplings are flavor diagonal. For left-handed leptons the analysis proceeds similar to the quarks.There are many ways of parameterizing the CKM matrix in terms of four parameters. It is the purpose of this section to summarize the most popular representations.
The Standard Parameterization: The Standard Parameterization of {{formula:a247c6d7-f743-4873-a941-971dfeddc6d0}} is taken to be the one proposed by Chau and Keung , and advocated by the PDG . It is obtained by the product of three complex rotation matrices, where the rotations are characterized by the Euler angles {{formula:ed8e274b-b006-4643-9755-bb2370584ac4}} and {{formula:de2212ec-366d-4348-8d15-b2e0ffeb04eb}} , which are the mixing angles between the generations, and an overall phase {{formula:a69e7f0a-1a7c-457d-8ea3-83030e02a6ad}} : {{formula:009bd3ab-599d-4fb1-9722-fd39aa76e7ad}}where {{formula:dce7ab04-132a-409b-896a-f2d250a511f2}} , {{formula:27472c22-614f-4d95-99b7-259a7f031d75}} for {{formula:eaebb2fd-ca7e-4a6d-b36c-4d362b8f1b6c}} . This parameterization has the considerable advantage of being exact in the sense that it strictly satisfies the unitarity relation (REF ).
The Wolfenstein Parameterization: Following the observation of a hierarchy between the different matrix elements, Wolfenstein proposed a simple expansion of the CKM matrix in terms of the four parameters {{formula:4a17ee6a-377a-4e10-956e-b6e7e148b5be}} , {{formula:ff1591ca-d91f-4967-9969-039ad89be9e7}} , {{formula:1e040766-e98e-4ed9-b5d9-64a67d1f9095}} and {{formula:dda9e5cd-16d0-48b7-9013-084978f2b3cb}} ({{formula:0c4d6244-087f-4f8d-9429-e93157bd7f1e}} being the expansion parameter), which is widely used in contemporary literature. Using the convention of Ref. one has {{formula:2384dd7e-f551-492c-8931-23e677d26957}}It is obtained from Eq. (REF ) via the definitions {{formula:eca1f464-b532-4108-b9cf-8331c9793b50}}and is valid to the order {{formula:7f67c161-e38d-47e0-b374-bb0bf474e891}} .
Phase Invariance: It was shown by Jarlskog that the determinant of the commutator of the up-type and down-type unitary mass matrices (REF ) reads {{formula:4a9c976f-8fa6-457f-a963-b3bff7bc1491}}with {{formula:263a113c-c282-4e92-a3e8-515c68a26584}} , {{formula:40eb46d0-b531-47e0-9756-c1b1e9c2d8fd}} , being {{formula:889189a2-754b-45f5-aef2-e03d25ac8efc}}The phase-convention independent measure of CP violation, {{formula:02e10282-ddcb-4e69-be95-15ee54b200e8}} , is given by {{formula:9b1aba43-1ee3-4ef1-8482-2b4d9d1cf07d}}with the CKM matrix elements {{formula:c1604579-4d49-4d49-b43d-03441785fdc9}} and {{formula:0e037dce-ff83-4bcf-9ef5-8d030737668f}} being the total antisymmetric tensor. One representation of Eq. (REF ) reads, for instance, {{formula:2c6ff4a3-0fad-46a1-b366-d998bf7a6a84}} . A non-vanishing CKM phase and hence CP violation necessarily requires {{formula:d57497db-bcb4-4d0c-9a1c-a0ff5dff038e}} . The Jarlskog parameter expressed in the Standard Parameterization (REF ) reads {{formula:4e5a19b9-e060-4b08-9cb1-9fd26b674d58}}and, using the Wolfenstein approximation (REF ), valid to the order {{formula:10c47e51-6527-434d-ae50-39b42dbadddd}} , one finds {{formula:d84a4c8c-4396-40dd-9bd1-d574fb801305}}The empirical value of {{formula:606a7083-98bf-4677-904d-70043eea0520}} is small compared to its maximum of {{formula:bf3a2e2b-8b9a-486f-96c0-1360e827a055}} showing that CP violation is suppressed as a consequence of the strong hierarchy exhibited by the CKM matrix elements. It is the remarkable outcome of Eq. (REF ) that CP violation requires not only {{formula:aa0d85b0-addf-4389-89db-05c9a30f00db}} to be non-zero, but also the existence of a non-degenerated mass hierarchy. Equal masses between at least two generations of up-type or down-type quarks would necessarily remove the CKM phase.Phase convention invariance of the {{formula:ffa60a00-31a6-4830-ac18-3dc1d68361fa}} -transformed quark wave functions is a requirement for physically meaningful quantities. Such invariants are the moduli {{formula:b9bb0061-c74a-4396-abb6-0265ee7212de}} and the quadri-products {{formula:158fb863-a9da-4f74-8432-3090b70f97fc}} (c.f., the Jarlskog invariant {{formula:e6aa8b64-a304-4584-8e53-1411e0e65cc0}} (REF )). Non-trivial higher invariants can be reformulated as functions of moduli and quadri-products (see, e.g., Ref. ). Indeed, Eq. (REF ) expresses the fact that, owing to the orthogonality of any pair of different rows or columns of {{formula:3b5ade09-4133-4c01-b69d-fee3038edfe9}} , the imaginary parts of all quadri-products are equal up to their sign. We will use phase-invariant representations and formulae throughout this paper We are indebted to K. Schubert for drawing our attention to this point..
The Unitarity Triangle: The allowed region in {{formula:d929e1b8-c501-485c-8f5f-f34f8425935a}} space can be elegantly displayed using the unitarity triangle (UT) described by the rescaled unitarity relation between the first and the third column of the CKM matrix {{formula:ef1cbab3-647e-496f-9dc2-8c1de48e59eb}}Note that twice the area of the non-rescaled {{figure:719ed5b2-9252-4efa-9969-7fddc4aba1ea}}UT corresponds to the Jarlskog parameter {{formula:f89275ce-7a97-48fc-acdd-2aafadbbce16}} . This identity provides a geometrical interpretation of the phase convention invariance of {{formula:38f88c33-1890-465b-99a0-311a04f6ecf5}} : a rotation of the CKM matrix rotates the UT accordingly while leaving its area, and thus {{formula:6843c7db-43dc-40ef-868c-336874926956}} , invariant. It is the remarkable property of the UT (REF ) that its three sides are governed by the same power of {{formula:ca4ff65e-10e1-4130-afc2-dda4ed2651cc}} and {{formula:14fed11c-4f48-42da-8ff3-fc8abdf32cb0}} {{formula:56ab8426-d7e7-4053-9b49-6e7b4e866523}}which predicts large CP asymmetries in the {{formula:2e97dbf3-b17a-41e0-8678-6ef6fd330931}} sector . As a comparison, the corresponding UT for the kaon sector is almost flat {{formula:6a0282fa-6642-40a6-be86-60b7c150b6fc}}exhibiting small CP asymmetries. {{figure:c4930676-a47a-4bde-a69f-3664dc9477fd}}The UT (REF ) is sketched in Fig. REF in the complex {{formula:f0757511-ba27-4092-ab6a-e784b65aaf56}} plane ({{formula:90fb6f93-8bca-4e6d-8884-5763c4430f5d}} , {{formula:6d6a3865-543f-46c6-839f-355236425b5d}} ) of the Wolfenstein parameterizationThe length of the vector to the triangle apex is given by {{formula:ce3eb4e7-da4b-489a-832f-424edda2f864}} so that the replacements {{formula:2eb9b21a-d064-4674-adc8-ad27602bcf99}} and {{formula:fe1dd92d-4705-453d-bef3-e9fe9dd20561}} , where {{formula:956636f4-5c2a-4795-be5c-171d6d0ac79e}} , improves the precision of the apex coordinate in the Wolfenstein approximation .. The sides {{formula:aa95f4be-e361-4aed-8f46-0cf8545ce73f}} and {{formula:4e34528b-69e4-4273-acd1-9f346a01445b}} (the third side being normalized to unity) are given by {{formula:dbfe20d7-f7ad-4fcd-a55c-f706c46f06ee}}and the three angles, {{formula:355983e9-6b80-4f6f-aa4d-0a311ffd2f32}} , read {{formula:9b08ccaa-82e0-4987-b022-19129dc23a9a}}where {{formula:e10afe9c-1337-4d3c-947f-06cd10702458}} in the Standard Parameterization. The angles and sides of the UT obey the trigonometric relation, {{formula:81ed4d66-90e1-4ddd-92b9-93079589dd38}} .The relations between the angles and the {{formula:57c14d6a-21d1-4660-aa66-9fd2cdcdf4f1}} , {{formula:6bdc787c-d7cc-4cf9-bee2-6e61f79d07ee}} coordinates are given by {{formula:c01b15c7-dc04-45b4-9d8f-f6c1d351366b}}A graphical compilation of the most relevant present and future constraints sensitive to the CP violating phase {{formula:68aaac29-b910-4681-b510-e1345c56c397}} is displayed in Fig. REF . We simplify the representation by assuming a measurement of {{formula:ab904ddb-878d-4a1a-ac74-d5a2bd3d24d8}} whereas, in principle, the UT angle {{formula:a046244f-526e-4899-a831-9a3f7bd30857}} can be directly determined from {{formula:d5db14c7-d930-4b92-aca8-0daccf19ec67}} decays. For the third UT angle {{formula:56c04303-fa1b-4bab-9518-2955debaf1a0}} , we assume a measurement of {{formula:639c2b78-9eb2-4f05-b22f-4c1a7cd6587e}} , even though charmless {{formula:a46f350a-b54c-433a-a9e2-1a49e8e4d3b4}} decays may allow a non-ambiguous determination of {{formula:46ad003f-d612-4ef7-bf62-dbe02198e75a}} . A more detailed elaboration of future measurements is given in Ref. . Some “standard” set of theoretical parameters is used for this exercise in order to reproduce compatibility between the constraints. The present experimental values for the observables and their dependence on the CKM matrix elements in the framework of the SM are discussed in Section .Over-constraining the unitary CKM matrix aims at validating or not the SM with three generations. The interpretation of these constraints requires a robust statistical framework which protects against misleading conclusions. The next section describes to some detail the statistical approach applied for the analysis reported in this work.
The Statistical Framework: We are considering an analysis involving a set of {{formula:50433985-b8dc-4cf3-b061-bcbed5166567}} measurements collectively denoted by {{formula:503a8ff4-d9b2-4210-8c13-91cbad493f25}} {{formula:46445830-45a7-402b-bb31-738df9fa85dc}} , described by a set of corresponding theoretical expressions {{formula:fec8234a-6aeb-478c-9f01-abf1b24aa9df}} {{formula:e166f18f-4178-4ea2-b859-2e1e8561847f}} . The theoretical expressions {{formula:dc110b11-2ecb-4f3d-80be-09c42be5c160}} are functions of a set of {{formula:882ff961-b618-471a-abca-0306849e06ff}} parameters {{formula:81159ae4-33a1-4814-8e9e-88839861ca50}} . Their precise definition is irrelevant for the present discussion (c.f., Section for details) beside the fact that:a subset of {{formula:7f4f3489-d9be-46f8-9910-0c7590af19b8}} parameters within the {{formula:8ab7d669-9287-4f82-abff-d95667659387}} set are fundamental, and free, parameters of the theory (i.e., the four CKM unknowns in the SM, the top quark mass, etc.) and are denoted {{formula:28453dbc-8ced-4a64-8e59-d1072f4533e4}} , where {{formula:01055c8b-1140-404f-8446-ecee0b09e326}} . the remaining {{formula:b3b39190-e90b-4584-b7dd-668b32157788}} parameters, which appear due to our present inability to compute precisely strong interaction quantities (e.g., {{formula:0d745fba-c0cd-4dd9-8e4a-153b2790d1b9}} , {{formula:2edadc66-7769-47b5-aaf3-12d321fa91bb}} , etc.), are denoted {{formula:7011cf6e-4d06-4db2-b400-5cf65481c78e}} , where {{formula:6d7ce3dd-2a2e-4cc9-9709-9764a606ab74}} .There are three quite different goals the analysis aims at:Within the SM, to achieve the best estimate of the {{formula:1f7ef5ae-31e7-40f5-90e7-701159e0cbda}} parameters: that is to say to perform a careful metrology of the theoretical parameters, for later use. Within the SM, to set a confidence level (CL) which quantifies the agreement between data and the theory, as a whole. Within an extended theoretical framework, e.g., Supersymmetry, to search for specific signs of new physics by pinning down additional fundamental, and free, parameters of the theory.These three goals imply three statistical treatments all of which rely on a likelihood function meant to gauge the agreement between data and theory.

(REF ) is a commodity which can be misleading. In general, denoting "{{formula:10dc551d-28b4-47ee-a892-4b89ab86ba81}} " the well known routine from the CERN library, one cannot infer a CL from the above {{formula:8ce45245-a2e5-40cd-89c0-58cd23fc7b5e}} value using {{formula:453dd0e8-faea-4072-a440-59789f988edb}}This is because neither {{formula:7c01f9c8-bc71-4f6e-bd82-19282ebcc814}} nor {{formula:2be670d4-6a49-4601-aee7-158ee483b4fe}} (they are further discussed in the sections below) are built from purely Gaussian measurements:In most cases {{formula:23e53479-2f5a-4910-8f1e-78c4ea0d5e0c}} should handle experimental systematics, and, in some instance, it has to account for inconsistent measurements. In practice, {{formula:ff9c3e03-e553-4ce3-bc44-eb85bf034322}} relies on hard-to-quantify educated guessworks, akin to the ones used to define experimental systematics, but in most cases even less well-defined.The first limitation is not specific to the present analysis and is not the main source of concern, here. The second limitation is the most challenging: its impact on the analysis is particularly strong with the data presently available. The statistical treatment advocated below, denoted Rfit, is designed to cope with both of the above limitations. Notwithstanding its attractive features, the Rfit scheme does not offer a treatment of the problem at hand free from any assumption: an ill-defined problem cannot be dealt with rigorously. However, the Rfit scheme extracts the most out of simple and clear-cut a priori assumptions.The alternative statistical treatments discussed in Section differ from the Rfit scheme by the procedure used to define the CL from the above {{formula:39193705-f9f9-4339-8214-eb08e1b18aeb}} , or by the content and interpretation of {{formula:f0530842-9189-4899-bfa0-7944d84462e7}} .
The Experimental Likelihood: The experimental component of the likelihood is given by the product {{formula:f8503435-473a-4152-be3b-7a26035eed23}}where the individual likelihood components account for independent measurementsFeatures marked by {{formula:beae214d-f0f2-4dc2-96a0-c7138d147aeb}} in the following item list are not issued in the analysis presented in this work, but may become important in future CKM profiles..
The Likelihood Components:: Ideally, the individual likelihood components {{formula:c8f54cb4-7104-43f0-a1cf-7889741d3fd5}} would be pure Gaussians {{formula:00e00006-097d-47bf-9ee3-dd60cd671c13}}each with a standard deviation given by the experimental statistical uncertainty {{formula:1941b6d4-17ff-4f08-a9bf-91faf5378b85}} of the {{formula:22be963a-ba15-4497-b575-95c7b6f46719}} measurement. However, in practice, one has to deal with additional experimental and theoretical systematic uncertainties.
Experimental Systematics:: An experimental systematics is assumed to take the form of a possible biasing offset, the measurement could be corrected for, were it be known. Their precise treatment is discussed in Section . There, a natural extension of the usual method of adding linearly or in quadrature statistical and systematic uncertainties is proposed.
Theoretical Systematics:: Theoretical systematics, when they imply small effects, are treated as the experimental ones. However, because most theoretical systematics imply large effects and affect in a non-linear way the {{formula:f37f23c7-43ac-43cd-a1c3-460c8435bbab}} prediction, most of them are dealt with through the theoretical likelihood component {{formula:fa223024-2143-44ad-86d8-0ced71edb5c4}} (c.f., Section REF ).
Model Dependent Measurements{{formula:6857040d-9517-4e34-9549-f56f43db53e3}} :: When theoretical systematics cannot be expressed as a dependence on not perfectly known parameters, but are expressed as a set of measurements based on alternative models, labelled by the index {{formula:0aa47762-6d16-4000-8913-adec9277cc66}} , (e.g., the exclusive {{formula:ca3271e4-21d4-4b3a-a1bc-d15eec4a504e}} measurement exhibits such a model dependence) {{formula:b94530f3-70b2-4d75-a0c6-6960f9047d4b}} is defined by {{formula:cad4f512-a45d-40bf-88d2-7f09a6b5ade4}}and {{formula:8297c3f3-8040-499e-96e8-acd8277a6692}} is treated as an additional {{formula:de6f7f39-2f53-4a81-aeb9-4b9d5464dbc8}} parameter, taking only discrete values.
Identical Observables and Consistency:: When several measurements refer to the same observable (e.g., various measurements of {{formula:b4094e9a-f831-4117-998e-00f3813a5b08}} ) they have to be consistent, independently of the theoretical framework used for the analysis.Similarly, when several measurements refer to different observables which are linked to the same {{formula:34b29d02-a395-4492-82c7-66675b9c7005}} parameter, e.g.., {{formula:d385374f-924d-4897-bb18-cbc112eb0d9b}} and {{formula:e815c984-749c-4f6d-9ddd-62bcc8b24a3e}} , or determinations of {{formula:444fb093-7d8a-46ff-bba6-911247d87a06}} stemming from different observables, or measurements of {{formula:87a9bae8-4fd7-4d31-8f88-7e5b5fffa98c}} obtained from similar {{formula:0c237088-ff64-4313-967a-20feefb38def}} decays, one may decide to overrule possible disagreement by imposing the measurements to be consistent. By doing so, one is deliberately blinding oneself from possible new physics effects which may have revealed themselves otherwise. Clearly, such overruling should be applied with great caution, and it should be well advertized whenever it occurs.The method to deal with this imposed consistency is to account for the measurements at once, by merging them into a single component, usually obtained from their weighted mean. A more refined treatment is needed when this set of measurements is clearly inconsistent. A general method to handle a set of measurements, whether they are consistent or not, is proposed in Ref. , . Yet, for “not too large” inconsistencies, the proposed method yields similar results as the {{formula:f520c375-39f0-4995-8cbc-eb74f8bccf5d}} rescaling approach adopted by the PDG . To clarify the presentation of the Rfit scheme, we use the latter: when N inconsistent measurements appear in this analysis, the error obtained for their weighted mean is rescaled by the factor {{formula:3ffea08e-d259-47aa-a809-188ddc37d6bd}} , where {{formula:e69beaab-a729-45af-a3d4-37404d1c55ce}} is the weighted mean {{formula:5d9920e9-8c53-4d1b-8673-845d4d119c4a}} .
Related Observables and Consistency{{formula:16bfad21-8363-4656-8f9d-a9ea8b87b821}} :: In some instances, several observables, although not identical, are functionally related in a way independent of the theoretical framework used for the analysis. The number of such instances is denoted {{formula:a8a3171f-e186-4d92-a48e-24492eccd5a1}} , and the effective number of measurements, the one to be used to compute degrees of freedom, is defined by {{formula:55c94152-40fd-4959-ac69-45f131888077}}An example is provided by the set of measurements yielding separately {{formula:aa3d8896-55f3-4bb1-ad61-7d05d5e899fb}} , {{formula:c20941b4-946b-4057-b69d-3973f276a36d}} and {{formula:e9d1d8fa-506d-44f4-9631-d6c8ee8eb0bd}} . The ratio of the first two should be compatible with the third measurement, whether or not the SM is valid. Since the measurements are not referring to a unique observable they cannot be merged simply into a single component, as above. One should normalize their contribution to ensure that they do not contribute to the overall {{formula:da5045c5-cad9-450b-968e-97b2d62ee614}} value, if they are in the best possible mutual agreement, independently of the theoretical framework used for the analysis. This normalization is in fact what is done in the case of identical observables. It is irrelevant for the metrological phase of the analysis, and for the third phase, where one searches for specific sign of new physics: then, any constant can be added to the {{formula:7437e826-c730-4aac-bd23-8c06990d8300}} without affecting the result. However, it is relevant for the second phase, where one probes the SM: a statistical fluctuation in the set {{formula:fde14f66-05c8-4257-82f0-d922a8747f8a}} , {{formula:f3322430-fb09-441c-82a1-8cb2fb9acc45}} and {{formula:8f588a6b-349d-461e-a181-92d20f8def7f}} which makes them violate their functional relation should not trigger a claim for new physics. In this example, the normalization constant is obtained as the maximal value of the function of the two variables {{formula:ad4b1f99-d2ad-4f33-8f1c-1a2db372fd79}} , {{formula:c64d6abe-55b9-4122-8220-45ee34832591}} {{formula:a661dfda-549b-4683-88a5-1b6ee6130550}}Here as well, care should be taken not to normalize that way the contributions of observables the functional connection of which is model dependent. For instance, the measurements leading to {{formula:db81a180-6f05-484e-9030-ce19417bbe6b}} and {{formula:e1a702dc-c3bd-43e8-b31d-6852e2bc9b29}} are sensitive to new physics because their measured values may violate the SM functional relation {{formula:d6ebe454-2d04-499f-8e80-422b3e327a17}} It is worth pointing out that an apparent functional violation is present (since long ago) in the available data (c.f.. Normalization:: More generally, the normalization of each individual likelihood component is chosen such that its maximal value is equal to one. This is not important for the analysis, but it is convenient: it ensures that a measurement does not contribute numerically to the overall {{formula:c6e04d68-9798-4b9f-a903-e4c2972c1c49}} value if it is in the best possible agreement with theory, and that the (so-called) {{formula:9d586f10-4e8c-4ace-a377-52fdb0a31bd1}} takes only positive values. In the pure Gaussian case, it implies simply to drop the normalization constant of Eq. (REF ): one is thus recovering the standard {{formula:89185024-e58e-4f36-acc9-5e643418ffee}} definition.

Supersymmetric Extensions of the Standard Model: Having considered both metrology and probing the SM with the present data set, one is now led to attempt an example analysis within an extended theoretical framework. This section aims to illustrate the search for specific new physics within a simple, predictive supersymmetric (SUSY) extension of the SM.There exist a considerable number of SUSY models in which new phases appear in the coupling between supersymmetric and SM fields. However, these models remain unpredictive as long as the additional phases are unconstrained. We therefore cannot forecast how the shape of the UT is affected by the new fields. As a starting point, one can use restrictive assumptions which lead to more predictive models. In particular, one may only retain models which do not involve additional CP violating phases, so that flavour-changing processes are described by the same quark flavor mixing matrix {{formula:75166bc7-24dc-4979-b69e-df52beabf530}} as in the SM. Supersymmetric contributions to the transitions between the down-type quarks ({{formula:011ad885-ba9e-4022-b4fa-ba69336736f6}} , {{formula:4436e9f0-37a9-4030-9b5e-ed94767ee4d4}} , {{formula:4f817db8-3232-4d96-93af-0efe1eef7be1}} ) are then proportional to the SM CKM matrix elements. Conclusions: We present a new approach to a global fit of the CKM matrix. It is denoted Rfit and is based on frequentist statistics. We emphasize the thorough statistical definition of the method and discuss differences from Bayesian statistics , and from the {{formula:c1ed95b9-519c-4898-a56b-c97698177489}} CL Scan method . The choice for the fit input parameters, their values and errors are discussed to some detail; in cases of doubts we favor the more conservative estimates. The CKM analysis is formally subdivided into three distinct phases: a metrological phase in which the Standard Model is assumed to be valid and confidence levels for the parameters are computed; a probing phase addressing the issue of the validity of the Standard Model description of data; a probing phase for new physics relying on predictive parameterizations. For the first phase of the analysis, graphical results are displayed in several one and two dimensional representations and numerical results are given for relevant CKM parameterizations, CKM matrix elements, Standard Model predictions of rare {{formula:d0818e54-a372-448a-a236-9caa8275d245}} and {{formula:5f766c8f-e87b-47c7-9d91-2fcd672f1037}} meson decays, and selected theoretical parameters. For the parameters related to the CP violating phase of the CKM matrix, we find for the different parameterizations (the fit includes the present world average of {{formula:70331e54-165f-4bb8-ae77-2690adcf6be7}} measurements) {{formula:27fb3140-48dd-474b-aba0-c60426b1b698}}where the {{formula:25f70a9b-a0fe-4462-9f84-c48729f967f9}} confidence level ranges are quoted. The second phase of the analysis provides an upper bound for the validity of the Standard Model, {{formula:a7d9a8e0-4c74-419e-a5eb-2b0a39d87154}}A simple predictive supersymmetric extension of the Standard Model has been studied in the third analysis phase.

Critical Issues of the Bayesian Approach: The Bayesian approach injects in the analysis pieces of information in the form of probability density distributions for the {{formula:ae8e679f-9cf6-41c5-961b-0afb7321d636}} parameters. The Rfit scheme proposed in the present paper advocates a non-Bayesian approach because most theoretical uncertainties on the {{formula:a657732b-b167-4bec-826b-e41398715727}} parameters do not stem from statistical fluctuations. The {{formula:37ce5847-cffd-42cc-b471-e523fa6acbd7}} parameters are not random variables following probability density functions: there are poorly known, but fixed, parameters. The following examples serve the purpose to illustrate in a simplified framework the impact of using the Bayesian approach.Let {{formula:9f09e34f-5fd5-4b8f-b34b-8d74cde3026f}} denote {{formula:c0799acc-aa40-45ef-bf74-93907f38de67}} {{formula:7cc7ca82-1be5-4207-8519-28737e998820}} parameters taking their values in identical allowed ranges {{formula:c91229e8-17dc-43bc-b4a9-d0d8ed6592bd}} . These {{formula:61da3a30-af1a-4d5d-abcd-0567116be747}} {{formula:a5f9be86-9215-4f77-9f8a-a8266f83d6fa}} parameters are assumed to combine to form {{formula:942dcd6a-a6c6-49f9-98f8-998123cb77a7}} , the theoretical prediction for an observable, as followsThis is not an academic exercize: products of {{formula:28149f1a-9ebb-45a5-a10b-4493ccc69cdc}} terms are not rare in the theoretical predictions. For example, the {{formula:1cd7cd85-71c8-4b87-90d4-2ad9dd75d8e2}} expression (c.f., Eq. (REF ) of Section REF ) involves the product of {{formula:bea92cb8-d385-4193-a751-b086d4c94c1b}} , {{formula:45f0c7ad-3950-4879-aeac-ec0a95ffa04b}} and {{formula:e68f5866-156f-4d40-9245-089e89150ad3}} . However, the choice of {{formula:5aa75e52-02a1-4598-8162-683630e58924}} ranges containing the origin is not met in practice. This choice is made here to highlight the difference between the Rfit scheme and a PDF-based Bayesian approach. However, the singularity discussed below is present when Gaussian PDFs are used, as a matter of principle, whether or not {{formula:63abdaf4-37a2-41bf-bfc2-cda1850980e6}} ranges contains the origin. {{formula:4eb72366-a8bc-4132-b468-0067715185d8}}The theoretical prediction {{formula:cad8a2ab-3618-4ea3-9627-86d6d44d3fb2}} enters in the analysis as an unique {{formula:8381de54-6ea9-4c1c-bf44-93401ef17a9d}} parameter, whichwithin the Rfit scheme, is characterized by its allowed range {{formula:c22a84e4-ad03-4908-9379-1a43d615a351}} within the Bayesian approach, is characterized by its PDF {{formula:67cc36b3-4f5c-4d37-a788-7e2ed88ae97e}} where we assumed that identical PDFs, {{formula:364bca85-04cc-4b67-9912-f9c64a6b979c}} , were attributed to the {{formula:662fe0ed-817a-4b84-b9d8-2b24f6e7afa4}} quantities.Independently of the details of the shape of {{formula:23110f95-8fa9-4a31-b98c-2705554f5303}} , if this PDF is non-zero at the origin, {{formula:3229b1d6-bfb0-4efa-ab23-b5e755636909}} will exhibit a singularity at {{formula:d4c36d21-381e-45cd-b191-28be5502e613}} with leading term {{formula:27a13de4-51b3-48be-b89f-567378b81c75}} . Hence, the larger {{formula:9d7eae68-3121-48c3-8460-edcc3adfa00d}} is, the more pronounced the peak at the origin of {{formula:a4870a80-02ce-44b1-9f24-5673c382b372}} is. {{figure:efe5e727-5a2a-4ee6-9848-bf3eb22fe646}}If one chooses a uniform distribution {{formula:53ab88ea-8670-4d04-a786-c5a6d83a1402}} , that is to say the PDF the “closest” to the Rfit assumptions (albeit being a fundamentally different object), one obtains a striking result. For {{formula:be482d65-0048-4bc6-b153-c1d674221e42}} , the Bayesian approach and the Rfit scheme are equivalent (though not for the associated CLs), insofar no other variable is involved: both state that the value of {{formula:a6f40e09-91f6-436f-9606-f2d5cd719d7e}} is simply within the allowed range {{formula:c0fba64f-0de6-43c9-974e-22d09b892ab1}} . However, though originally no {{formula:fd4d0747-89e3-4a5f-93b3-20294aaed44f}} values were favored, the Bayesian approach departs drastically from Rfit as soon as {{formula:b89d6579-865f-4bd9-9549-393ac3d6247a}} : it states that {{formula:3fd9e625-1357-4588-8aa9-16903c986c02}} is most likely close to zero. In effect, when the number of {{formula:8adaf800-692d-4b80-a1bd-ee49f37e3015}} parameters entering the computation of the theoretical prediction increases, and hence when our knowledge of the corresponding observable decreases, the Bayesian approach claims the converse.This is less a consequence of the initial ad hoc choice for the PDF {{formula:04a62062-5121-412f-826b-5a2dcf6b3b73}} , than a consequence of the inescapable properties of Eq. (REF ), when applied to a product of terms. For instance, the peaking effect remains present for a sum of terms, but it is far less pronounced. The above generalities are illustrated, for {{formula:19027ae2-cf09-42bc-ad3b-d925d2fc2ada}} and {{formula:9d975ba6-2602-4b56-8855-23f80c23141c}} , in Fig. REF . The choice {{formula:61bf7fd7-9c02-465c-b917-072036cd7c8e}} is made because the resulting allowed ranges for the product {{formula:95b1fd39-59b4-4712-ab2e-b853814ee747}} and for the sum {{formula:4cd1921a-2c2b-4e58-b42d-dc5b8ad107c2}} are identical when using Rfit, namely {{formula:d74499b5-cbbe-47b3-af1f-4a80120659f4}} . For both, the sum {{formula:55ab78a3-f066-435c-95ce-a5aa4b2ff6e4}} and the product {{formula:f10775da-78c8-45ed-b96b-887412aa6994}} , the uniform and the Gaussian PDFs yield similar {{formula:b4a84ab4-ae5a-4759-a9e7-6c1da404cfde}} distributions, because their RMS are chosen identical. The still noticeable difference between the two {{formula:574011e1-70e2-49cf-b053-70d419e67c34}} PDFs is damped away by Eq. (REF ), even for such a moderate number like {{formula:486c73cd-d055-442f-8a74-f2c14f667f14}} . As a consequence, when following the Bayesian approach, it is not a particularly conservative choice to adopt a uniform PDF instead of a Gaussian PDF.It is a remarkable difference between the two treatments that, whereas within the Rfit scheme the two theoretical predictions {{formula:392097d8-af61-4502-bb2f-dc374741f91c}} and {{formula:c2562203-175f-4294-9c75-131a7fc834c5}} are genuinely indistinguishable, they yield sharply different PDFs in the Bayesian approach. This shows that, even more than the ad hoc choice made to ascribe PDF to the {{formula:7a50a2ee-8e3f-4dc3-95ce-d94ea85424d1}} parameters, it is the functional dependence of the theoretical predictions in these parameters, and the interplay between the various theoretical predictions within the complete CKM analysis, which play the central role. The attractiveness of the Bayesian approach, offering a straightforward procedure for analyses, is fallacious. The deep implication of ascribing PDFs to non-random variables is hidden inside an apparently innocuous convolution, the outcome of which reflects, more than anything else, the mathematical structure of the problem at hand.
Critical Issues of the 95% CL Scan Method: The 95% CL Scan method REF presents several unwelcome features which are reviewed below.
Drawing features:: Its final graphical result depends strongly on the choices made for {{formula:7396c34b-fb8c-4109-a245-85bae27fdca3}} , the selection threshold used to retain models, and for {{formula:9c0363f0-94f8-4168-9e39-dfc608d1090c}} , the constant defining the contours to be drawn. It is not possible to infer how a given drawing is modified by changing these choices. Regions of weak statistical confidence, just barely passing the selection threshold, and thus retained, bear the same graphical weight than regions of fair CL. Similarly, regions of lower CL, barely not passing the selection threshold, and thus not retained, are ignored.
Contour features:: The relevance of drawing the contours is not obvious. Whereas a given contour has a clear-cut meaning, the message it carries is to show how precise the determination of {{formula:a5d87561-5907-41d7-9d07-40590fa6dc47}} would be, in the academic situation where all theoretical uncertainties would supposedly be resolved. These contours are not ellipses in general. For instance, in the case of the measurement of {{formula:f4e1d8fc-b520-4d57-ba1f-bc3e85567e97}} alone, they are built from straight lines (c.f., Section REF ). They can take complicate shapes, depending on the choice made for the {{formula:e4b9f3da-d1bd-457e-bacb-5c860a5a107c}} variables, and depending on the presence of sizeable secondary minima. In simple situations, using the 95% CL Scan method yields awkward results. For instance, in the first example given in Section REF , where a standard situation is considered, the method would conclude by a set of short intervals in {{formula:cf0222cd-c325-4789-864e-be591355d2f6}} , each obtained for a fixed {{formula:8892f5f6-16b1-44a8-9add-e1f3ca9ada82}} value instead of providing the overall allowed interval, i.e., applying the Rfit scheme.
Envelope features:: In the {{formula:72df148d-0f3d-4af7-b6f6-f88141d4e412}} space no information can be carried about possibly more or less favored regions: a point is either within the envelope of the countours, and thus acceptable, or outside, and thus not acceptable. The envelope of the contours can be unstable with respect to change of {{formula:f2f533de-5717-430c-b5af-d1c2bacf376a}} . Indeed, the envelope can be a discontinuous function of this parameter: if lowering {{formula:39aa7c78-f032-439e-9b84-044b4241a6c1}} allows an outsider model to be selected outside of the envelope, this outsider model surfaces in the {{formula:87a18050-82fa-45d5-9c8b-3276520b5dd2}} space with its full contour and thus lead to an abrupt change of the envelope. The envelope provided by the 95% CL Scan method tends to be over-conservative. For the example of Section REF , the method yields for the envelope of the {{formula:1578f54a-1aba-4d9f-b453-ea84bb0bd232}} intervals: {{formula:981f7667-de62-4975-a0d3-fdb6b3a0a194}}which is always larger than the correct result given by Eq. (REF ) (the two limiting cases {{formula:a72293ae-d539-42ad-8cf2-ab731b00c30f}} and {{formula:d7b97a0a-a59a-4195-a21a-e7427fde45e3}} excepted).
Comments on Statistics of Normal Ratios: Ratios of branching fractions of rare {{formula:93b05fa5-0d0d-48c2-b829-63081f848a28}} transitions have attracted much attention in recent theoretical and experimental analyses, by virtue of their potential to constrain the unitarity angle {{formula:bd429217-4f07-4990-b425-a62185ed5e45}} (see Section REF ). It is shown in this section that the extraction of physical observables out of ratios of normally (Gaussian) distributed quantities, e.g., branching fractions, requires some precaution.
